q: In the Gull Rock messages, what changes from one message to the next?
a: Only a few values, and only by a little
why: The skeleton — keys, quotes, colons, commas — is identical every time; the values drift slowly. So each message is mostly predictable from the one before.
title: Notice anything?

q: Roughly what share of a Gull Rock message is new compared with the message just before it?
a: About 4 % — a handful of digits out of 148 bytes
wrong: None of it — messages repeat exactly
why: The highlighter figure counts it — typically three to eight changed characters per 148-byte message.
title: Notice anything?

q: What does lossless compression promise?
a: The original is rebuilt exactly, bit for bit
wrong: The original is rebuilt approximately, but looks the same
The data always becomes at least twice as small
Only the important parts are kept
why: Lossless means exact reconstruction. Lossy compression (JPEG, 2-bit KV quantization) keeps only an approximation. This site is only about lossless.
title: Notice anything?

q: A 148-byte Gull Rock message, compressed by itself with DEFLATE, comes out at about…
a: 124 bytes — a saving of about one sixth
why: Run the compression figure. Even though about 96 % of each message repeats the one before, one message alone barely shrinks.
title: Notice anything?

q: Where is the redundancy that DEFLATE misses when it compresses one message at a time?
a: Between messages — each is predictable from its predecessors
wrong: Inside each message — it repeats its own words
why: Each message has few internal repeats; what repeats is the skeleton shared by all messages, which a one-message compressor never sees.
title: Notice anything?

q: What does LZ matching write in place of a string of bytes that appeared earlier?
a: A short instruction — copy this many bytes, starting that many bytes back
wrong: Nothing — repeated strings are simply dropped
A shorter synonym from a fixed word list
why: The receiver has already rebuilt everything before this point, so it can follow the pointer and copy the bytes itself.
title: Why one message alone won't shrink

q: Compressed alone, why does one Gull Rock message barely shrink?
a: Inside one message there are only a few short repeats to copy from
why: Alone, only about a fifth of the message is covered by copies, all three to five bytes long. The long repeats are in the other messages, which the compressor never sees.
title: Why one message alone won't shrink

q: How is the 15:00 message written when it follows the 14:30 message in the same file?
a: Five copies of 149 bytes back plus seven literal characters
wrong: As one copy of the whole message
As the difference of every number
why: Everything except a few digits (and the line break) is a copy from exactly one message back.
title: Why one message alone won't shrink

q: Compressed as one log file, the 48 messages of a whole day cost about how much per message?
a: About 13 bytes
wrong: About 124 bytes, as when compressed alone
why: 642 bytes for 48 messages. The first message costs about 124 bytes; every later one finds its twin 149 bytes back and adds only about 11.
title: Why one message alone won't shrink

q: Why can’t Gull Rock simply send its log in daily batches?
a: Each message must arrive soon and be readable on its own
wrong: Because a batch compresses worse than single messages
Because DEFLATE accepts at most 148 bytes at a time
Because the mainland cannot store a whole log
why: A storm warning cannot wait a day, radio messages get lost, and a reader may want one old message without unpacking a whole day.
title: Why one message alone won't shrink

q: In compression, what is a dictionary?
a: Information both ends hold in advance, shared by many items, so each item can travel short
wrong: A list of words and their meanings
The compressed form of one message
A table the receiver rebuilds from every message
why: The dictionary is sent (or installed) once. Every later item can then point into it, as if the compressor had already seen it.
title: The trained dictionary

q: What does the receiver need to rebuild a message from its delta?
a: The very same dictionary the sender used
wrong: A copy of the raw message
why: A delta is full of pointers into the dictionary. Only with the same dictionary do the pointers lead to the right bytes.
title: The trained dictionary

q: With a dictionary of 24 messages from day one, a day-two message (147 bytes) compresses to about…
a: 22 bytes on average, instead of 125 alone
wrong: 125 bytes — dictionaries do not help DEFLATE
why: Measured live on all 48 day-two messages; the best is 14 bytes, the worst 27.
title: The trained dictionary

q: Why does a dictionary of just one sample message already do most of the work?
a: That one message holds the skeleton every message shares — keys, quotes, station name, date
wrong: Because DEFLATE only reads the first message of a dictionary
Because one message contains every possible reading
Because the dictionary is compressed first
why: Alone, a message costs 125 bytes; with one sample it costs 30. More samples add only value strings such as “heavy rain”, down to about 22.
title: The trained dictionary

q: Besides frequent fragments of sample text, what does a zstd trained dictionary carry?
a: Ready-made statistics for the second stage, and an ID number
wrong: The compressed messages of the last day
A list of every possible message
A password that encrypts the messages
why: The statistics spare each tiny message from describing its own symbol frequencies; the ID lets the receiver check it holds the right dictionary.
title: The trained dictionary

q: The same 48 messages cost 124 bytes each compressed one by one, but 13 bytes each compressed as one log. What explains the difference?
a: Only how the data is cut up and read — one by one, or as one stream
wrong: The log is compressed with a stronger compressor
The log throws away repeated values
Single messages contain more information than the log
why: Same bytes, same compressor. One by one, each message has nothing earlier to copy from; in the log, each finds its twin 149 bytes back.
title: Three lessons from the dictionary

q: A 3,522-byte dictionary saves about 103 bytes per message. After how many messages has it paid for itself?
a: About 34 messages — some 17 hours of Gull Rock
wrong: Never — the dictionary always costs more than it saves
why: Break-even = dictionary bytes ÷ bytes saved per message = 3,522 ÷ (124.7 − 22.1) ≈ 34.
title: Three lessons from the dictionary

q: A bigger dictionary gives smaller deltas but pays off later. What decides the best size?
a: How many messages will share it
wrong: The speed of the radio link
why: Per message, you pay dictionary bytes ÷ messages sharing it, plus the delta. Few messages favour a small dictionary; many favour a large one.
title: Three lessons from the dictionary

q: What happens when a delta is decoded with an almost-right dictionary?
a: Out comes a plausible message with wrong values, and nothing complains
wrong: The right message comes out, since the dictionaries nearly match
why: The pointers land on slightly different bytes. Raw DEFLATE has no check; zstd writes the dictionary’s ID into every message to catch this.
title: Three lessons from the dictionary

q: Using the previous message as the dictionary compresses well. What is the catch?
a: Every message then depends on the one before; lose or skip one and the chain breaks
wrong: It compresses far worse than a trained dictionary
A previous message is too short to be a dictionary
why: It averages 21 bytes, as good as the trained dictionary — but to read one message you need all the messages before it.
title: Three lessons from the dictionary

q: Why can’t DEFLATE shrink the twelve rows of readings stored as binary numbers?
a: Neighbouring numbers are close but almost never equal, and LZ matching only copies exact repeats
wrong: Because twelve rows are too few bytes to compress
Because DEFLATE only works on text
why: Only 2 of 44 numbers equal the one above, never two side by side. 108 bytes go in, 108 come out.
title: Our files are lists of numbers

q: When the items are lists of numbers, what can the dictionary be?
a: A few numbers — for example, each column’s typical value
wrong: A stack of old rows to copy byte strings from
Nothing — numbers cannot share a dictionary
why: Four typical values, sent once, turn every row into small leftovers. Copying is replaced by guessing.
title: Our files are lists of numbers

q: Subtracting each column’s typical value from the twelve rows cut the binary digits per row from 46 to…
why: The leftovers are small (pressure within ±1.74 hPa, for instance), so each needs fewer binary digits than the full reading.
title: Our files are lists of numbers

q: Which part of the zstd picture does NOT carry over from text messages to lists of numbers?
a: Copying exact byte strings
wrong: Paying for the dictionary once and sharing it
The receiver needing exactly the right dictionary
why: Matching turns into predicting. The economics and the need for the right dictionary stay the same.
title: Our files are lists of numbers

q: Which two conditions, together, make a dictionary the tool for the job?
a: The items are alike, and they are fetched as tiny, independent pieces
wrong: The files are large, and the link is fast
The data is random, and the link is slow
The data is text, and loss is acceptable
why: Alike items give a dictionary something to capture; tiny independent fetches are what stop an ordinary compressor from capturing it by itself.
title: The profile of a dictionary problem

q: The items are alike, but they are always read as one big stream. What is the right tool?
a: An ordinary compressor run over the whole stream
why: The day’s log compresses to 13 bytes per message with plain DEFLATE. A dictionary only earns its cost when the pieces travel alone.
title: The profile of a dictionary problem

q: In the LLM version of the story, what plays the part of one tiny Gull Rock message?
a: One small piece of the LLM’s memory, fetched to the GPU on its own
wrong: One word of the LLM’s answer
why: Sparse attention fetches a few small pieces of memory per step, scattered over a long history — the access pattern of lesson 1.
title: The profile of a dictionary problem

q: On this site, “similarity”, “redundancy” and “mutual information” between an item and a dictionary are…
a: Names for one quantity, in bits — how much shorter the item’s code gets when the dictionary is known
wrong: Three different quantities that must be measured separately
Measures of how random the item is
why: More of it means the item is more predictable. Part II defines it as mutual information.
title: The profile of a dictionary problem

q: The old site used one word both for a run of token positions and for the set of data one dictionary serves. What does this site say?
a: A stretch for a run of token positions, and a punnet for the set of cherries one dictionary serves
wrong: A slice for the positions and a cherry for the data
why: A run of positions is a knob we choose; the cherries cut from it under one slice are what one compress call sees. Two objects, two words.
title: The profile of a dictionary problem

q: The old site used one word both for what the indexer selects and for what the compressor shrinks. What does this site say?
a: A pick when the indexer names it, a cherry when the receiver asks for it and the compressor shrinks it
why: The indexer selects positions; the scenario delivers fixed-shape sub-arrays. One old word hid two things.
title: The profile of a dictionary problem

q: Why does the “Back to school” Part use a weather station instead of an LLM?
a: So each idea can be learned on a toy whose behaviour is easy to picture, before it is applied to an LLM’s memory
wrong: Because the project is about weather data
Because LLMs do not use bits
Because an LLM’s memory cannot be described with these ideas
why: Every concept is introduced on a small, concrete toy first; the LLM and its orchard only arrive in Part III, when the vocabulary is ready.
title: Why go back to school?

q: In the toy world, what plays the role of an expensive, slow link?
a: The radio link from Gull Rock to the mainland, paid per byte
why: Paying per byte is what makes bits worth counting; later the link becomes the wire between host memory and the GPU.
title: Why go back to school?

q: Which five families of ideas does the primer cover?
a: Information, coding, statistics & vectors, number formats, machines (memory and caches)
why: These are the five columns of the concept map on this page.
title: Why go back to school?

q: How many yes/no questions does it take to pin down one of 16 equally likely wind directions?
why: Each halving question cuts the candidates in two: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. That is log2​16=4 questions.
title: Bits: twenty questions

q: Why is “Is it north?” a poor first question about the wind direction?
a: Its answer is almost always “no”, so it rules out only one direction of sixteen
wrong: It cannot be answered with yes or no
Its answer takes two bits to write down
North is the most common wind at Gull Rock
why: A good question is one whose answer you cannot guess in advance. A 50/50 question halves the candidates; a lopsided one barely dents them.
title: Bits: twenty questions

q: How many different things can 10 bits tell apart?
why: Every extra bit doubles the count: 210=1024.
title: Bits: twenty questions

q: When many decimal digits are sent together, about how many bits does each digit cost?
a: About 3.32 bits
why: Three digits have 1,000 possibilities and fit in 10 bits (1,024), so 3.33 bits each. In the limit it is log2​10≈3.32. One digit alone needs 4.
title: Bits: twenty questions

q: Gull Rock sends 48 wind directions a day. Sent as 4 bits each instead of the JSON text “wind_dir”:“WSW”, a day costs…
a: 192 bits instead of 6,144
why: The JSON text is 16 characters, 128 bits. Four bits a report × 48 reports = 192 bits.
title: Bits: twenty questions

q: Fog has probability p=1/8 at Gull Rock. What is the surprisal of a fog report?
a: 3 bits
why: Surprisal is log2​(1/p)=log2​8=3 — a one-in-eight event is like naming one of eight equally likely things.
title: Surprise

q: What is the surprisal of an outcome that is certain (p=1)?
a: 0 bits
why: News you knew already tells you nothing: log2​(1/1)=0.
title: Surprise

q: A sunny report on one day and a fog report on another, unrelated day. What is their total surprisal?
a: 4 bits
why: Independent probabilities multiply (½ × ⅛ = 1/16) and their logarithms add: 1 + 3 = 4 bits.
title: Surprise

q: What must the probabilities of a distribution add up to?
why: A distribution lists every possible outcome, and in the long run one of them always happens. Their shares add to one whole.
title: Surprise

q: If an outcome becomes half as likely, its surprisal…
a: grows by exactly 1 bit
why: log2​(2/p)=log2​(1/p)+1. Each halving of the probability is one more fair yes/no question.
title: Surprise

q: What is the entropy of the Gull Rock sky (sunny ½, cloudy ¼, rain ⅛, fog ⅛)?
a: 1.75 bits per report
why: ½·1 + ¼·2 + ⅛·3 + ⅛·3 = 1.75: the surprisals, weighted by how often each report comes.
title: Entropy: the average surprise

q: For a source with four possible outcomes, when is the entropy highest, and how high?
a: When all four are equally likely — 2 bits
wrong: When one outcome is certain — 2 bits
When all four are equally likely — 4 bits
When the probabilities are ½, ¼, ⅛, ⅛ — 1.75 bits
why: Equal odds leave nothing to exploit: log2​4=2 bits. Any imbalance lowers the entropy; a certain outcome brings it to 0.
title: Entropy: the average surprise

q: What does order-0 entropy ignore?
a: The context — which symbols came before
why: It is computed from symbol frequencies alone. Shuffle the reports and it does not change, so it cannot see that fog tends to follow fog.
title: Entropy: the average surprise

q: Entropy estimated from the histogram of a small sample tends to be…
a: too low
why: A small sample often misses or under-counts rare outcomes, so it looks more predictable than the source really is.
title: Entropy: the average surprise

q: The sky’s entropy is 1.75 bits. What is its perplexity?
a: About 3.36
why: Perplexity is 2H=21.75≈3.36: as unpredictable as a fair die with 3.36 faces.
title: Entropy: the average surprise

q: With the season almanac at both ends, how many bits per sky report does the Gull Rock station need on average?
a: About 1.59 bits
why: The average of the four seasons’ entropies, ¼ × (1.42 + 1.19 + 1.76 + 1.98) ≈ 1.59. That is H(X∣Y); it saves 0.16 bits against the 1.75 of the year.
title: Side information

q: In winter, the sky’s entropy is 1.98 bits — more than the 1.75 bits of the whole year. Does that contradict “conditioning never increases entropy”?
a: No — the rule holds on average over the seasons, not in every season
wrong: Yes — the almanac must be wrong
Yes — so the almanac should not be used in winter
No — winter is simply too rare to count
why: Knowing that it is winter makes the sky harder to guess. Averaged over all four seasons, the almanac still saves 0.16 bits per report.
title: Side information

q: When does knowing the season save nothing at all, H(X∣Y)=H(X)?
a: When every season’s sky looks exactly like the whole year’s
wrong: When the seasons are equally long
When the sky has four possible reports
When the almanac is printed only once
why: Then the season and the sky are independent. In the figure, this is almanac sharpness 0.
title: Side information

q: What must be true for side information to make the station’s messages cheaper?
a: The receiver must already have it when the message arrives
wrong: It must be sent along with every message
It must be exactly correct every day
It must have more entropy than the message
why: The office decodes a summer-coded report with its own copy of the almanac. Without that copy the cheap message is unreadable.
title: Side information

q: The sky has H(X)=1.75 bits and H(X∣Y)=1.59 bits with the season almanac. What is the mutual information I(X;Y)?
a: About 0.16 bits
why: Mutual information is the saving: I=H(X)−H(X∣Y)=1.75−1.59.
title: Mutual information

q: How much does one sky report tell the harbour about the season?
a: The same 0.16 bits that the season tells about the sky
wrong: Nothing — information flows only from season to sky
2 bits, the full entropy of the season
1.75 bits, the full entropy of the sky
why: Mutual information is symmetric: H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=2−1.84=0.16 bits.
title: Mutual information

q: When is I(X;Y)=0?
a: When knowing Y does not change the probabilities of X at all
wrong: When X and Y are equal
When Y has more entropy than X
why: Then the two are independent, and the conditional entropy equals the plain entropy.
title: Mutual information

q: In the sticky-sky toy (stickiness 0.8), which side information saves more bits per sky report?
a: The previous report, about 1 bit — six times the season’s 0.16
wrong: Neither — side information cannot lower entropy
why: Half an hour ago is a much closer neighbour than “it is summer”. The nearest neighbour usually knows the most.
title: Mutual information

q: As two things become more similar, what happens to the conditional entropy of one given the other?
a: It goes down
why: Similarity is mutual information, the bits saved. More saved means fewer bits still needed, i.e. lower conditional entropy.
title: Mutual information

q: Which of these does “conditioning never hurts” NOT promise?
a: That every single message gets cheaper
wrong: That the average cost does not go up
That independent side information leaves the cost unchanged
That the saving is measured in bits
why: The promise is about the average. In winter the sky report costs more with the almanac than the year’s average does.
title: Mutual information

q: Which code does Huffman’s recipe give for the Gull Rock sky (sunny ½, cloudy ¼, rain ⅛, fog ⅛)?
a: sunny 0, cloudy 10, rain 110, fog 111
why: Merge rain and fog (⅛ + ⅛), then that node with cloudy (¼ + ¼), then with sunny. Reading from the top gives lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 — the surprisals.
title: Codes and Huffman

q: What does the prefix property of a code guarantee?
a: A stream of codewords can be cut back into symbols without separators
wrong: Every codeword has the same length
The code reaches the entropy exactly
why: No codeword is the beginning of another, so the decoder knows a codeword has ended the moment it matches one.
title: Codes and Huffman

q: In Huffman’s recipe, which two items are merged at each step?
a: The two least likely
wrong: The most likely with the least likely
why: The rarest items end up deepest in the tree and get the longest codewords.
title: Codes and Huffman

q: In summer (sunny ¾, cloudy ⅛, rain and fog 1/16 each) the entropy is 1.19 bits. What does the Huffman code average?
a: 1.375 bits
why: Codeword lengths are whole bits (1, 2, 3, 3). Sunny’s surprisal is only 0.415 bits, but its codeword costs a whole bit.
title: Codes and Huffman

q: A codeword of length 3 bits implicitly assumes its symbol has probability…
why: A codeword of ℓ bits behaves as a bet on probability 2−ℓ. When the true probability differs, the code pays extra.
title: Codes and Huffman

q: About how many bits does arithmetic coding need for a whole message?
a: About the sum of the surprisals of its symbols
wrong: One whole bit per symbol, at least
The number of symbols times the entropy of the alphabet’s largest symbol
why: Each symbol shrinks the interval by its probability; naming a number in an interval of width u takes about log2​(1/u) bits — the sum of the surprisals.
title: Arithmetic coding and rANS

q: A summer fortnight of noon reports (12 sunny, 2 cloudy, 1 rain, 1 fog). Huffman needs 22 bits. Arithmetic coding with summer’s probability table needs about…
a: 19 bits
why: 12 × 0.415 + 2 × 3 + 4 + 4 ≈ 19.0 bits. The 12 sunny reports cost 5 bits instead of 12.
title: Arithmetic coding and rANS

q: Summer data coded with the year’s probability table costs 1.375 bits per report; summer’s entropy is 1.19. What is the 1.375 called?
a: The cross-entropy of summer data under the year’s table
why: Cross-entropy is the average cost when the data follow one distribution and the code another. It is never below the entropy.
title: Arithmetic coding and rANS

q: Can a cross-entropy ever be smaller than the entropy of the data?
a: No — a wrong table can only cost extra
wrong: Yes, if the table is sharper than the data
why: The entropy is the floor for any code. The gap between the two is the price of the wrong table.
title: Arithmetic coding and rANS

q: Why can’t you decode report number 1,000 of an rANS stream without decoding the 999 before it?
a: The entropy coder carries a running state, and that state depends on every earlier report
wrong: rANS writes the reports in reverse order
rANS stores reports in fixed 4-bit slots
rANS needs the probability table of the next report
why: The state after report 999 is only known by decoding reports 1 to 999. Variable-length codes like Huffman hide the position of report 1,000 in the same way.
title: Arithmetic coding and rANS

q: How many different values can an n-bit fixed-length slot hold, if one code is reserved as the escape marker?
a: 2n−1 values (0 to 2n−2)
wrong: 2n values
n values
2n values
why: An n-bit slot has 2n codes. The top one, all ones, means “look in the escape stream”, which leaves the rest for ordinary values: 0 to 30 in a 5-bit slot.
title: Fixed-length codes and escapes

q: For the 1,024 Gull Rock wind readings, which width gives the fewest bits in total, escapes included?
a: 5 bits, about 5.54 bits per reading
why: At 5 bits only the 31 gales escape (ε = 3.0 %), adding 0.54 bits per reading. At 4 bits, 201 ordinary breezes escape as well (232 escapes in all), and the escapes cost more than the bit saved.
title: Fixed-length codes and escapes

q: What is random access?
a: Being able to decode any single item without decoding the items before it
wrong: Reading the items in a random order to improve compression
Choosing the code width at random
Storing the items at random positions
why: With n-bit slots, item i starts at bit in. With an entropy-coded stream, you must decode from the start to find it.
title: Fixed-length codes and escapes

q: With n=5, ε = 3.0 % and 18 bits per escape, what is the cost per reading?
a: About 5.54 bits
why: n+ε×18=5+0.030×18≈5.54.
title: Fixed-length codes and escapes

q: Compared with an entropy coder, what does the fixed-length code with escapes buy for the extra bit per wind reading?
a: Random access and decoding every reading independently, in parallel
wrong: No need for any side information
why: The entropy coder gets 4.54 bits per reading, the fixed-length code 5.54. The extra bit pays for knowing where every reading starts.
title: Fixed-length codes and escapes

q: What is a residual?
a: The exact difference between a value and its prediction, r=x−x^
wrong: The part of a value that is thrown away
The average of the last few values
The prediction made by the receiver
why: The receiver makes the same prediction and adds the residual back, x=x^+r, so nothing is lost.
title: Predict, then send the surprise

q: What may a prediction use?
a: Only things the receiver already knows, such as earlier readings
wrong: Anything the sender knows, including the current reading
Future readings, if they are available
why: The receiver must be able to make exactly the same guess, or it cannot add the residual back.
title: Predict, then send the surprise

q: Predicting every temperature with the 28-day average leaves the entropy at 6.53 bits — unchanged. Why?
a: Subtracting a constant moves the histogram but does not narrow it
wrong: Residuals are always more expensive than values
The average is not known to the receiver
why: Entropy depends on the spread of the values, not on where they sit. A guess has to follow the ups and downs to save bits.
title: Predict, then send the surprise

q: How many bits per reading does the “previous value” predictor save on the Gull Rock temperatures?
wrong: Nothing — it only moves the histogram
why: The residuals spread over about ±0.3 °C instead of ±2.4 °C, which is three halvings of the spread, about 2.9 bits.
title: Predict, then send the surprise

q: What do DPCM, FLAC and PNG have in common?
a: They predict each value from its neighbours and code the exact residual
wrong: They all store values in fixed 8-bit slots
They all throw away small details
They all use a trained dictionary of byte strings
why: They all do lossless predictive coding — predict, take the exact integer residual, entropy-code it.
title: Predict, then send the surprise

q: What does the standard deviation σ of a set of residuals measure?
a: Their typical distance from the mean
wrong: How many of them are zero
why: It is the square root of the variance, the average squared distance from the mean μ.
title: The shape of a residual

q: The residuals’ standard deviation is halved. Roughly how many bits per value does that save?
a: One bit
why: For a bell-shaped residual, bits ≈ log2​σ + a constant, and log2​(σ/2)=log2​σ−1.
title: The shape of a residual

q: About how many bits does a Gaussian residual with σ = 4 integer steps cost?
a: About 4.05 bits
why: log2​4+2.05=4.05; the figure’s exact sum and its Monte Carlo run agree to within 0.01 bit.
title: The shape of a residual

q: For a fixed standard deviation, which shape costs the most bits?
a: The Gaussian
wrong: A shape with all values equal to the mean
why: For a given spread the bell curve is the most unpredictable shape, so it is the honest worst case; the pointier Laplace costs about 0.1 bit less.
title: The shape of a residual

q: What is a Monte Carlo check?
a: Testing a claim by simulating many random samples and measuring the result
wrong: A gambling-based estimate of the mean
why: The figure draws 20,000 random residuals of each shape, counts them, and compares their entropy with the formula.
title: The shape of a residual

q: Why can no predictor bring the Gull Rock temperature residuals down to zero bits?
a: The sensor’s own noise cannot be predicted from anything
wrong: Because residuals are always at least 1 °C
Because the entropy coder adds a bit per value
Because the first reading is sent in full
why: Even a perfect guess of the true temperature misses the noise of the reading itself, about 1 tenth of a degree here — roughly 2.1 bits per reading.
title: The shape of a residual

q: A predictor explains 75 % of the variance of bell-shaped values. How many bits per value does it save?
a: 1 bit
why: ½ log₂(1/(1 − 0.75)) = ½ log₂ 4 = 1. The residual’s σ is half the original.
title: The exchange rate: variance explained → bits

q: About what share of the variance must a predictor explain to save 2 bits per value?
a: About 94 %
why: Two bits means the residual’s σ is a quarter of the original, so its variance is 1/16: R² = 15/16 ≈ 93.75 %.
title: The exchange rate: variance explained → bits

q: A predictor explains a share R2 of the variance σ2. What variance does the residual keep?
a: (1−R2)σ2
wrong: R2σ2
(1−R2)σ
σ2/R2
why: R² is the share explained; the rest, 1 − R², stays in the residual.
title: The exchange rate: variance explained → bits

q: Predicting every temperature with the 28-day average gives which R²?
why: The average is a constant; the residual has exactly the spread of the values. No variance explained, no bits saved.
title: The exchange rate: variance explained → bits

q: Going from one bit saved to two bits saved, by how much must the unexplained variance shrink?
a: By a factor of 4
why: Each bit halves σ, and halving σ quarters the variance. So 25 % unexplained becomes 6.25 %.
title: The exchange rate: variance explained → bits

q: The 14:30 reading with the mast thermometer is r = np.array([11.4, 10.8, 0.82, 1012.6, 14.0]). What are r.shape and r[3]?
a: (5,) and 1012.6, the pressure
why: Five elements in a one-dimensional array; elem_id counts from 0, so position 3 is the barometer.
title: Vectors, elements and furrows

q: What is a furrow on this site?
a: One element position followed across many vectors: one column of the stacked table, R[:, elem_id]
wrong: One whole reading: one row of the table, R[i]
The radio wire a message travels over
A single number in one reading
why: A row is a vector, a cell is an element, a column is a furrow. Per-furrow statistics are computed separately for each column.
title: Vectors, elements and furrows

q: Twelve readings of five elements are stacked into R. What is R.shape, and what is R.mean(axis=0).shape?
a: (12, 5) and (5,): one mean per furrow
why: axis=0 averages down the rows, so one number survives per column, which is per furrow.
title: Vectors, elements and furrows

q: Writing each reading with a fixed-length code, how many bits per reading did subtracting each furrow’s mean save on the afternoon’s twelve readings?
a: From 45 to 21 bits per reading
why: The pressure furrow alone drops from 15 bits (10 126 steps of 0.1 hPa) to 6 bits once its mean is removed.
title: Vectors, elements and furrows

q: Why does subtracting one mean of all 60 numbers make the code longer instead of shorter?
a: The furrows live at very different typical values, so one shared shift is wrong for every furrow
wrong: Because subtraction always adds a sign bit
Because the global mean is not a whole number
Because the radio cannot send negative numbers
why: One shift of 210.1 turns a humidity of 0.82 into −209.32, which needs 16 bits. The typical value belongs to the furrow, never to the reading.
title: Vectors, elements and furrows

q: Does subtracting each furrow’s mean lower the entropy of the readings?
a: No. Shifting by a known constant never changes entropy; it shortens fixed-length codes and prepares the data for later tricks
wrong: Yes, by about one bit per element
No, it raises the entropy by the size of the means
why: An entropy coder that knows each furrow’s distribution gains nothing from a shift. A fixed-length code, and every method that assumes centred data, does.
title: Vectors, elements and furrows

q: For one reading, the foot thermometer is 2 °C above its mean and the top one is 1.5 °C above its own. What does this reading add to the covariance?
a: A positive product, +3 °C², pulling the covariance up
wrong: Nothing; only readings below the mean count
why: Covariance is the average of (distance from mean) × (distance from mean). Both on the same side gives a positive product.
title: Furrows that move together

q: What is the correlation of the two Gull Rock thermometers over ten days?
a: About 0.99
why: The covariance 2.94 °C² divided by the two spreads, 1.73 × 1.72, gives 0.992. Not exactly 1: each sensor has its own small noise.
title: Furrows that move together

q: A correlation of 0.992 means the best straight-line prediction of one thermometer from the other explains how much of its variance, and saves how many bits?
a: About 98 % of the variance, worth about 2.9 bits on that furrow
wrong: About 99 % of the variance, worth about 0.5 bit
About 50 % of the variance, worth about 1 bit
All of it, worth an unlimited number of bits
why: R2 is the correlation squared, 0.983, and the exchange rate of II.12 gives 21​log2​1−0.9831​≈2.95 bits.
title: Furrows that move together

q: R holds 480 readings of 5 elements. What does np.cov(R.T) return, and what sits on its diagonal?
a: A (5, 5) array; the diagonal holds the variance of each furrow
wrong: A (480, 480) array; the diagonal holds each reading’s length
A (5, 5) array with zeros on the diagonal
why: np.cov wants one variable per row, so the furrows (the columns of R) are handed over transposed. The covariance of a furrow with itself is its variance σc2​.
title: Furrows that move together

q: Why is the covariance matrix of the raw Gull Rock readings hard to read at a glance?
a: Its cells carry the furrows’ own units, so pressure’s big numbers dwarf humidity’s tiny ones
wrong: Because covariances can only be positive
Because it has more rows than furrows
why: The pressure variance is about 29.5 hPa², the humidity variance about 0.002. The correlation matrix (standardized furrows) removes the units.
title: Furrows that move together

q: When you rotate the axes of a 2-D cloud, what stays the same?
a: The total spread — the sum of the variances along the two axes
wrong: The covariance between the two coordinates
The number of bits needed per reading
why: A rotation moves no point; it only changes which numbers we write down. The sum of the variances stays 5.94 °C² at every angle, while its split between the axes changes.
title: Turning the axes (KLT)

q: Why does a lopsided split of the same total spread cost fewer bits?
a: Bits grow with the logarithm of each variance, so one big and one tiny variance cost less than two medium ones
wrong: Because the big variance is sent with fewer bits
Because a rotation removes noise from the data
Because lopsided data needs no sign bit
why: By the Gaussian rule each number costs about ½ log₂ of its variance plus a constant, so the total depends on the product of the variances: 2.99 × 2.95 ≈ 8.8 before, 5.91 × 0.025 ≈ 0.15 after.
title: Turning the axes (KLT)

q: What is an eigenvalue of a covariance matrix?
a: The variance of the data along one of its natural axes (an eigenvector)
wrong: The largest number in the matrix
why: Turned to the eigenvectors, the coordinates are uncorrelated, and the variance along each one is its eigenvalue λ. For the thermometers: 5.91 and 0.025 °C².
title: Turning the axes (KLT)

q: How do the KLT and PCA differ?
a: Not in their mathematics — both rotate to the eigenvectors; they differ in what is done next (PCA usually drops the small axes, the KLT for coding keeps them all)
wrong: The KLT works only in two dimensions
PCA is lossless, the KLT is lossy
why: Same eigenvectors, two traditions. Lossless coding cannot drop anything, so on this site we say KLT.
title: Turning the axes (KLT)

q: Turning the thermometer axes to the KLT saves 2.95 bits per reading. What else gives exactly 2.95 bits?
a: Predicting the top thermometer from the foot one with a straight line (the exchange rate at R² = 0.983)
wrong: Rounding both thermometers to whole degrees
why: In two dimensions the two are the same redundancy measured two ways. The difference coordinate is the residual of that prediction in disguise.
title: Turning the axes (KLT)

q: What is the transform coding gain, per element, of a KLT on standardized data with eigenvalues λ1​…λd​?
a: 21​log2​(AM/GM) of the eigenvalues
wrong: log2​λ1​, from the largest eigenvalue
21​log2​d
21​log2​(λ1​/λd​)
why: Each coordinate costs about ½ log₂ of its variance. Before the rotation all variances are 1 (their average); after it they are the λ’s. The difference, averaged, is ½ log₂ AM/GM.
title: What the rotation buys

q: Which spectrum gives the larger coding gain on vectors of 64 standardized elements?
a: 8 directions at variance 50 and 56 at 0.1 — about 2.4 bits per element
wrong: 8 directions at variance 10 and 56 at 1 — about 2.4 bits per element
64 directions all at variance 1 — about 1 bit per element
Both give the same gain, since both have 8 strong directions
why: The geometric mean is dragged down by the small eigenvalues. 10 vs 1 gives only 0.34 bit; 50 vs 0.1 gives 2.43 bits.
title: What the rotation buys

q: What does “low rank” mean for a cloud of vectors?
a: Its spread lives mostly in a few directions — a few large eigenvalues, the rest small
wrong: It has been rounded to few bits
why: The sharper the drop from the large eigenvalues to the small ones, the more a KLT saves.
title: What the rotation buys

q: Why can a KLT computed in floating point not simply be rounded to make it lossless?
a: Rotated whole numbers are generally not whole numbers; rounding them cannot always be undone exactly
wrong: Because a rotation changes the total spread
Because floating point cannot store negative numbers
Because the KLT is only defined for two elements
why: Lifting fixes this by splitting the rotation into steps that each change one number by a rounded function of the others — undone by subtracting the same rounded amount.
title: What the rotation buys

q: In the integer average-and-difference transform, how is the original foot reading recovered from s and d?
a: foot = s − ⌊d/2⌋, then top = foot + d
wrong: foot = s + d, then top = s − d
why: Each lifting step is undone by subtracting exactly what it added, in reverse order — no rounding error survives.
title: What the rotation buys

q: What is a centroid?
a: The average point of a group of vectors
wrong: The first vector of a group
why: For the calm readings, the centroid is (7.7 kn, 69.9 %): the average wind and the average humidity of the calm group.
title: Clusters and codebooks (VQ)

q: What are the two steps that k-means repeats?
a: Assign every vector to its nearest centroid; move every centroid to the average of its vectors
wrong: Sort the vectors; split them in half
Rotate the data; drop the smallest axis
Pick the k largest vectors; delete the rest
why: Each step can only reduce the total squared distance, so the loop settles down — though not always in the best possible place.
title: Clusters and codebooks (VQ)

q: How many bits does naming one centroid out of a codebook of C=8 cost?
a: 3 bits per vector
why: The index tax is log2​C bits per vector. Spread over d elements, it is log2​C/d bits per element.
title: Clusters and codebooks (VQ)

q: In lossless VQ, what plays the role of the prediction, and what is sent?
a: The nearest centroid is the prediction; the index and the exact residual are sent
wrong: The index is the prediction; only the centroid is sent
The residual is the prediction; only the index is sent
Nothing is predicted; the centroid replaces the vector
why: Lossless VQ is predictive coding with a menu of C predictions. Plain (lossy) VQ would send only the index and accept the error.
title: Clusters and codebooks (VQ)

q: On the weather-regime data (wind and humidity, d=2), what does a 3-centroid codebook net per element?
a: About 1.46 bits — 2.26 saved minus 0.79 of index tax
wrong: About 2.26 bits — the tax is paid only once
About 0.05 bits — the same as a rotation
About −0.79 bits — the tax always wins
why: The residual spread shrinks to about 0.04 of the original per furrow, saving 2.26 bits per element; the index costs log₂ 3 / 2 = 0.79.
title: Clusters and codebooks (VQ)

q: Run k-means on the bell-shaped two-thermometer cloud. What does the codebook end up doing?
a: Lining its centroids up along the cloud’s long axis — rediscovering the rotation, but paying an index tax for it
wrong: Placing all centroids at the mean
Beating the rotation by about one bit per element
why: Its best net, 1.36 bits per element at C = 64, stays below the 1.47 bits the KLT gets with no tax.
title: Codebooks versus rotations

q: In rate–distortion terms, how much can each bit spent describing a bell-shaped (Gaussian) value shrink the error, at best?
a: It can at best halve the error’s standard deviation
wrong: It can at best divide the error by ten
It can remove the error completely
It can at best shrink it by one percent
why: Each extra bit at best divides the error variance by 4. So log₂ C bits of index per vector save at most log₂ C / d bits per element — exactly the tax.
title: Codebooks versus rotations

q: On which kind of data can a VQ codebook beat a rotation (KLT)?
a: Clustered data, where the vectors fall into separate lumps
wrong: Data whose elements are all independent
Any data, given a large enough codebook
why: A rotation only sees straight-line structure. On the weather regimes VQ nets 1.46 bits per element; the KLT gets 0.05.
title: Codebooks versus rotations

q: Product quantization splits a 64-element vector into nsub​=8 pieces with 256 centroids each. What is the index tax?
a: 64 bits per vector, 1 bit per element
why: Each piece costs log₂ 256 = 8 bits; eight pieces cost 64 bits, spread over 64 elements.
title: Codebooks versus rotations

q: Does product quantization escape the bound that stops a codebook from beating a rotation on Gaussian data?
a: No — the bound adds up piece by piece, so the same economics apply
wrong: Yes — splitting removes the index tax
Yes — the pieces are always clustered
No — product quantization is lossy, so the bound does not apply
why: Each sub-codebook is an ordinary VQ on its piece, facing the same bits-versus-error trade-off.
title: Codebooks versus rotations

q: In INT8 with a scale of 0.25 °C, what values can be stored, and how far off can a temperature be?
a: Multiples of 0.25 °C from −31.75 to +31.75; at most 0.125 °C off
wrong: Multiples of 0.25 °C from 0 to 63.75; at most 0.25 °C off
why: INT8 stores a whole number k between −127 and 127 and means k × scale. The grid is even, so the rounding error is at most half a step everywhere.
title: Integers and floats

q: Why does a uniform 8-bit grid suit rainfall rate (0.1 to 100 mm/h) so badly?
a: Its step, about 0.8 mm/h, is bigger than a whole drizzle — every light rain rounds to 0 or 0.8
wrong: Because 100 mm/h does not fit in 8 bits
why: With 127 steps up to 100 mm/h, the step is 100/127 ≈ 0.79 mm/h. Drizzle (0.1–0.5 mm/h) is lost entirely; the top of the range is measured far more finely than anyone needs.
title: Integers and floats

q: What do the exponent and the mantissa of a floating-point number do?
a: The exponent picks the power of two (the binade); the mantissa picks the position inside it
wrong: The exponent stores the sign; the mantissa stores the value
The exponent stores the digits; the mantissa the decimal point
Both store halves of an ordinary integer
why: Value = sign × (1 + fraction) × 2^exponent. Inside one binade the steps are equal; each binade up, they double.
title: Integers and floats

q: What does BF16 look like, bit by bit?
a: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 7 mantissa bits
wrong: 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits
1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits, 11 mantissa bits
why: BF16 keeps the 8-bit exponent of a 32-bit float, so it has the same range, but only 7 mantissa bits: 11.4 becomes 11.375.
title: Integers and floats

q: In ten days of BF16 temperatures from Gull Rock, how much information do the 8 exponent bits carry together?
a: About 0.22 bits — only two exponents ever occur
wrong: About 8 bits — one per exponent bit
About 4 bits — half of the field
Exactly 0 bits — the exponent never changes
why: All temperatures lie between 4 and 16 °C, so only the binades [4, 8) and [8, 16) appear. The mantissa bits, by contrast, look like coin flips.
title: Integers and floats

q: How are the 8 bits of an FP8 E4M3 number used?
a: 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits
wrong: 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits
8 bits of a whole number with a scale
1 sign bit, 3 exponent bits, 4 mantissa bits
why: E4M3 = 4 exponent, 3 mantissa bits. Its largest value is 448. The other common FP8 format, E5M2, has 5 exponent and 2 mantissa bits.
title: Eight-bit floats and index space

q: What is quantization, as this site uses the word?
a: Rounding numbers to the nearest point of a fixed grid of representable values
wrong: Counting how many values a format can represent
Coding numbers with fewer bits without any loss
Measuring the spread of a furrow
why: It happens once, before our lossless compressor arrives; the rounded 8-bit values are the originals it must reproduce bit for bit.
title: Eight-bit floats and index space

q: In E4M3 index space, how many steps apart are 12 and 11, and how many are 0.1 and −0.1?
a: 1 step, and 58 steps
why: Near 12 the E4M3 grid has one value per unit; between −0.1 and 0.1 it is packed with 57 values. A small difference near zero crosses many rungs.
title: Eight-bit floats and index space

q: In E4M3 (above its smallest numbers), how many index steps is a doubling of the value, anywhere on the line?
a: 8 steps
wrong: It depends on the size of the value
why: Each binade (a doubling) holds 8 values, one per mantissa pattern: 0.5 → 1 is indices 48 → 56, 100 → 200 rounds to 96 → 192, indices 108 → 116.
title: Eight-bit floats and index space

q: Roughly how many of E4M3’s 253 values lie between −1 and 1?
a: 111 — almost half
why: The logarithmic grid spends as many codes on each binade below 1 as above it, so codes pile up near zero.
title: Eight-bit floats and index space

q: What is a cache?
a: A small, fast store that keeps copies of some items from a big, slow one
wrong: A compressed copy of the whole archive
A queue of asks waiting to be served
The slow memory where everything is kept
why: The desk is the cache, the archive is the big slow store. An ask found on the desk is a hit; otherwise it is a miss and the lift must fetch it.
title: The forecaster's desk

q: On the storm morning (24 asks, 8 different logbooks), why can no desk of any size get fewer than 8 misses?
a: Each logbook’s first ask must miss — it has never been fetched before
wrong: Because the desk always loses 8 logbooks to eviction
Because LRU makes a mistake on every eighth ask
Because the lift carries only 8 logbooks a morning
why: First-time asks miss whatever the policy or the desk size. Only repeat asks can hit.
title: The forecaster's desk

q: The desk is full and a new logbook arrives. Which logbook does LRU send back down?
a: The one whose last use was longest ago
wrong: The one that arrived on the desk first
The one requested least often overall
why: Least recently used. “Arrived first” is FIFO; “requested least often” is a different policy (LFU).
title: The forecaster's desk

q: On the storm morning with a 4-logbook desk, how many misses do LRU and FIFO make?
a: LRU 10, FIFO 14
why: FIFO throws out Gull Rock and Seal Point simply because they arrived early, although they are needed every few asks. LRU keeps them because they are always recently used.
title: The forecaster's desk

q: In the asks G S H G, what is the reuse distance of the second G?
a: 2 — two other logbooks (S and H) were used since the first G
why: Reuse distance counts distinct other items since the previous use, not elapsed asks. Repeats of the same item count once.
title: Reuse distance

q: Under LRU with B slots, exactly when does an ask miss?
a: When its reuse distance is at least B (or it is a first ask)
wrong: When its reuse distance is at most B
When its reuse distance is exactly B
When more than B asks have passed since its last use
why: LRU keeps the B most recently used items. An item with distance u sits at position u+1 in recency order, so it is on the desk only if u+1≤B.
title: Reuse distance

q: What does the miss-rate curve m(B) give you?
a: The LRU miss rate for every cache size at once, read off one histogram of reuse distances
wrong: The miss rate of the best possible policy
How the miss rate changes over time
The miss rate of one cache size, measured very precisely
why: m(B) is the fraction of asks whose reuse distance is at least B. One pass over the asks gives the whole curve.
title: Reuse distance

q: On the round-robin sweep G S H L N G S H L N …, how many of 24 asks miss with 4 slots under LRU, and under Bélády?
a: LRU 24 (all of them), Bélády 9
why: Every reuse distance is 4, so with 4 slots LRU always evicts exactly the logbook needed next. The clairvoyant policy keeps most of them.
title: Reuse distance

q: Why is Bélády’s policy useful if it is impossible to run?
a: It bounds what any eviction policy could achieve, so the gap to LRU shows how much a smarter policy could still win
wrong: It is used by real caches with a small delay
It is always twice as good as LRU
why: Bélády needs the future. Comparing it with LRU on recorded asks tells you whether to work on the policy or buy a bigger cache.
title: Reuse distance

q: What is the difference between bandwidth and latency?
a: Bandwidth is how much a link moves per second once data flows; latency is how long one ask takes to start arriving
wrong: They are two names for the same speed
Bandwidth is the size of a memory; latency is its price
Latency is the bandwidth of a single wire
why: The lift carries up to 50 logbooks per trip (bandwidth) and each trip takes 2 minutes however much it carries (latency).
title: Wires and memories

q: The forecaster needs ten logbooks. How long does it take to order them one at a time, waiting for each, versus all at once?
a: 20 minutes versus 2 minutes
wrong: The same either way — the lift has the same speed
why: One at a time pays the 2-minute latency ten times. Ordered together, they share one trip.
title: Wires and memories

q: Roughly how fast is PCIe Gen5 ×16, the link between host memory and the GPU, compared with the GPU’s own HBM?
a: About 64 GB/s per direction (≈ 50 in practice) against several TB/s — roughly 100× slower
wrong: About the same speed — both are a few TB/s
why: An H200’s HBM delivers about 4.8 TB/s; 4.8 TB/s ÷ 50 GB/s ≈ 96.
title: Wires and memories

q: What is host DRAM, in the harbour-office picture?
a: The archive downstairs — the big, slower memory where everything is kept
wrong: The radio link to Gull Rock
why: HBM is the desk (small, fast, next to the GPU), host DRAM the archive (big), PCIe the lift between them.
title: Wires and memories

q: Why can many small scattered reads still use most of a link’s bandwidth?
a: If enough of them are in flight at once, their latencies overlap and the link stays full
wrong: Because small reads have no latency
Because the link compresses small reads automatically
They cannot — small reads always waste most of the bandwidth
why: Delivered rate ≈ (reads in flight × read size) ÷ latency, up to the bandwidth. GPUs keep thousands of reads in flight; a forecaster waiting for each logbook keeps one.
title: Wires and memories

q: A season ticket costs 300 crowns; a single trip costs 12. After how many trips does the season ticket pay off?
a: 25 trips
why: Break-even = fixed cost ÷ saving per item = 300 ÷ 12 = 25.
title: Pay once, use many times

q: What is the per-item cost of a fixed cost shared by n items?
a: The fixed cost divided by n
wrong: The fixed cost, whatever n is
The fixed cost divided by its square root
why: That is all amortization is. It falls as 1/n — a straight line of slope −1 on log–log axes.
title: Pay once, use many times

q: The regime codebook of II.17 costs 96 bits to send once and saves about 2.9 bits per reading. When does it break even?
a: After about 33 readings
wrong: Never — a codebook always costs more than it saves
why: 96 ÷ 2.92 ≈ 33. Beyond that, every reading is profit; before it, the codebook is a loss.
title: Pay once, use many times

q: A dictionary weighs as much as w items and is shared by b items, with every number stored in 8 bits. What does it cost per number?
a: 8w/b bits
wrong: 8b/w bits
wb/8 bits
8w bits, whatever b is
why: It is w/b items’ worth per item, and an item’s worth is 8 bits per number.
title: Pay once, use many times

q: Which three moves recur through the whole primer?
a: Predict then send the residual; use side information both ends already have; pay fixed costs once and share them
why: Residuals, codebooks and rotations are ways of predicting; dictionaries, almanacs and codebooks are side information; every one of them is a fixed cost to amortize.
title: School’s out: a cheat sheet

q: Which of these is not measured in bits on this site?
a: Reuse distance
why: Reuse distance counts distinct items between two asks for the same item. It describes which items are wanted, not what is inside them.
title: School’s out: a cheat sheet

q: In Part III, what does the stack of readings R of II.13 become, and what does a furrow become?
a: The orchard v of shape (n_tokens, n_kv_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim); a furrow becomes v[:, layer_id, head_id, elem_id]
wrong: A list of tokens; a furrow becomes one token
The dictionary; a furrow becomes one delta
The hot cache; a furrow becomes one slot
why: Same idea, two more axes: one element position followed along the token axis, with a layer and a head fixed.
title: School’s out: a cheat sheet

q: What links the exchange rate of II.12 to the KLT of II.15?
a: Both convert explained variance into bits with the same Gaussian rule: for two thermometers they give the same 2.95 bits
wrong: Nothing; one is about prediction, the other about rotation
The KLT is only defined when R² is below 0.5
The exchange rate is the KLT applied to one furrow
why: Bits ≈ ½ log₂ variance + constant. Prediction shrinks one variance; rotation reshuffles variances so their product shrinks. Same currency.
title: School’s out: a cheat sheet

q: In the toy world, what do the desk, the lift and the archive become in Part III?
a: HBM next to the GPU, the PCIe link, and host DRAM
wrong: The CPU, the radio and the disk
The LLM, the tokens and the prompt
The codebook, the index and the residual
why: Small and fast, the link, big and slow: about a hundred times apart in speed.
title: School’s out: a cheat sheet

q: What is a token?
a: The unit of text an LLM reads and writes, a word or a piece of one; its position in the sequence is token_pos_id
wrong: One byte of the text file
why: Common words are usually one token; rare words are split into pieces. An LLM produces exactly one token per decode step, at position token_pos_id.
title: How an LLM writes

q: What is a sequence on this site?
a: One conversation’s tokens as the LLM sees them, from its first token to now
wrong: The order in which cherries are stored
why: A sequence is one LLM context. A serving system runs many sequences at once, and each grows its own orchard.
title: How an LLM writes

q: Qwen3.5-2B has 24 layers. How many of them are KV layers?
a: 6: only those keep keys and values for every token, and only they get a layer_id in the orchard
why: The other 18 layers carry a fixed-size state and have nothing per token to store. layer_id counts KV layers only: 0 … 5.
title: How an LLM writes

q: What happens in prefill, and what in decode?
a: Prefill reads the whole prompt at once; decode then writes the answer one token per step
wrong: Prefill writes the answer; decode reads the prompt
Both read the prompt one token at a time
Prefill compresses the prompt; decode decompresses it
why: Prefill can work on all prompt tokens in parallel. Decode is sequential, because each new token depends on the one before.
title: How an LLM writes

q: With a time per output token of 30 ms, roughly how many tokens per second does one sequence get?
a: About 33
why: 1 s ÷ 0.030 s ≈ 33 tokens per second, for each sequence the machine serves.
title: How an LLM writes

q: In attention, what is compared with what?
a: The new token’s query is compared with the key of every stored token
wrong: The new token’s value is compared with every stored value
Each stored key is compared with every other stored key
The query is compared with the values
why: The score of stored token t is the dot product of the query and that token’s key. The values are only used afterwards, mixed by the weights.
title: Attention: looking back

q: Scores 1, 2 and 3 go into a softmax. Roughly what weights come out?
why: Softmax exponentiates and normalises: e1,e2,e3=2.7,7.4,20.1, divided by their sum 30.2.
title: Attention: looking back

q: In decode_step, what is the shape of key on the Bench, and what is K after np.stack?
a: (2, 256), one vector per KV head; K is (pos+1, 2, 256), every stored key of the layer
why: Qwen3.5-2B keeps 2 KV heads of 256 elements per layer. K stacks the pos+1 stored keys of the layer along a new first axis.
title: Attention: looking back

q: A layer has 8 query heads and 2 KV heads (grouped-query attention). How many key vectors does one token store at that layer?
a: 2, one per KV head
wrong: 16, one per query head and KV head
why: With GQA, groups of query heads share one KV head: head_id = qh // (n_q_heads // n_kv_heads). Only the KV heads are stored.
title: Attention: looking back

q: In the decode step, which line makes the stored memory grow with every step?
a: k[layer_id].append(key); v[layer_id].append(val)
why: Every step, at every KV layer, one more key and one more value are appended, and never removed.
title: Attention: looking back

q: Why does an LLM store keys and values instead of recomputing them at every step?
a: A token’s key and value never change once computed, so recomputing them every step would waste work
wrong: Because keys and values change at every step
Because the LLM cannot compute them again
Because storing them makes the output more accurate
why: A key depends only on its own token and earlier ones. Later tokens cannot change it, so it is computed once and kept.
title: The orchard

q: What is the orchard?
a: Every key and every value one sequence has grown at every KV layer: k, v of shape (n_tokens, n_kv_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim), kept in host memory
wrong: The hot cache of recently used picks on the GPU
why: It grows one row per token at every KV layer and is never pruned. It is a store, not a cache, whatever its usual name says.
title: The orchard

q: In the fixed index order, what does v[t, l, h, :] select?
a: One V vector: token t, KV layer l, KV head h, every element
wrong: One token’s values at every layer
why: The order is always [token_pos_id, layer_id, head_id, elem_id]. Fixing the first three and taking all elements is one head’s vector, (head_dim,).
title: The orchard

q: How many bytes are one token’s values at one layer on the Bench, and across all its KV layers?
a: 512 B and 3 072 B
why: 2 heads × 256 elements × 1 byte = 512 B per layer; × 6 KV layers = 3 072 B. On the Pin the same two numbers are ≈ 640 B and ≈ 50 KB.
title: The orchard

q: What is v[:, layer_id, head_id, elem_id]?
a: One furrow: one element position of one head, followed along every token of the sequence
wrong: One token’s values at one layer
The whole value half of the orchard
why: Fixing everything but token_pos_id leaves a column of n_tokens numbers: 225 000 on the Bench.
title: The orchard

q: What does RoPE do to a key before it is stored?
a: Turns each pair of its elements by an angle that grows with the token’s position
wrong: Adds the position number to every element
Shuffles its elements in a random order
why: Because both query and key are turned, their dot product depends only on how far apart the two tokens are. Keys are more regular before the turn than after it.
title: Two wrinkles: RoPE and MLA

q: The orchard holds rope(key, pos, theta). Can the key before the turn be recovered?
a: Yes, exactly: rope(stored, -pos, theta) undoes it, because the position is known
why: A rotation is reversible, and token_pos_id is known to both sides. A lossless compressor may therefore store keys before RoPE and turn them on the way out.
title: Two wrinkles: RoPE and MLA

q: What does MLA store per token per layer?
a: One latent vector, from which keys and values are rebuilt by a matrix multiplication
wrong: Nothing; it recomputes keys and values
Only the keys, never the values
One key and one value per query head
why: Multi-head latent attention keeps a single latent (576 elements in DeepSeek-V3, ≈ 640 on the Pin). For this site it is still one fixed-size row of the orchard per token per KV layer.
title: Two wrinkles: RoPE and MLA

q: On the Pin, why is v.shape written (100_384, 78, 1, 640) although GLM-5.1 has no separate value heads?
a: Its one latent per token per layer is treated as one head of 640 elements, so the same four index names fit both settings
wrong: Because GLM-5.1 has exactly one KV head
Because the latent is 640 values and no keys
why: The latent holds keys and values together; writing it as (1, 640) keeps the orchard’s index order [token_pos_id, layer_id, head_id, elem_id] the same on both settings.
title: Two wrinkles: RoPE and MLA

q: In top-k sparse attention, how many positions does one layer read at one decode step?
a: k, the ones the indexer picked (2048 in DSA)
wrong: k per KV head, so k times the number of heads
why: The indexer names a pick set S of k positions per layer per step; attention scores and mixes only those.
title: Sparse attention and the indexer

q: What does the indexer do?
a: Cheaply scores every stored position and keeps the k best, before attention touches any key or value
wrong: It decides which layers to skip
It sorts the tokens of the prompt alphabetically
why: In DSA it uses its own tiny keys in a low-precision format, so scanning everything is cheap compared with full attention.
title: Sparse attention and the indexer

q: What is a pick?
a: One (layer_id, token_pos_id) the indexer names at one decode step: one position wanted at one layer
wrong: The whole pick set of a step
why: A pick is the unit of demand. What it covers differs by LLM: one layer in DSA, a group of layers in GLM-5.1, four squeezed tokens in DeepSeek-V4.
title: Sparse attention and the indexer

q: Does sparse attention shrink the memory a sequence needs?
a: No; every row of the orchard must still be kept, because any position may be picked at a later step
wrong: Yes, to k rows per layer
why: The picks drift from step to step. A position skipped now may be picked later, so nothing can be thrown away.
title: Sparse attention and the indexer

q: Which property of sparse attention does this project build on?
a: At every layer of every step, the indexer announces exactly which positions attention will read, before their bytes are touched
wrong: Sparse attention makes keys more compressible
Sparse attention reads positions in order
why: That advance notice is a precise demand signal, which a cache (and a compressor) can plan around.
title: Sparse attention and the indexer

q: How big is the orchard of one 128K-token sequence of GLM-5.1, in BF16?
a: About 13 GB
why: 131 072 tokens × about 100 KB per token (78 KV layers × 1.28 KB) ≈ 13.1 GB. At 8 bits, half of that.
title: Everything must be kept

q: In the harbour office of Part II, what plays the role of the GPU’s HBM?
a: The forecaster’s desk, small, fast, close at hand
wrong: The radio link to Gull Rock
why: The archive is host DRAM (big, slow to reach) and the lift is the link between them.
title: Everything must be kept

q: Keeping the orchard in host memory and fetching every pick at every step: how many bytes per step for one GLM-5.1 sequence (BF16)?
a: About 204 MB
why: k×NL​×e=2048×78×1.28 KB ≈ 204 MB per step.
title: Everything must be kept

q: At 30 ms per step, what link bandwidth does that plan need per sequence, and how many sequences fill a 50 GB/s link?
a: About 6.8 GB/s per sequence, so about 7 sequences
wrong: About 68 GB/s, so less than one
why: 204 MB ÷ 0.030 s ≈ 6.8 GB/s; 50 ÷ 6.8 ≈ 7 (about 9 at the nominal 64 GB/s). HiSparse’s paper says “a dozen”.
title: Everything must be kept

q: Where does HiSparse keep each sequence’s complete orchard?
a: In host DRAM, on the CPU side of the link
why: Host DRAM is big enough for every orchard. The GPU keeps only a small hot cache per sequence per layer.
title: HiSparse: a library with a reading desk

q: What is B?
a: The number of pick slots in one hot cache, per sequence and per layer
wrong: The number of picks per step
The number of sequences per GPU
why: With k=2048 picks per step, HiSparse found B between 4096 and 8192 most useful; its headline numbers use B=4096.
title: HiSparse: a library with a reading desk

q: When the hot cache is full and a pick is missing, which pick does HiSparse evict?
a: The least recently used pick that is not in this step’s pick set
wrong: The pick with the smallest attention weight
The oldest token of the sequence
why: It is LRU with one guard: nothing the current step needs may be thrown out. In the listing, next(x for x in hot_cache if x not in S).
title: HiSparse: a library with a reading desk

q: Does HiSparse change what the LLM writes?
a: No; attention reads exactly the same picks, only where they are kept changes
wrong: Yes, slightly, because old rows are approximated
Yes, it skips some picks to save time
Only for prompts longer than 128K tokens
why: Every pick is in the hot cache before attention runs, either because it was already there (a hit) or because it was just fetched (a miss).
title: HiSparse: a library with a reading desk

q: What does one miss cost in HiSparse?
a: One raw pick of e bytes moved over the link
wrong: One byte per element of the sequence’s context
why: The hot cache holds raw picks, so a miss fetches the full e bytes from host memory into a free or evicted slot.
title: HiSparse: a library with a reading desk

q: At step 1 of the toy trace the hot cache holds 1, 10, 13, 2, 5, 9 (oldest first) and the indexer picks 2, 5, 9, 14. Which pick is evicted?
a: 1, the least recently used pick that is not wanted now
why: 14 is the only miss and needs a slot. The oldest resident pick not in the pick set is 1.
title: Watching the hot cache work

q: At step 3, position 5 is not picked, yet it stays and 13 is evicted. Why?
a: 5 was used at step 2, so it is more recent than 13
why: LRU evicts by last use: 13 was last used before step 1; 5 was last used at step 2.
title: Watching the hot cache work

q: In the toy trace, what share of all picks are hits?
why: Every step has three hits and one miss.
title: Watching the hot cache work

q: Which two prices does HiSparse leave untouched?
a: A miss costs one raw pick (e bytes) on the link; a slot costs one raw pick (e bytes) of GPU memory
wrong: The number of misses and the number of hits
The time of attention and the time of the indexer
The size of the prompt and the size of the answer
why: HiSparse lowers how many misses there are by caching well; what each miss and each slot costs stays at the raw row size.
title: Watching the hot cache work

q: What does the Lucky Louis property say?
a: From one decode step to the next, the indexer re-picks mostly the same positions
wrong: Neighbouring rows of the orchard have similar contents
The indexer always picks the newest tokens
A position picked once is never picked again
why: It is a statement about which picks are wanted, step after step. That is why a cache betting on recent picks keeps winning.
title: The Lucky Louis property

q: Keeping only the current top-k on the GPU misses 30 % of each step’s picks. What does that say?
a: On average, 70 % of a step’s picks were also picked at the step before
wrong: 30 % of the positions are never picked
The indexer is wrong 30 % of the time
70 % of the orchard is in the cache
why: A cache that holds exactly the previous step’s picks hits exactly the re-picked ones.
title: The Lucky Louis property

q: On HiSparse’s trace, what miss rate does LRU reach with B=4096 slots, and what does the clairvoyant Bélády policy reach?
a: 13.4 % for LRU, 8.2 % for Bélády
why: Even a policy that knows the future still misses 8.2 %; LRU is within about 5 points of it.
title: The Lucky Louis property

q: The indexer stably re-picks the same positions. What does that tell us about the bytes stored in those rows?
a: Nothing; it is about which picks are wanted, not about what they contain
wrong: That neighbouring rows are nearly identical
That the rows are all zeros
why: In the figure the keys are pure random numbers, and the picks still repeat. Similar contents would be a separate property, to be measured on its own.
title: The Lucky Louis property

q: Through HiSparse’s three LRU points, the miss rate falls roughly as m(B)∝B−1.08. What happens to the misses when the hot cache doubles?
a: They fall to about 47 %, roughly halved
why: 2−1.08≈0.47.
title: One curve behind every cache number

q: Under LRU with B slots, when does a pick miss?
a: When its reuse distance is at least B
wrong: When it was never picked before
When its position is larger than B
When its attention weight is small
why: The reuse distance counts the distinct other positions picked since its last pick; once B of them have come in, it has been pushed out. So m(B) is the share of picks with reuse distance ≥B.
title: One curve behind every cache number

q: Clairvoyant Bélády eviction at 4096 slots misses 8.2 %. About how many LRU slots would give the same miss rate, according to the fitted curve?
a: About 6 700, some 60 % more slots
why: Solve 0.294(B/2048)−1.08=0.082: B≈6700. A perfect eviction policy is worth what 60 % more desk space buys.
title: One curve behind every cache number

q: Within HiSparse, what is the only way to cut misses much further?
a: More hot-cache slots, each costing one raw pick of GPU memory
why: Eviction is within five points of the clairvoyant bound, so the remaining route is a bigger cache, paid in GPU memory, B×e per layer per sequence.
title: One curve behind every cache number

q: Why freeze a reference setting instead of using the best numbers for each question?
a: So every estimate on the site is comparable, and conclusions can be stated as ratios that carry over to other machines
wrong: Because GLM-5.1 is the best LLM
Because other machines do not use sparse attention
why: The point is not this rig; the point is that all pages use the same one, and name it.
title: Two reference settings: the Pin and the Bench

q: What is one token’s row at one layer on the Pin, and on the Bench?
a: 640 B on the Pin (one MLA latent, keys and values together); 512 B of values on the Bench, with keys another 512 B
why: The Pin’s 640 B is derived from GLM-5.1’s 50 KB per token at 8 bits over 78 layers. The Bench’s 512 B is 2 heads × 256 elements, values alone; 50 KB and 3 072 B are the per-token totals over all KV layers.
title: Two reference settings: the Pin and the Bench

q: Which quantities does the Bench lack that the Pin has?
a: Picks per step k, the miss rates and the time per output token: no indexer ever ran on it
wrong: The row size and the number of KV layers
The link bandwidth and the GPU memory
The stretch length and the storage format
why: The Bench is the data-side setting. It has shapes, bytes and measured ratios; the miss side of the economics needs an indexer and a decode loop.
title: Two reference settings: the Pin and the Bench

q: What is a stand-in LLM?
a: A small open LLM whose orchard is measured in place of the real sparse-attention target
wrong: A smaller copy of GLM-5.1 with the same weights
The LLM that runs the indexer
A probability table used by an entropy coder
why: Qwen3.5-2B on the Bench stands in for GLM-5.1. Whether its statistics transfer is itself a risk, and the site says so wherever a Bench number is carried to the Pin.
title: Two reference settings: the Pin and the Bench

q: What does the setting switch in the top bar change?
a: The hover reminders of terms and symbols, every live number written with the [[@key]] macro, and the figures that read the setting
wrong: The miss rates of HiSparse’s trace
why: Prose typed for one setting keeps its numbers and names the setting; only what was written to follow the switch follows it.
title: Two reference settings: the Pin and the Bench

q: On the Pin with B=4096, how many misses does one layer have per decode step?
a: About 274
why: m×k=0.134×2048≈274, each a scattered read of 640 bytes.
title: Three numbers and a deadline

q: At B=4096, about how many sequences can a 50 GB/s link feed on misses alone?
a: About 110
why: 274 misses × 78 layers × 640 B ≈ 13.7 MB per step; over 30 ms that is 0.46 GB/s per sequence; 50 ÷ 0.46 ≈ 110.
title: Three numbers and a deadline

q: At B=8192, which wall binds, and at about how many sequences?
a: GPU memory, at about 73 sequences
wrong: Neither; the GPU can serve unlimited sequences
why: Each sequence then holds 78 × 8192 × 640 B ≈ 409 MB of hot cache, and 30 GB ÷ 409 MB ≈ 73. The link could feed about 219.
title: Three numbers and a deadline

q: How long is one layer’s share of a 30 ms decode step on the Pin?
a: About 0.38 ms
why: 30 ms ÷ 78 layers ≈ 0.38 ms; each layer’s misses must arrive within that slice.
title: Three numbers and a deadline

q: Why must a decoder on the miss path run at least ten times faster than the link?
a: So that decoding a layer’s misses takes a small fraction of the 0.38 ms in which the link is already busy
wrong: Because the link is ten times faster than the GPU
Because decoding must happen ten times per step
Because the decoder reads every pick ten times
why: With 110 sequences the link needs the whole 0.38 ms for 19 MB of misses. At 500 GB/s, decoding them takes 39 µs, a tenth of the window.
title: Three numbers and a deadline

q: What are the four subproblems of kvblockdiff?
a: The compression scenario (bytes per cherry), the pick trace and the hot-cache replay (which picks miss and where they land), the decoder’s speed (does a cold decode fit the step), and the economics (sequences per GPU and dollars)
wrong: Keys, values, queries and the indexer
why: Each supplies one factor of the application’s bill, depends on different data, and has its own clean statement and its own measurement.
title: The project, and its four subproblems

q: Why is the compression scenario studied apart from the serving system?
a: Because the bytes a cherry needs depend only on the orchard and the dictionary, not on the indexer, the cache or the link, so they can be measured on a dump of orchards with no serving system at all
wrong: Because serving systems cannot be simulated
Because the compression scenario is the whole project
why: The factor it supplies, the delta share against dictionary weight, is a property of the data. The traffic factors come from a different source, the indexer’s picks.
title: The project, and its four subproblems

q: Why does the scenario insist on one cherry at a time, decoded cold, under a leash?
a: Because the miss path fetches one scattered pick now, with nothing decoded before it, and a dictionary that quietly contains the punnet would make the measurement answer a different question
wrong: Because the leash makes compressors faster
Because the campaigns’ harness could not do otherwise
why: Every rule of the scenario is the access pattern of the application written down, so that its numbers mean what the bill needs them to mean.
title: The project, and its four subproblems

q: In the compression scenario, what does the receiver ask for?
a: One cherry at a time, at any position, in any order
wrong: The whole orchard of a sequence, once
One stretch at a time, in order
why: The scenario models the miss path of sparse decoding, where one scattered piece is wanted now. Everything about it follows from “one at a time, at random”.
title: One cherry at a time

q: Which of these is part of the compression scenario?
a: A dictionary the receiver holds before it asks
wrong: The hot cache and its LRU eviction
why: The scenario keeps only what decides how many bytes a cherry costs. Caches, links and indexers return in Part VI, when the scenario’s numbers are mapped onto a serving system.
title: One cherry at a time

q: Why study the scenario apart from the application?
a: Because it is a clean information-theory question whose answer the application needs, and which can be measured on data we already have
wrong: Because the application is impossible to build
Because compressors cannot run on a GPU
Because the scenario is what HiSparse already does
why: The scenario can be run today on a dump of Qwen3.5-2B’s orchard, with no serving system. Its results then feed every application design.
title: One cherry at a time

q: Token position 13 in a sequence cut into stretches of stretch_len = 4 belongs to which stretch?
a: Stretch 3
why: stretch_id = token_pos_id // stretch_len = 13 // 4 = 3; stretch 3 holds positions 12 to 15.
title: The stretch: a knob, not a fact

q: Why does this site call the stretch “a knob, not a fact”?
a: Because we choose its length; nothing in the orchard marks where a stretch ends
wrong: Because stretches are fixed by the LLM’s architecture
Because the indexer decides the stretches
Because the GPU chooses the stretch length at run time
why: Defining a hypothesis as “cherries are alike within a stretch” would bake our design choice into the science. The orchard has distances and repeats, not stretches.
title: The stretch: a knob, not a fact

q: What does a stretch say about which layers, heads or elements are in play?
a: Nothing; a stretch is a range of token positions only
why: The stretch is one of three independent choices. Which coordinates are in play is the slice; how they are diced is the cherry shape.
title: The stretch: a knob, not a fact

q: What does a slice name?
a: Which coordinates of the orchard are in play for a scenario: K and/or V, which layers, which heads, which elements
wrong: How many token positions are in a stretch
How the data is cut into cherries
why: The slice is the “what is compressed” choice. The stretch is “which positions”; the cherry shape is “cut into what”.
title: The slice: what is in play

q: The campaigns of Part VIII compressed which slice of Qwen3.5-2B’s orchard?
a: The values only, v[:, :, :, :], at every KV layer and both heads (C1 only layer 0, head 0)
why: Values alone, so one token at one layer in play was 512 bytes, not the 1024 the old plan assumed for keys plus values.
title: The slice: what is in play

q: Why can keys and values be treated as separate scenarios?
a: Because a slice may name either; the receiver may ask for a key cherry without a value cherry
wrong: Because values are always compressed better
Because the LLM reads keys at a different step
why: Keys and values have different statistics (keys are rotated by RoPE, values are not). A slice of keys and a slice of values are two scenarios; a slice of both is a third.
title: The slice: what is in play

q: What is a cherry?
a: One unit of ask-and-answer: a fixed-shape sub-array of the slice that the receiver asks for and the sender answers with one delta
wrong: One token position of the sequence
