why: The receiver asks for cherries one at a time. Every cherry of a scenario has the same shape, known in advance to both sides.
title: The cherry and its shape

q: A slice puts the values of KV layers 1 and 3, head 0, in play. With the cherries v[t, 1, 0, :] and v[t, 3, 0, :] (256 elements each), how many cherries does one token position yield, and of how many bytes?
a: Two cherries of 256 bytes each (one per layer)
why: The slice gives 2 × 256 elements per position; each cherry takes one layer’s vector, so there are two per position. With v[t, [1, 3], 0, :] (512 elements) there would be one of 512 bytes.
title: The cherry and its shape

q: Why are “two cherries v[t, 1, 0, :], v[t, 3, 0, :] per token” and “one cherry v[t, [1, 3], 0, :] per token” different scenarios, though the same bytes are in play?
a: Because the receiver may ask for one layer’s vector without the other in the first, and never in the second; and a compressor can use what is inside one cherry for free
wrong: They are the same scenario written two ways
Because the first has a bigger dictionary
why: What one ask returns, and what a decode may use without paying, both change with the cherry shape. The campaigns measured the difference: joining the two heads into one cherry saved 0.032 of ratio.
title: The cherry and its shape

q: What is a punnet?
a: All the cherries of one stretch under one slice and one cherry shape; what one compress call sees and one dictionary serves
wrong: A range of consecutive token positions
The whole orchard of one sequence
why: A stretch is positions; a punnet is cherries. The punnet is the unit of compression; the cherry is the unit of delivery.
title: The punnet: what one dictionary serves

q: Slice v[:, [1, 3], 0, :], stretch_len = 4096, cherries v[t, 1, 0, :] and v[t, 3, 0, :] (256 elements each). How many cherries are in one punnet, and how many raw bytes?
a: 8192 cherries, 2 097 152 bytes
why: Two cherries of 256 bytes per token position × 4096 positions = 8192 cherries × 256 B = 2 MiB.
title: The punnet: what one dictionary serves

q: Which statement about a punnet is false?
a: A punnet contains every value of its stretch
wrong: A punnet is served by exactly one dictionary
Two scenarios can cut the same stretch into punnets of different sizes
A punnet is never a whole orchard
why: A punnet contains what the slice puts in play, which may be one head of one layer. The rest of the stretch’s values are not in the punnet.
title: The punnet: what one dictionary serves

q: What are the two functions of the contract?
a: deltas, dictionary = compress(punnet) once, and decompress(deltas[i], dictionary) for any cherry i
why: The sender compresses a whole punnet once; the receiver decompresses one cherry at a time. The harness supplies everything else.
title: The contract

q: What does “decoded cold” mean?
a: The receiver rebuilds a cherry from nothing but its own delta, the dictionary and the scenario’s constants, without having decoded any other cherry first
wrong: The decoder runs on the CPU instead of the GPU
The dictionary is reloaded before every cherry
The cherry is decoded twice and compared
why: One cherry at a time, at random, means no neighbour has been decoded before. A compressor that needs the previous cherry first breaks the contract.
title: The contract

q: Which of these may a dictionary contain?
a: Anything at all: statistics, a basis, a codebook, an entropy-coder table, reference cherries, the weights of a small network
wrong: Only bytes copied from the punnet
why: The dictionary is opaque to the scenario. The scenario counts its bytes and checks the leash; what a compressor does with it is the compressor’s business.
title: The contract

q: Which of these is charged by the scenario?
a: The bytes of the dictionary
wrong: How the sender stores and catalogues the deltas
The length field of each delta
why: How the sender stores and catalogues its deltas is not charged (host memory is not the bottleneck), delta lengths are not counted by ruling, and the scenario’s constants are known to both sides in advance.
title: The contract

q: A compressor’s dictionary is 0.52 of the punnet’s raw bytes and its deltas, summed, are 0.11 of them. Its MDL ratio and its bits per element?
a: 0.63, about 5.1 bits
why: MDL ratio = dictionary share + delta share = 0.52 + 0.11 = 0.63; bits per element = 8 × 0.63 ≈ 5.1.
title: The score: the MDL ratio

q: Which number does a miss on the link care about?
a: The delta share, every delta of the punnet summed over the punnet’s raw bytes
why: A δ-miss moves one delta. The dictionary was moved earlier and is on the shelf; its cost is paid differently (Part VI).
title: The score: the MDL ratio

q: Why does the dictionary share not measure how much the cherries of a punnet share?
a: Because a compressor may file reference cherries in the dictionary or in deltas and the ratio barely moves; the share is where bytes were filed, not what is shared
wrong: Because the dictionary is never charged
Because it does measure it, exactly
why: Moving every cherry into the dictionary changed one compressor’s ratio by 0.00004. What measures sharing is the gain over solo coding (Part VIII).
title: The score: the MDL ratio

q: Two compressors score 0.6449 and 0.6461 on two different screens. Which is better?
a: Unknown; scores from different samples of punnets cannot be subtracted
wrong: The second, because its screen was harder
Whichever has the smaller dictionary share
why: What makes a punnet hard is its text. Compare compressors only on the same punnets, as a paired difference.
title: The score: the MDL ratio

q: Without the leash, where does the best MDL ratio end up?
a: With every cherry stored in the dictionary and every delta empty, which is stream compression of the punnet
wrong: With a dictionary of exactly half the punnet
why: Campaign C1 watched the optimum slide to that corner within a day: 0.6705 at 4096 positions with empty deltas. To hand over one cherry the receiver had to decode the punnet.
title: The leash

q: What does the leash limit?
a: The distinct dictionary bytes one cold decode of one cherry may touch: at most the leash of the stretch length, 293 cherries’ worth at 4096 positions
wrong: The total size of the dictionary
The number of cherries per punnet
The GPU memory a shelf may use
why: It is a cap on reads per cherry, checked for every cherry. The dictionary itself may be large; a decode may not wander through it.
title: The leash

q: Why does each stretch length have its own leash?
a: Because how strict a leash is depends on how many cherries the punnet holds: 137 of 512 cherries is 26.8 % of the punnet, 293 of 4096 is 7.2 %
wrong: It does not; the leash is the same at every stretch length
Because the GPU has a fixed memory
Because the leash doubles with the stretch
why: The leash is counted in the scenario’s own cherry bytes and limits the share of the punnet one decode may read, so the pair (stretch length, leash) is one scenario axis: 512/137, 4096/293, 16 384/1103, whole sequence/14 503.
title: The leash

q: How is the leash checked?
a: For every single cherry, decoded cold in a fresh process, recording the distinct dictionary bytes it touched; a sample of cherries is not enough
wrong: On the mean over eight sampled cherries per punnet
By comparing the dictionary size with the leash
Only on the first cherry of each punnet
why: The rule was first stated on the mean; the human then set it on every cherry, and the old eight-cherry samples had run up to 26 % below the true worst cherry.
title: The leash

q: A dictionary weighs w = 256 cherries’ worth. How many bits per element does it add in a punnet of b = 512 cherries?
a: 4 bits, half of the raw 8
why: 8w/b=8⋅256/512=4. No residual saving is that large; a codebook that size needs punnets of 8K cherries or more.
title: Who pays for the dictionary: scope

q: Which scope’s dictionary adds nothing to the score?
a: Global scope, a shared table fitted on dev sequences or a separate training corpus and shared by every sequence
wrong: Stretch scope, because punnets are small
Sequence scope, because it is loaded once
None; every scope pays the same
why: A shared table is side information, held by both sides before any sequence is seen, so no byte of it enters the score. It must be fitted on dev sequences or a separate corpus, never on a holdout sequence.
title: Who pays for the dictionary: scope

q: How does sequence scope relate to stretch scope?
a: It is stretch scope with one stretch as long as the sequence
why: The same compress call on a punnet of the whole sequence’s slice. One control checks this to the bit.
title: Who pays for the dictionary: scope

q: What is a calibration corpus for?
a: Fitting shared tables and solo tables on the dev sequences or a separate training corpus, never on a holdout sequence
why: A shared table fitted on the holdout sequences would be a hidden dictionary; fitting it on dev sequences or a separate corpus rules that out.
title: Who pays for the dictionary: scope

q: What is the first reason to run many scenarios?
a: Each best compressor, and each difference between scenarios, is a measurement of the orchard’s information: which axes share bits, and how many
wrong: To find the one scenario with the lowest ratio
To make the harness run faster
Because the LLM changes between scenarios
why: The compressor is the instrument and its score is the reading. Comparing cherry shapes on the same elements measured how many bits the two heads share.
title: Why we vary the scenario

q: Why do DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.1 call for different scenarios?
a: V4’s indexer picks per layer, GLM-5.1’s picks once for a group of layers; one maps to one-layer cherries with a dictionary per layer, the other to multi-layer cherries or a shared dictionary
wrong: V4 does not use a hot cache
why: What a pick covers decides what one ask must return, hence the cherry shape and what a dictionary must serve.
title: Why we vary the scenario

q: How is a scenario written on this site?
a: As a line like V at one KV layer, v[t, l, :, :] · stretch 4096 · leash 293
wrong: By the name of the compressor
By the campaign’s track id alone
why: The line names the cherry as an index expression (which fixes the slice), the stretch length and the leash; format, LLM and corpus are stated once per page when they do not vary.
title: Why we vary the scenario

q: What is a compressor on this site?
a: One concrete compress/decompress pair, built as a dataflow graph of stages from raw cherries to dictionary bytes and delta bytes
wrong: Any program that reduces file size
why: The scenario is the problem; the compressor is one attempt. The campaigns wrote 126 of them, mostly by swapping or adding one stage to an earlier one.
title: Compressors: a graph of stages

q: Which stage does every lossless compressor on this site end with?
a: An entropy coder or a fixed-length code with escapes, on exact integer residuals
why: Predict, take the exact residual, code it. A quantiser may appear only on the dictionary side; deltas are never rounded.
title: Compressors: a graph of stages

q: What is the solo family?
a: Compressors with an empty dictionary: each cherry coded on its own with a fixed table
wrong: Compressors that use one reference cherry
The best compressors of the campaigns
why: Solo is the baseline every dictionary must beat: 0.778 on the Bench’s values, from per-furrow order-0 tables fit on a calibration corpus.
title: Compressors: a graph of stages

q: Two people report “1.4× on 8-bit orchards”. Which difference makes the claims impossible to compare?
a: One charged the dictionary’s bytes to the cherries that use it, the other did not
wrong: One used Python, the other Rust
One ran on keys first, the other on values first
One printed the ratio, the other the bits per element
why: A dictionary that is not paid for makes any compressor look good. The harness charges every byte by one rule, so the numbers mean the same thing.
title: The harness: the referee

q: What does the harness check about a compressor’s decompress?
a: That every cherry of every punnet comes back bit for bit from its own delta and the dictionary alone, in a separate decoder-only process, with its reads counted
wrong: That the mean error is below one FP8 step
That a sample of eight cherries per punnet decodes correctly
That the dictionary is smaller than the deltas
why: That is what “verified” means. A quick trial skips the separate process and can never hold a record.
title: The harness: the referee

q: What must happen to a gain under the shuffle control?
a: It must vanish, if it came from neighbours being neighbours
why: Shuffling tokens across sequences destroys every neighbourhood. A gain that survives the shuffle was never about neighbours; it is a bug or a global property.
title: The harness: the referee

q: Why is “compress the whole sequence’s orchard with zstd” not a scenario?
a: Because one ask must return one cherry decoded cold; a stream compressor must decode everything before it
wrong: Because the orchard is too large for zstd
why: The scenario’s access pattern is one cherry at a time, at random. Bulk compression answers a different question (bulk transfer between machines) and is read about in Part IX.
title: What the scenario is not

q: Does the scenario account for GPU memory?
a: No; it charges a dictionary’s bytes and measures reads, and leaves residency to the application
why: The leash keeps the search out of the trivial corner; it is not a memory budget. Whether a dictionary fits on a shelf is Part VI’s question.
title: What the scenario is not

q: How does a pick relate to cherries?
a: One pick asks for one or more cherries, depending on the scenario’s cherry shape
why: The indexer names picks; the scenario delivers cherries. The mapping between them is the first page of Part VI.
title: What the scenario is not

q: What are the three steps every lossless compressor on this site performs on a cherry?
a: Predict it from the dictionary, take the exact integer residual, code the residual so that the delta decodes alone
wrong: Quantise it, round it, store the rounded value
Rotate it, drop the small coordinates, store the rest
Sort the punnet, deduplicate it, compress it with zstd
why: Predict, subtract exactly, code. Exact integer residuals in index space make the round trip bit for bit; how good the prediction is decides how small the residual is.
title: The shape of every compressor, and its bill

q: What is the per-cherry tax?
a: Whatever a stage makes every delta carry besides its residual, such as which centroid, which reference cherry, or a flag
wrong: The dictionary’s bytes divided by the punnet size
A fee for loading the dictionary onto the GPU
why: The dictionary is paid once per punnet. The tax is paid again by every cherry and travels in every delta.
title: The shape of every compressor, and its bill

q: A stage saves 0.40 bit per element on residuals, charges a 12-bit tax per 512-element cherry, and weighs 64 cherries over a punnet of 4096. Net saving?
a: About 0.25 bit per element
wrong: It loses about 0.1 bit per element
title: The shape of every compressor, and its bill

q: How many bits of information does one 8-bit E4M3 value of the Bench’s values hold when coded alone?
a: About 6.2 bits, so a dictionary must earn its keep from the remaining structure, counted from 6.2 and never from 8
wrong: 8 bits; the codes are used evenly
4 bits; half the codes are never used
About 1 bit; the mantissa is all that matters
why: Solo coding reaches 0.778 of raw on the Bench, 6.22 bits per element. A dictionary that brings an element from 8 to 6.4 bits has won nothing.
title: The shape of every compressor, and its bill

q: What does a solo compressor use to code an element?
a: One fixed table per furrow, fit once on a calibration corpus and shared by every sequence
wrong: The punnet’s own furrow statistics, charged to the punnet
The previous cherry of the same furrow
A table fit to each sequence at prefill
why: The Hermit never looks at context. Its per-furrow tables are global, so they weigh nothing on the bill and nothing has to be loaded.
title: Solo: the Hermit

q: A punnet’s values sit around a typical value of their own, and the Hermit codes them with its global table. Averaged over punnets, how many extra bits per element does it pay?
a: ½ log₂ 1/(1 − R²), where R² is the share of variance the punnet locations explain
wrong: Nothing; a global table is always optimal
One bit per element, whatever the drift
log₂ of the number of punnets
why: The extra cost of a wrong table is a cross-entropy penalty. Averaged over punnets it is the exchange-rate formula, exactly what a furrow-statistics dictionary could win back.
title: Solo: the Hermit

q: What did the campaigns measure as the solo floor on the Bench’s values, and what did the best real solo compressor reach?
a: 0.778 ideal over the six KV layers (0.7999 at layer 3, head 0), tables uncharged; 0.8039 with a two-number table per furrow
why: 0.778 is the per-punnet, per-furrow order-0 entropy of the stored bytes over six layers. Compressor 09 stores a centre and a width per furrow and pays 0.004 of ratio for them. zlib on the punnet reached only 0.909.
title: Solo: the Hermit

q: What does the furrow-statistics stage write into the dictionary, and into each delta?
a: A location and a scale per furrow into the dictionary; nothing into the deltas beyond the residual
wrong: A rotation matrix into the dictionary; its coefficients into each delta
A codebook into the dictionary; an index into each delta
Nothing into the dictionary; a pointer into each delta
why: Two numbers per furrow, so about two cherries’ worth. Every cherry of the punnet is predicted by the same locations, so nothing needs to be said per cherry.
title: Furrow statistics: the Anchor

q: A furrow’s values have total variance 4 across punnets and variance 1 inside each punnet. What does the Anchor save on it, for an ideal entropy coder?
a: 1 bit per element
wrong: Nothing; subtracting a constant never helps
why: ½ log₂(4/1) = 1 bit. Punnet locations explain 75 % of the variance. A single global location would save nothing, because entropy depends on the shape of a histogram and not on where it sits.
title: Furrow statistics: the Anchor

q: What did the campaigns find when per-furrow statistics were fit per punnet and charged?
a: They are the solo baseline itself, 0.804 against the uncharged ideal 0.800; on their own they added nothing beyond solo
wrong: They could not be made to decode cold
why: Compressor 09 is a centre and a width per furrow per punnet. The gain the campaigns found came from reference cherries and linear prediction stacked on top of those statistics.
title: Furrow statistics: the Anchor

q: How much does a full KLT basis weigh for cherries of d elements, stored in BF16?
a: 2d cherries’ worth (d × d numbers at 2 bytes each)
why: A cherry is d bytes at 8 bits per element; a d×d matrix in BF16 is 2d2 bytes, 2d cherries. For the Bench’s 512-element cherry that is w=1024; a rank-16 partial basis is 32.
title: KLT: the Compass, at work

q: 64 standardised furrows: 8 directions with variance 10, the other 56 with variance 1. The KLT gain is about…
a: 0.34 bit per element
why: AM = (80 + 56)/64 = 2.125; GM = 10^(8/64) = 1.33; ½ log₂(2.125/1.33) = 0.34. “Low-rank-ish” is not enough; the weak directions must be nearly empty.
title: KLT: the Compass, at work

q: By how much did fixed rotations (DCT, Hadamard, random) lose on the Bench’s values, and why?
a: By 0.28 to 0.32 bit per element: rotating then rounding costs about a quarter of a bit, and element numbers carry no neighbourhood for a DCT to use
wrong: By 2.5 bits, the weight of a full basis
They won by 0.25 bit on the middle layers
By 0.004, the same as joining the layers
why: Rounding after a rotation costs the lattice constant, 0.2546 bit per coordinate (measured 0.29 to 0.32). Linear prediction subtracts a guess and never rounds the vector, so it never pays.
title: KLT: the Compass, at work

q: What per-cherry tax does a VQ stage with C centroids charge, and what does its dictionary weigh?
a: log₂ C bits per cherry for the index; C cherries’ worth for the codebook
wrong: log₂ C bits per element; nothing for the codebook
C bits per cherry; log₂ C cherries’ worth
why: The index tax of II.17, spread over the cherry’s d elements: 8/512 = 0.016 bit per element for 256 centroids. The codebook is 8C/b bits per element: 0.5 bit at b=4096.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: On bell-shaped (Gaussian) data, how does the best possible VQ compare with an untaxed rotation?
a: It cannot beat it; its index buys at most log₂ C / d bits per element beyond the rotation, exactly what the index costs
wrong: It always beats it, because centroids adapt to the data
They are equal only when C = 2
VQ wins once C is large enough
why: The rate–distortion bound of II.18. With its codebook charged as well, VQ nets at most the KLT gain minus 8C/b. Only clustered data escapes it.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: Stacked on a reference tree and linear prediction, how often did the encoder choose a codebook when free to pick one by exact bits?
a: On 0 of 72 punnets
why: A codeword is stored only to help others; a reference cherry is stored anyway, so it costs a pointer and nothing more. Offered codebooks of 4, 16 or 64 words or none, the encoder took none every time.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: What does the sibling stage write into the dictionary, and into each delta?
a: Nothing beyond real cherries of the punnet; a pointer to the reference, log₂ b bits, into each delta
wrong: C centroids; log₂ C bits per cherry
One location per furrow; no tax
why: The “codebook” is the punnet itself. The pointer is cheap per element on long cherries: 12 bits over 512 elements is 0.023.
title: Siblings and reference trees

q: Why does predicting a cherry from a random sibling cost about half a bit per element more than predicting it from its furrow locations?
a: The residual is the difference of two independent noises, so its variance doubles
wrong: Because the pointer costs half a bit
Because siblings are stored in E4M3
Because the sibling is from another punnet
why: Variances of independent parts add: 2σ² instead of σ², and ½ log₂ 2 = 0.5 bit per element. A true twin, whose own part is the same, is the only sibling that helps.
title: Siblings and reference trees

q: Why not predict every cherry from its nearest other cherry in the punnet?
a: 51 % of cherries are mutual nearest neighbours; two cherries that point at each other can never be decoded
wrong: Searching for the nearest cherry is too slow
The nearest cherry is usually in another punnet
The nearest cherry is a centroid, not a real cherry
why: The decodable optimum for one reference per cherry is the punnet’s minimum spanning tree, which connects everything without a cycle. That is the reference tree.
title: Siblings and reference trees

q: What does linear prediction, as the campaigns used it, guess a value from?
a: Elements of the same cherry that the decoder has already read, as a weighted sum added to the reference cherry’s value
wrong: The same element of the adjacent token
why: The rule is a table of which earlier elements and which weights, stored once per punnet; the delta codes the exact correction to the guess.
title: Linear prediction across elements

q: A rotation (the KLT) also mixes elements. Why did prediction win where fixed rotations lost?
a: A rotation transforms the whole vector and rounds it, about a quarter of a bit per element; prediction subtracts a guess from the original values and never rounds the vector
wrong: Rotations cannot be stored in a dictionary
Prediction uses more elements than a rotation
The KLT needs the adjacent token
why: The rounding tax is the cost the KLT page of the first plan missed; prediction pays no such tax because the stored values stay on their original grid.
title: Linear prediction across elements

q: At stretch 512, which linear-prediction rule scored best, and why?
a: A rule the decoder learns from cherries it has already decoded (0.6894), because a punnet of 512 cannot pay for a fully stored table (0.6960)
wrong: The fully stored rule, as at every stretch length
No rule at all; prediction loses below 4096
A rule fit on another sequence
why: The stored table costs 8w/b bits per element, and at b=512 that is too much; at 4096 the paid rule leads again.
title: Linear prediction across elements

q: Tokens were shuffled so that each punnet became a random sample of a layer’s tokens. What happened to the two gains?
a: The reference-tree compressor worsened from 0.6907 to 0.7520; the linear-prediction gain stayed within 0.002
wrong: The prediction gain vanished and the tree gain survived
why: Repeats live on nearby text and the shuffle destroys them. The rule lives on the LLM’s weights, which the shuffle cannot touch.
title: Linear prediction across elements

q: What does context modelling do with a prediction?
a: It uses the prediction to choose the probability table for the value, instead of subtracting it
wrong: It subtracts the prediction and codes the difference
It stores the prediction next to the value
It discards values that differ from the prediction
why: The cost of a value becomes −log₂ p(x | x̂), averaging H(X | X̂), which is never more than H(X).
title: Context modelling never loses

q: In the exact toy, below roughly which share of variance explained is subtraction in E4M3 index space worse than no prediction at all?
a: About 0.70
why: With one table for all residuals, the wide residuals of predictions near zero spoil the narrow ones. Context modelling stays below the no-prediction line at every R².
title: Context modelling never loses

q: Why can context modelling not replace a fixed-length miss path?
a: Its code lengths depend on the context’s table, so it needs an entropy coder; it serves the entropy-rate column
wrong: Because it needs a dictionary of hundreds of cherries
Because it cannot use the punnet’s prediction
why: On E4M3, contexts near zero genuinely need wide codes; the gain lives in variable-length coding.
title: Context modelling never loses

q: Why is “rotate in floating point, then round to integers” not lossless?
a: Rounding can send two different inputs to the same integer point, and then no decoder can tell which one it was
wrong: Because floating-point rotations are not exact
Because a rotation changes the variance of the data
Because integers cannot be rotated at all
why: In the figure, 12 of the 81 points vanish into collisions at 45°. A many-to-one step cannot be undone.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: Why can the shear x1​←x1​−round(ax2​), with a fixed slope a, be undone exactly?
a: It leaves x2​ unchanged, so the decoder recomputes the very same rounded shift and adds it back
wrong: Because rounding errors cancel on average
Because the slope is always an integer
Because the decoder stores the rounding error separately
why: The rounded amount depends only on the coordinate that did not move. The inverse is the same step with the opposite sign.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: Why did the campaigns never build a lifted KLT?
a: Code-length estimates showed every rotation losing 0.28 to 0.32 bit per element, about a quarter of it the price of rounding a rotated vector, which lifting makes reversible but not free
wrong: Because lifting cannot run on GPUs
Because a KLT is always lossy
Because the basis would not fit in the leash
why: Lifting answers “can it be undone?”, not “does it pay?”. Linear prediction took the same cross-element structure without rounding the vector.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: For a bell-shaped furrow stored in E4M3 with no predictor, what do sign, exponent and mantissa cost?
wrong: About 4 bits, mostly in the sign
why: The exponent is the only field with easy, context-free redundancy (4 bits stored, 2.5 of information). The mantissa is nearly uniform.
title: Splitting the bit fields

q: A value −3 is predicted as 6. How far apart are they on an INT8 grid with a step of 2, and on the E4M3 grid in index space?
a: 5 steps on INT8, 144 steps on E4M3
why: E4M3’s grid is dense near zero, so a residual that crosses zero walks past every tiny value in between. INT8’s grid is even.
title: Splitting the bit fields

q: Which single measurement showed that the linear structure of the values is hidden by the FP8 grid?
a: A shared-bits estimate on values matched real code lengths (0.278 against 0.263, r = 0.9993), while the same estimate on the FP8 code index read 0.104, three times too low
wrong: The mantissa kept 2.80 of its 3 bits
The skew of the error was −0.03
why: The structure is in the values. Counting in grid steps hides two thirds of it; the campaigns’ tables are built in value units and integrated over each code’s cell.
title: Splitting the bit fields

q: What does the entropy rate measure?
a: What an ideal entropy coder (arithmetic coding, rANS) would pay for the residuals, plus the tax and the amortised dictionary
wrong: The width of the fixed-length code
The raw size of the cherry
The size of the dictionary alone
why: It is the scientific number, the floor any compressor with the same table could reach.
title: Two rates: entropy and fixed-length

q: In the harness’s fixed-length format, how is an escaped element marked?
a: Its field holds the one value the width rule never uses, −2n−1, and its raw code follows the cherry’s fields
wrong: By a separate list of positions in the punnet
By setting the field to zero
It is not marked; escapes are dropped
why: The width rule allows residuals with magnitude below 2n−1, so the most negative field value is free to mean “escaped”. An escape then costs its 8 raw bits and no position, and every delta stays decodable alone.
title: Two rates: entropy and fixed-length

q: For Laplace-shaped residuals at 5 to 7 bits per element, how far apart are the two rates?
a: About one bit per element with the best width, about 1.5 with the harness’s 99.5 % coverage rule
why: A fixed width rounds up to whole bits and must cover the tail. SplitZip’s BF16 numbers show a gap of the same size in bits (0.9 to 1.5); it reads as 10 to 15 % only because a BF16 element has 16 bits to divide by.
title: Two rates: entropy and fixed-length

q: Which of the two rates did the campaigns measure on the Bench?
a: Only the entropy rate: every compressor is one rANS stream per cherry, and no fixed-length rate was measured
wrong: Only the fixed-length rate, for the GPU decoder
Neither; the campaigns measured reads only
why: The best numbers, 0.636 at 4096 and 0.618 at 16 384, are entropy rates; a one-bit gap would put the engineering number near 0.76.
title: Two rates: entropy and fixed-length

q: A predictor explains R² = 75 % of an element’s variance. For bell-shaped data, how many bits per element does it save?
a: 1 bit
why: ½ log₂ 1/(1 − 0.75) = ½ log₂ 4 = 1. Two bits need 94 %, three bits need 98.4 %.
title: The exchange rate, applied

q: Ten furrows of a 512-element cherry are predicted almost perfectly (R² = 0.99, 3.3 bits each); the rest not at all. What is saved per element of the cherry?
a: About 0.06 bit
why: Bits add up per element: 10 × 3.3 = 33 bits spread over 512 elements is 0.06 bit each. Owning most of the variance is not owning most of the bytes.
title: The exchange rate, applied

q: The two KV heads of a layer have cosine about 0.05 at the same element, yet share about 0.85 bit per element. How?
a: Their distances between tokens correlate up to 0.92; they are two views of one vector, and bits count what one view says about the other, not the angle between same-index elements
wrong: They share no bits; 0.85 is the index tax
Because head 1 is a copy of head 0
why: A cosine is one number about one pair of elements; mutual information counts everything. Joining the two heads into one cherry saved 0.0322 of ratio on 20 of 20 sequences.
title: The exchange rate, applied

q: What is a code-length estimate?
a: The code length a probability table would reach, computed exactly on the data without building the compressor; a lead, not a result
wrong: A verified score from a separate decoder process
The mean of a screen’s punnets
A compressor whose encoder rounds its weights exactly
why: The campaigns’ grades run from bound and code-length estimate, through quick, to verified. Only the last rebuilds every cherry in a separate process with its reads counted.
title: Bounds before building

q: In the memory table, what did the intact LLM pay per value, and what did it pay with far attention cut and the linear-attention state reset?
a: 1.35 bits intact; 5.16 bits with both removed, about what a real compressor with no LLM pays (5.13)
why: What a punnet’s dictionary can hold is roughly what the LLM knows from the last few thousand tokens; the rest of the value’s bits are decided by memory the punnet does not contain.
title: Bounds before building

q: When can vector quantization beat the rate–distortion bound computed for Gaussian data?
a: When the data is genuinely clustered, which a Gaussian table cannot describe
wrong: When the codebook is large enough
why: The bound is a statement about Gaussian data. With 32 real clusters, VQ netted +1.45 bits where a rotation got +0.68; on the Bench, clusters existed only in a minority of cherries.
title: Bounds before building

q: Why rehearse the measurement on synthetic punnets before touching a real orchard?
a: Their structure is known, so the method must recover what was planted and find nothing where nothing was planted
wrong: Synthetic data compresses better, so the results look good
Real orchards cannot be read from a GPU
why: A known answer turns the data itself into a test of the code. It says nothing about orchards.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: In the rehearsal, at which stretch length is the furrow-statistics rate lowest, and why?
a: At 2048 tokens, the true length of the planted stretches
wrong: At 256 tokens; smaller punnets always fit better
At 4096 tokens; the dictionary is cheapest there
It does not depend on the stretch length
why: Shorter stretches pay more for their dictionaries and fit noisier statistics; longer ones straddle two planted stretches and fit neither.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: After shuffling tokens across sequences, the sequence-scope gain fell to 0.13 bit instead of zero. What is that?
a: The calibration gap, the global table fit on 8 other sequences being slightly off for these; it shrinks with more calibration sequences
why: With 2, 8 and 32 calibration sequences the shuffled sequence gain is 0.22, 0.12 and 0.07 bit. Gains are read against the shuffled curve, never against zero.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: How does a pick relate to the cherries of a scenario?
a: The indexer names a pick; the scenario’s cherry shape says how many cherries rebuild it, one on the Pin, one or two on the Bench
wrong: A pick is always exactly one cherry
Picks and cherries are the same word for the same thing
why: A pick is (layer_id, token_pos_id). Under cherry v[t, l, :, :] that is one cherry; under v[t, l, h, :] it is two; a design that moves keys and values together needs the cherries of two slices.
title: From the scenario to the serving system

q: In the mapping between the tiny files of Part I and kvblockdiff, what plays the role of one tiny file?
a: One cherry, the unit a miss fetches alone
wrong: The whole orchard of a sequence
why: A tiny file is compressed alone against a shared dictionary; a cherry is delivered alone as a delta against its punnet’s dictionary. Same shape of problem.
title: From the scenario to the serving system

q: What does kvblockdiff change about a hot-cache miss?
a: A miss whose punnet dictionary is on the GPU moves a delta instead of the raw pick, and the GPU rebuilds the pick bit for bit
wrong: It makes misses rarer with a better eviction policy
It moves a lower-precision copy of the pick
It skips the missed pick and attends to the rest
why: The indexer, the hot cache, every hit and every eviction stay as in HiSparse. Only the bytes per miss change, and the LLM’s outputs do not change at all.
title: From the scenario to the serving system

q: Which number of Part IV does a miss on the link care about?
a: The delta share ρ: a δ-miss moves ρe bytes
why: The dictionary was moved earlier and sits on the GPU; what crosses the link at miss time is one delta per cherry of the pick.
title: From the scenario to the serving system

q: How many bytes does one punnet of kvblockdiff occupy in host memory?
a: we+bρe: one dictionary plus b deltas
wrong: be, the same as raw
wbe, a dictionary per cherry
ρwe, the dictionary only
why: The dictionary is stored once per punnet; each of the b cherries adds its delta of ρe bytes on average.
title: How big is each piece?

q: With b=4096 and the light compressor of Part VIII (w≈86, ρ=0.665), what share of the stored punnet is dictionary?
a: About 3 %
why: w/(w+bρ)=86/(86+2724)≈3 %. At the reference-tree point (w≈2150, ρ=0.112) it is about 82 %.
title: How big is each piece?

q: All costs included, what is a cherry of kvblockdiff worth, as a fraction of a raw cherry?
a: ρ+w/b
wrong: ρ exactly
ρ×w
1−ρ
why: Divide the punnet’s bytes we+bρe by its b cherries and by e. The dictionary adds w/b, the dictionary share of Part IV.
title: How big is each piece?

q: Why does the dictionary’s share of a cherry shrink as the stretch grows?
a: The dictionary is paid once per punnet, so it is shared by more cherries
wrong: Deltas get larger and hide it
The GPU caches long stretches for free
why: That is amortization, a fixed cost divided by the number of items sharing it. The data, not the formula, limits how long a useful stretch can be.
title: How big is each piece?

q: What is the dictionary shelf?
a: A per-sequence, per-layer set of nD​ punnet dictionaries kept in GPU memory next to the hot cache
wrong: A second hot cache of raw picks
The host-memory copy of every dictionary
A cache of the indexer’s picks
why: The hot cache of raw picks stays exactly as in HiSparse; the shelf is the one structure kvblockdiff adds.
title: The shelf, and two kinds of miss

q: A pick is not in the hot cache, and its stretch’s dictionary is on the shelf. What crosses the link?
a: Only its delta, ρe bytes on average: a δ-miss
wrong: Nothing; it counts as a hit
why: The GPU rebuilds the pick from the delta and the resident dictionary, then places it in the hot cache as usual.
title: The shelf, and two kinds of miss

title: Stereo similarity (head axis)

q: Why does the shared information fall from 0.85 to 0.21 bit when each head gets its own reference cherry?
a: Two different earlier tokens no longer line up, so the heads’ residuals stop sharing what the references already explained
wrong: Because the second reference costs 0.64 bit
Because head 1 is noise after a reference
Because the bound only holds for one head
why: One reference serving both heads keeps 0.54 bit in common; separate references keep 0.21. One reference per token per layer is the natural unit.
title: Stereo similarity (head axis)

q: A serving design fetches each KV head of a layer as its own pick. What does stereo similarity say about it?
a: It pays for the 0.85 bit the heads share unless its dictionary carries the other head; a design whose picks cover both heads gets the saving for free
wrong: Nothing, picks are about the indexer
It saves more, because cherries are smaller
It must use a cosine threshold
why: The saving exists only inside a cherry or a dictionary that holds both views. The cherry shape decides who gets it.
title: Stereo similarity (head axis)

q: Which stereo questions are still unmeasured?
a: Stereo on keys, their two heads joined under the frontier compressor, and stereo across layers, a map from one layer’s cherry into another’s
wrong: Whether the two heads share anything at all
Whether the join holds on more than one sequence
Whether the cosine between the heads is really near zero
why: The join is 20 of 20 sequences and the cosine rests on 36 punnets; what is open is keys, whose heads were coded jointly for one night only, and the cross-layer map.
title: Stereo similarity (head axis)

q: In a punnet of KV layer 0 values, what is a cherry’s nearest other cherry, most of the time?
a: The same token again, 55 % of the time in 512-token punnets and 78 % in 4096-token punnets
wrong: A random cherry: in 256 dimensions all cherries are equally far
why: The text repeats, and a repeated token in a similar context gives nearly the same cherry. The adjacent token shares only 0.058 bit per element there.
title: Echo similarity (repeats)

q: Where do the reference tree’s links point at KV layers 0, 4 and 5?
a: Mostly far away: only 9, 7 and 12 % of links stay within 8 tokens, against 37 to 47 % in the middle layers
wrong: Within 8 tokens about half the time
why: The first and last KV layers build hubs where many far-apart repeats of one token hang off one copy (largest degree 12 to 22); the middle layers build chains (6 to 10).
title: Echo similarity (repeats)

q: Tokens were shuffled so each punnet became a random sample of a layer’s tokens. What happened to the reference-tree compressor?
a: Its ratio went from 0.6907 to 0.7520, about 70 % of its gain over solo gone
wrong: It improved, because the shuffle spread the repeats
why: The shuffle keeps every cherry and destroys its neighbourhood. A gain that lives on nearby repeats must vanish, and did.
title: Echo similarity (repeats)

q: Why is the echo verdict stated with a caveat about the text?
a: It was measured on coding-agent transcripts, which repeat unusually often; tool calls repeat about 1.4 times more than prose
wrong: Because only one sequence was used
Because echoes cannot exist in prose
why: In-stretch repeat rates were 56 to 59 % for tool calls and outputs against 38 to 42 % for prose. Prose and a second LLM are unrun scenarios.
title: Echo similarity (repeats)

q: HiSparse’s LRU hot cache hits about 87 % of picks at B = 2k. What is that number evidence about?
a: Which positions the indexer keeps picking from step to step
wrong: How alike neighbouring cherries’ bytes are
How many bits a stretch dictionary would save
why: A hit means “picked again soon”. It compares one step’s query with the next step’s query; it never compares one stored cherry with another.
title: Two localities, kept apart

q: In the toy, the stored bytes are shuffled across positions while the picks stay the same. What happens?
a: The hit rate stays at 89 %; the bits saved by a neighbour fall from 1.61 to about 0
wrong: The hit rate falls; the bits stay at 1.61
why: Picks depend on the indexer’s query, not on the bytes. Shuffling destroys neighbour similarity and leaves every pick where it was.
title: Two localities, kept apart

q: Which which-question does the shelf design genuinely need answered?
a: Whether misses pile into a few heavy stretches that stay in use for many steps
wrong: Whether the LRU hit rate is above 80 %
Whether neighbouring cherries have similar bytes
Whether the indexer is DSA or NSA
why: Stretch dictionaries are cheap to keep on the GPU only if misses concentrate in a few long-lived stretches. That is a question about picks, answered from a pick trace.
title: Two localities, kept apart

q: Which side of the which/what split did the campaigns measure?
a: The what side only: the bytes, in bits, with a shuffle control; no indexer ran on the Bench
why: The Bench’s dump has values and pre-RoPE keys but no queries and no picks. The which side on the Bench waits for a stand-in indexer.
title: Two localities, kept apart

q: Misses spread evenly over 25 stretches, and the shelf holds 4 dictionaries. Roughly what is the δ-miss fraction?
a: About 16 %
wrong: 100 %, every miss has a dictionary somewhere
why: Only misses that land in one of the 4 on-fire stretches are δ-misses: 4 / 25 = 0.16.
title: Lucky Louis, stretch by stretch

q: How does the stretch form of the Lucky Louis property differ from the ordinary one?
a: The ordinary one says the same positions are re-picked; the stretch form says the misses also crowd into a few stretches that stay busy for many steps
wrong: The stretch form is about the bytes inside cherries
The stretch form is about the layer axis
why: Picks can repeat while being scattered over the whole sequence. Then each miss lands in a different stretch, and a few shelved dictionaries help little.
title: Lucky Louis, stretch by stretch

q: One dictionary load costs about as much link traffic as how many raw misses?
a: w, its weight in cherries’ worth
why: A load moves we bytes, a raw miss e. Against about 274 misses per layer per step on the Pin, loads × w must stay well below 274.
title: Lucky Louis, stretch by stretch

q: Why is the heavy-stretch question unmeasured on the Bench?
a: No indexer ran; the dump has values and keys but no queries and no picks
wrong: Because the stretch length was never fixed
Because the campaigns ran out of time
why: The question is a statistic of a pick trace. A stand-in indexer built from recomputed queries would produce one.
title: Lucky Louis, stretch by stretch

q: What are the three rungs of the ladder, from top to bottom?
a: A cherry against everything, against its sequence, against its surrounding stretch
wrong: Against its layer, its head, its element
Against the hot cache, host memory, the link
why: Each rung narrows what the cherry is compared with, and so, intuitively, makes it less surprising. The rungs are the three dictionary scopes.
title: The cat-sequence ladder

q: Why is H(E)≥H(E∣sequence)≥H(E∣stretch) guaranteed?
a: Conditioning never increases entropy on average, and knowing the stretch also tells you the sequence
wrong: Because stretches are shorter than sequences
It is not guaranteed; it is a hypothesis
why: Side information can only help on average. The stretch rung refines the sequence rung, so it can only help further. What is not guaranteed is the size of each step.
title: The cat-sequence ladder

q: What is “the jump” at the end of the argument?
a: Concluding from HiSparse’s high hit rate that the bottom rung is steep, so stretch dictionaries will work
wrong: Concluding that cats and dogs need different LLMs
Concluding that the sequence rung is useless
Concluding that the hot cache should be larger
why: The jump uses evidence about which picks are wanted as if it were evidence about how alike their bytes are. The leak page takes it apart.
title: The cat-sequence ladder

q: How much had the stretch rung bought, measured, by the end of the campaigns?
a: 1.14 bits per element over solo at stretch 4096, from 0.778 to 0.636
wrong: 0.37 bit, as the variance budget predicted
why: 8 × (0.778 − 0.636) = 1.14. The sequence rung above it is a bound so far (about 0.60 at 16K positions and 0.57 for a whole sequence), and the global rung is unmeasured.
title: The cat-sequence ladder

q: What does a high hot-cache hit rate tell you?
a: That the query ranks the orchard at step t+1 much as it did at step t
wrong: That neighbouring cherries hold similar numbers
That the LLM’s keys are low-rank
why: Hits need stable rankings, and stable rankings need a slowly moving query. Nothing about the keys resembling each other is required.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: In the live Monte Carlo the keys are drawn independently at random. How well does a key predict the next one?
a: Not at all; R² ≈ 0.000, so a neighbour saves no bits
wrong: It depends on the query drift
why: Independent keys share nothing. Yet with a slowly drifting query, overlap and hit rate look like HiSparse’s.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: What controls the hit rate in the toy: the query drift η or the similarity of neighbouring keys?
a: The query drift η
wrong: Neither; it is fixed by k
why: Switching to keys that are close copies of their neighbours (R² ≈ 0.9) leaves the hit-rate curve almost unchanged; moving η changes it completely.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: Can the leak be closed by a measurement?
a: No; it is a demonstration that the inference is invalid, and the bytes must be measured on their own
wrong: Yes, by measuring HiSparse’s hit rate more precisely
Yes, by a larger hot cache
Yes, by a shuffle control on the hit rate
why: The toy proves that hits do not imply alike bytes. The campaigns then measured the bytes directly, and found structure that came from echoes, not from the query.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: A predictor explains 75 % of an element’s variance. How many bits per element does it save, at the Gaussian exchange rate?
a: 1 bit
why: 21​log2​1−R21​=21​log2​4=1. Two bits need 94 %.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: With the budget 30 % global, 20 % sequence, 20 % stretch, 30 % noise, what is the stretch rung alone worth?
a: About 0.37 bit per element
why: 21​log2​0.31​−21​log2​0.51​≈0.87−0.50=0.37. The whole ladder is worth about 0.87 bit.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: Why can a few near-deterministic furrows save more than their share suggests?
a: The exchange rate rises steeply as R² approaches 1, so a furrow with 2 % noise saves about 2.8 bits
wrong: Because large furrows are stored with more bits
Because the noise floor does not apply to them
why: Bits per element are an average over furrows. ½ log₂(1/0.02) ≈ 2.8 bits on a tenth of the furrows adds about 0.28 bit to the average on its own.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: The best compressor won 1.14 bits per element over solo at stretch scope, more than the toy budget’s 0.37. Why?
a: The structure was concentrated, not spread: whole-cherry repeats and a linear map between the heads, which explain most of some cherries rather than a little of all of them
wrong: The exchange rate does not apply to FP8
The budget forgot the global rung
why: An echo explains almost all of a repeated cherry; head 0 explains 73 % of head 1’s residual at KV layer 4. The escape hatch, not the even spread, is what the data used.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: A pair of key furrows sits near the same point token after token. What does RoPE do to it?
a: It rotates the pair by an angle that grows with position, smearing the tight cluster into an arc or a whole ring
wrong: It adds random noise to every element
It shrinks the pair toward zero
why: RoPE rotates each pair of key elements by position × that pair’s speed. A location per furrow can no longer predict a value that keeps turning.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values apart

q: Why store keys before RoPE?
a: Before the spin the structured furrows are nearly constant and cheap to predict; the receiver rebuilds the pre-RoPE key exactly and applies the rotation for the known position
wrong: Because attention never uses rotated keys
Because pre-RoPE keys are smaller in bytes
why: The rotation after decoding is a cheap element-wise step. The Bench’s dump already holds keys with the rotation inverted.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values apart

q: How did pre-RoPE keys compress, compared with values at the same layer, in the first campaign?
a: About the same, with the same compressor family and the same stages in the same order; slightly lower ratios at every KV layer but the last
wrong: Keys did not compress at all
Keys compressed twice as well as values
Keys needed a completely different compressor
why: Keys against values at stretch 4096, head 0: 0.660 against 0.673 at KV layer 0, 0.701 against 0.740 at KV layer 2. Only KV layer 5 flips, because its values are unusually easy.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values apart

q: Why are keys a separate scenario rather than half of a K+V cherry?
a: Keys want their own reference tree (coding them on the values’ tree costs +0.0024), their shared structure with values needs a global-scope table, and a K+V cherry is a third scenario with its own numbers
wrong: Because keys are stored on a different GPU
Because keys cannot be compressed under a leash
why: The slice is the first axis of a scenario: k[...] and v[...] are different problems, and what they share (0.19 to 0.40 bit of the key) is not learnable per punnet.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values apart

q: Why does one pass over a trace give LRU’s misses at every cache size?
a: An LRU cache of B slots always holds exactly the top B items of the recency stack, so each ask’s depth in that stack says at once for which sizes it hits
wrong: Because the miss rate is the same at every size
Because the trace is replayed once per size in parallel
why: A smaller cache’s contents sit inside a larger one’s, Mattson’s inclusion property. Misses at size B are the asks with stack distance at least B.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: On the asks 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO misses 9 times with 3 slots. With 4 slots it misses…
a: 10 times, more with a bigger cache (Bélády’s anomaly)
why: FIFO’s contents at 3 slots are not a subset of its contents at 4, so it has no single stack curve. LRU and Bélády’s policy do.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: If the miss rate follows m(B)∝B−1.08, doubling the hot cache multiplies the misses by about…
why: 2−1.08≈0.47. HiSparse’s points: 30 % at 2048, 13.4 % at 4096, 6.7 % at 8192.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: What does a replay of a pick trace give that HiSparse’s three points do not?
a: The whole stack-distance histogram in one pass, so every cache size, the victim tier and the dictionary shelf are read off directly
wrong: Only the miss rate at B = 4096
The Bélády miss rate at every size
The hit rate of the indexer
why: One pass gives the full curve; the same pass over stretch ids gives the shelf’s curve.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: What is a campaign, in this Part’s sense?
a: One run of the autonomous research loop, with several AI researcher agents writing and testing compressors against one harness under one set of rules, every trial recorded
wrong: One compressor run over every punnet of the data
The GPU job that captured the orchard
A round of questions put to the human
why: Two campaigns ran: C1 with four researcher agents, C2 with about twenty-one. The harness, not an agent, kept the score.
title: A dispatch from the harness

q: How many compressors and trials did the two campaigns leave behind?
a: 126 compressors and about 390 recorded trials, in one night and one day
wrong: Four compressors and a dozen trials
why: C1 recorded 218 trials and left 62 compressors; C2 recorded 169 trials; 126 compressors exist in all, with 36 Rust components.
title: A dispatch from the harness

q: The best verified result at a stretch of 4096 tokens was a ratio of about 0.636. In bits per element of a value, that is…
a: About 5.1 bits of 8
why: Bits per element are 8 times the ratio: 8 × 0.636 ≈ 5.1. Solo coding sits at 6.22 (0.778), raw at 8.
title: A dispatch from the harness

q: By how much did the best compressors beat solo coding (0.778)?
a: By 1.1 to 1.3 bits per element: 0.636 at a stretch of 4096 tokens, 0.618 at 16 384
wrong: By nothing; solo coding was already the floor
title: A dispatch from the harness

q: Which statement about the data behind this Part is true?
a: Values only, one LLM, one kind of text, FP8 E4M3, six KV layers, most results on two sequences
wrong: Keys and values of several LLMs on books, code and chat
Values in BF16 on all 24 layers
A random sample of 1000 sequences from the web
why: The campaigns measured the value half of Qwen3.5-2B’s orchard on the author’s own coding-agent transcripts. Every finding carries that qualification.
title: A dispatch from the harness

q: A number in this Part is labelled “code-length estimate”. What does that mean?
a: A code length computed from a probability table on the data, without building the compressor; a lead, not a verified result
wrong: Every cherry was rebuilt bit for bit in a separate process
The number was confirmed on all 30 sequences
The compressor ran in exact integer arithmetic
why: Three grades appear here. Verified means every cherry came back bit-exactly from a separate decoder; a code-length estimate and a bound are what a compressor could reach.
title: A dispatch from the harness

q: How many of Qwen3.5-2B’s 24 layers are KV layers?
a: Six: every fourth layer (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23), which the orchard indexes as KV layers 0 to 5. The other eighteen are linear-attention layers with a fixed-size state
why: The LLM is a hybrid. A linear-attention layer carries one fixed-size summary forward instead of a memory of every token, so it has nothing per token to store or compress.
title: The data on the table

q: How big is one token’s values at one KV layer, at 8 bits?
a: 512 bytes: 2 KV heads × 256 elements, the cherry v[t, l, :, :]
why: One head is 256 elements; a layer has two KV heads. Across the six KV layers a token’s values are 3072 bytes.
title: The data on the table

q: What text produced the orchards?
a: Thirty of the author’s own coding-agent transcripts, about 225K tokens each, read by the LLM (prefill) but not continued
wrong: Two books, two code repositories, two transcripts and two LongBench prompts
why: The plan had asked for genre diversity. What was captured is one genre: 30 sequences of 219 678–229 360 tokens, prefill positions only, tool output 26–89 % of each.
title: The data on the table

q: Why does “one kind of text” matter for reading this Part?
a: Coding-agent transcripts are full of repeated tool output and tool calls; any gain that comes from repeats may be smaller on prose
wrong: Because the LLM cannot read other text
Because tool output is stored in a different number format
It does not matter; orchards are the same for any text
why: A later page finds that a punnet’s difficulty follows its share of repeated tokens. A novel repeats itself less than a transcript of file reads.
title: The data on the table

q: How was the FP8 copy of the values derived?
a: From the BF16 capture, with one power-of-two scale per layer and tensor, rounded to the nearest E4M3 value
wrong: Captured directly in FP8 by the LLM
why: The INT8 variant uses one scale per furrow instead; C2 coded the FP8 copy only.
title: The data on the table

q: Why do the stored keys differ from the LLM’s own keys by about one BF16 ulp in 64 of 256 elements?
a: The orchard held keys after RoPE; the rotation of the 64 rotary elements was inverted to recover the pre-RoPE keys, and BF16 rounding cannot be fully undone
wrong: The keys were quantized to FP8 first
The LLM uses a different RoPE for keys and queries
The exporter dropped the sign bit
why: Only 64 of the 256 elements are rotated (partial RoPE). The other 192 are bit-identical to the orchard; for lossless coding the recovered keys are simply the data.
title: The data on the table

q: The campaigns’ track s-layer-b4k-r293, in the site’s words, is which scenario?
a: V · all · cherry v[t, l, :, :] · stretch 4096 · leash 293, on a screen
wrong: K · KV layer 0 · cherry v[t, l, h, :] · stretch 293
V · all · cherry v[t, :, :, :] · stretch 4096 · no leash
V · head 0 · cherry v[t, l, :, :] · stretch 16 384 · leash 293
why: “layer” names the cherry shape (both heads of one KV layer), “b4k” the stretch length, “r293” the leash; the slice is always the values.
title: The rules of the game, as scenarios

q: What is a screen?
a: A fixed, cheap test: an evenly spaced tenth of the stretches of two (or five) sequences at one scenario
wrong: A full run over every stretch of every sequence
A trial whose reads were sampled
why: A screen is cheap enough to run hundreds of times. Nearly every number in this Part is a screen, and two screens read different punnets.
title: The rules of the game, as scenarios

q: Why can the scores of two screens not be subtracted?
a: They read different punnets; the token screen happened to sample punnets about 0.005 harder for every compressor than the layer screen did
wrong: Because one is in bits and the other in bytes
Because screens use different number formats
They can, as long as both are verified
why: The layer screen read 0.6449 and the token screen 0.6461, yet on the same elements v[t, :, :, :] cherries beat v[t, l, :, :] cherries by 0.0043 on 20 of 20 sequences. Only a same-window comparison ranks cherry shapes.
title: The rules of the game, as scenarios

q: A ledger row says verification: {isolated: true} and reads: {every_cherry: true}. What has been proved?
a: Every cherry of every punnet came back bit for bit from a separate decoder-only process, and the leash was checked on every cherry, not a sample
wrong: The dictionary is smaller than the deltas
The compressor is faster than the link
The score is better than solo
why: That is a verified result with the leash proved. A row without the second flag may hide a worst cherry up to 26 % hungrier than its sample showed.
title: The rules of the game, as scenarios

q: Why did the leash not exist when the first night began?
a: Nobody had written the one-cherry-at-a-time access pattern down as a rule; within the hour the search slid to “every cherry in the dictionary”, 0.6705, which is stream compression of the punnet
wrong: The harness could not count reads yet
The human forgot to copy it from Part IV
It existed but was set to 1 103
why: At 10:15 UTC the goal was clarified, at 11:00 the corner was called what it was, and by 11:20 the leash existed. Since 31 October it is counted for every single cherry.
title: The rules of the game, as scenarios

q: At KV layer 0 (the LLM’s layer 3), head 0, what did the campaign measure as the solo floor, and what did the best real solo compressor reach?
a: 0.7999 ideal (per-furrow statistics, tables uncharged); 0.8039 with a two-number curve per furrow
why: 0.7999 is the per-punnet, per-furrow order-0 entropy of that one head; 0.8039 is compressor 09, which stores a centre and a width per furrow. The six-layer ideal is the lower 0.778.
title: Night one: the twin ladder

q: In a punnet of KV layer 0 values, what is a cherry’s nearest other cherry, most of the time?
a: The same token again, 55 % of the time at a stretch of 512 tokens and 78 % at 4096
wrong: A random cherry: in 256 dimensions all cherries are equally far
why: Coding-agent transcripts repeat tokens, and the same token in the same kind of context gives nearly the same value cherry. The adjacent token shares only I = 0.058 bit per element at KV layer 0.
title: Night one: the twin ladder

q: Why not predict every cherry from its nearest other cherry in the punnet?
a: 51 % of cherries are mutual nearest neighbours; two cherries that point at each other can never be decoded
wrong: Searching for the nearest cherry is too slow
The nearest cherry is usually in another punnet
The nearest cherry is a centroid, not a real cherry
why: The decodable optimum for one reference per cherry is the punnet’s minimum spanning tree, which connects everything without a cycle. That is the reference tree.
title: Night one: the twin ladder

q: How did pre-RoPE keys compress, compared with values at the same KV layer?
a: About the same, with the same compressor family and the same mechanisms in the same order; slightly lower ratios at every KV layer but the last
wrong: Keys did not compress at all
Keys compressed twice as well as values
Keys needed a completely different compressor
why: Keys against values at a stretch of 4096: 0.660 against 0.673 at KV layer 0, 0.701 against 0.740 at KV layer 2. Only KV layer 5 flips, because its values are unusually easy.
title: Night one: the twin ladder

q: The lowest ratio of the night, 0.6705, was set aside. Why?
a: Every cherry sat in the dictionary, so rebuilding one cherry meant decoding about 1 490 cherries’ worth of it, which is stream compression of the punnet
wrong: It failed the exact round trip
It was measured on the wrong layer
It used a centroid codebook, which the rules forbade
why: The human called it serialized compression of the punnet: technically valid, useless when one cherry at a time is wanted. The leash was written the same morning.
title: Night one: the twin ladder

q: What does linear prediction, as the campaign used it, guess a value from?
a: Elements of the same cherry that the decoder has already read, as a weighted sum added to the reference cherry’s value
wrong: The same element of the adjacent token
why: The rule is a table of which earlier elements and which weights, stored once per punnet; the delta codes the exact correction to the guess.
title: Two kinds of structure

q: A rotation (the KLT) also mixes elements. Why did prediction win where fixed rotations lost?
a: A rotation transforms the whole vector and then rounds it, costing about a quarter of a bit per element; prediction subtracts a guess from the original values and never rounds the vector
wrong: Rotations cannot be stored in a dictionary
Prediction uses more elements than a rotation
The KLT needs the adjacent token
why: The rounding tax is the cost the toolbox’s KLT page warns about; prediction pays no such tax because the stored values stay on their original grid.
title: Two kinds of structure

q: On five sequences, compressor 121 against compressor 102 came out as…
a: −0.0088 on every sequence, with a spread of about 0.0001
wrong: −0.0088 on average, but better on only three of five
The same score; 121 only reads less
why: 0.62970 against 0.63848; per sequence −0.00883, −0.00887, −0.00861, −0.00874, −0.00886. The sequences themselves differ by ten times that.
title: Two kinds of structure

q: Tokens were shuffled so that each punnet became a random sample of a KV layer’s tokens. What happened to the two gains?
a: The reference-tree compressor’s score worsened from 0.6907 to 0.7520; the linear-prediction gain stayed within 0.002
wrong: The prediction gain vanished and the tree gain survived
why: Repeats live on the text and the shuffle destroys them. The rule lives on the LLM’s weights, which the shuffle cannot touch.
title: Two kinds of structure

q: A prediction rule fit on another sequence recovers how much of the gain?
wrong: Nothing: the rule is specific to each punnet
More than 100 %, because the other sequence is cleaner
why: The weights carry over almost whole. What does not carry over is the choice of which terms to keep; refitting another sequence’s pattern costs about 0.01 at KV layer 2.
title: Two kinds of structure

q: Why might the rule one day cost nothing to store?
a: It belongs to the LLM’s weights, so a table prepared in advance and held by both sides could carry it for every punnet
wrong: Because the rule has only a few terms
Because the decoder can always guess it from the first cherry
why: Storing the rule costs 0.013 to 0.021 at a stretch of 4096. A shared table was not allowed in the campaign; an estimate says it would take compressor 102 from 0.6407 to 0.6326.
title: Two kinds of structure

q: The layer screen scored 0.6449 and the token screen 0.6461. Why does that not rank the two cherry shapes?
a: Each screen samples its own punnets, and what makes a punnet hard is its text; on the same window the v[t, :, :, :] cherry is better by 0.0043
wrong: It does: v[t, l, :, :] cherries are better by 0.0012
Because the token screen used a different leash
why: The token screen happened to contain slightly harder text. Only a same-window comparison, the same values cut two ways, ranks cherry shapes.
title: Cutting the orchard: cherry shapes compared

q: The same element position in the two heads of a KV layer has a cosine of about 0.05. Do the heads share information?
a: Yes, 0.85 bit per element raw; the distances between tokens correlate up to 0.92 across heads, so they are two views of one vector
wrong: Only after a rotation aligns them
why: Copying head 0 onto head 1 is worse than guessing the mean, yet joining the heads saves 0.0322 on 20 of 20 sequences. Similarity scores are not bits; that is stereo similarity.
title: Cutting the orchard: cherry shapes compared

q: After the heads, what did joining all six KV layers into one cherry save, and how do the layers group?
a: A further 0.0043 of ratio (20 of 20); KV layers 0, 4, 5 behave alike and 1, 2, 3 behave alike, so by kind, not by nearness
wrong: A further 0.03; adjacent layers group together
0.0043, and only adjacent layers may be joined
why: Grouping KV layers 0+4+5 and 1+2+3 beat grouping 0+1+2 and 3+4+5 by 0.0015 on 7 of 7 sequences, although the second joins neighbours.
title: Cutting the orchard: cherry shapes compared

q: What is the verdict on upstairs similarity?
a: Small, and not by adjacency; given everything else, adjacent KV layers share 0.03 to 0.08 bit per element, distant ones about 0.01
wrong: Strong: one dictionary can serve four adjacent layers
why: The floor directly above is barely more alike than a floor far away. Floors come in two kinds instead.
title: Cutting the orchard: cherry shapes compared

q: Like for like, what did joining 2 and 4 adjacent tokens into one cherry cost?
a: +0.037 and +0.063 of ratio against the v[t, l, :, :] cherry
wrong: It could not be measured under a leash
why: The best trick is one pointer per token to an earlier similar token; a pair of tokens rarely has a good earlier pair to point at.
title: Cutting the orchard: cherry shapes compared

q: Where do the reference links point at KV layers 0, 4 and 5 (the LLM’s layers 3, 19 and 23)?
a: Mostly far away, to repeats of the same token; only 9, 7 and 12 % of links stay within 8 tokens, against 37 to 47 % in the middle layers
wrong: To the adjacent token, as fallen-apple similarity predicted
Within 8 tokens for about half the cherries, at every layer
why: Middle layers build chains along the text; the first and last layers build hubs of far-apart repeats. The right axis is repetition, not distance.
title: Cutting the orchard: cherry shapes compared

q: Stacked on a reference tree and linear prediction, how often did the encoder choose a codebook when it was free to pick one by exact bits?
a: On 0 of 72 punnets
wrong: Only on the KV layer 0 punnets
why: A codeword is stored only to help others; a reference cherry is stored anyway, so it costs a pointer and nothing more. Offered codebooks of 4, 16 or 64 words or none, the encoder took none every time (r26-t0010).
title: Codebooks and rotations

q: What is a code-length estimate?
a: The code length a probability table would reach, computed on the data without building the compressor; a lead, not a result
wrong: A verified score from the separate decoder
The mean of a screen’s punnets
A compressor whose encoder rounds its weights exactly
why: The campaign’s grades run from bound and code-length estimate, through encoder bytes and quick, to verified. Only the last rebuilds every cherry in a separate process.
title: Codebooks and rotations

q: By how much did the DCT, Hadamard and random rotations lose, and why?
a: By 0.28–0.32 bit per element: rotating then rounding costs about a quarter of a bit, and element numbers carry no neighbourhood for a DCT to use
wrong: By 2.5 bits, the weight of a full basis
They won by 0.25 bit on the middle layers
why: Rounding after a rotation costs the lattice constant, 0.2546 bit per coordinate (measured 0.29–0.32). Linear prediction subtracts a guess and never rounds the vector.
title: Codebooks and rotations

q: Compressor 129 has no reference tree. On the layer screen, how far behind the tree compressor 102 was it?
a: 0.041 of ratio, on 14 of 14 parts of the screen
why: 0.6863 against 0.6449. The gap is what the repeats in the text are worth once linear prediction has taken the geometry.
title: Codebooks and rotations

q: How much of the close-enough family of 62 techniques has a real compressor behind it?
a: 21 techniques; 18 have only a bound, 16 are untried, 7 do not apply
wrong: None; the branch was closed on bounds alone
21, and the other 41 were shown to lose
why: The branch is not closed. By the human’s rule, in this branch a bound is a lead and only a real compressor answers.
title: Codebooks and rotations

q: An order-8 filter along tokens, FLAC-style, saves up to 0.33 bit per element on its own. How much after a reference cherry?
a: At most 0.06 bit, and that is not a code that can exist
why: In the middle KV layers the reference very often is a token a few steps back, so it already collects what the filter would. The leftover needs the whole past, which no leash allows.
title: Sound, time and bits

q: Where do references point in the middle KV layers (1, 2, 3), compared with KV layers 0, 4 and 5?
a: 37–47 % within 8 tokens against 7–12 %; chains along the text against hubs on repeated tokens far apart
wrong: Uniformly over the punnet in every layer
To the first token of the punnet
why: Two kinds of tree. A pointer in a chain costs 6.6–7.4 bits; a pointer to a hub about 10.
title: Sound, time and bits

q: At a stretch of 512 tokens, what beat the best fully paid prediction rule?
a: A rule the decoder learns from cherries it has already decoded (0.68938 against 0.6960)
wrong: A neural network stored in the dictionary
why: At a stretch of 512 the punnet cannot pay for the rule: the amortization rule of II.24, in action. At 4096 the paid rule leads again.
title: Sound, time and bits

q: Which single measurement showed that the linear structure of the values is hidden by the FP8 grid?
a: A shared-bits estimate on values matched real code lengths (0.278 against 0.263, r = 0.9993), while the same estimate on the FP8 code index read 0.104, three times too low
wrong: The mantissa kept 2.80 of its 3 bits
The skew of the error was −0.03
why: The structure is in the values. Counting in grid steps hides two thirds of it, which is exactly the worry of the toolbox’s bit-fields page.
title: Sound, time and bits

q: The same prediction error, measured two ways. How skewed is it?
a: −0.03 in value, −1.60 in the code index
wrong: −1.60 in value, −0.03 in the code index
why: FP8 cells narrow toward zero, so a symmetric error in value looks lopsided in grid steps. A logistic in value, integrated over the cell, inherits the skew for free.
title: Sound, time and bits

q: Counting the leash for every single cherry cold (5.3 million cherries) instead of 8 sampled per punnet changed what?
a: 4 of 19 winners and no headline; the sampled maxima had run up to 26 % low
why: The worst cherry reads 1.1–3.7 times the mean because of long chains in the tree, so a sample of 8 per punnet missed it. The best compressors still fit 293.
title: Reading one cherry

q: What does the leash cost at its tightest setting, 137 cherries’ worth on v[t, l, :, :] cherries?
a: 0.0234 of ratio (compressor 97 at 0.65980 fits; compressor 121 at 0.63639 does not)
wrong: It cannot be met at all
why: No compressor was tuned for its worst cherry, so this is the most the rule costs today, not what it must cost.
title: Reading one cherry

q: Moving every cherry of a tree compressor into the dictionary, so that every delta was empty, changed the ratio by how much?
a: +0.00004 of ratio
why: A reference cherry costs the same per element inside the dictionary as outside (5.84 against 5.85 bits). Where the bytes sit does not change the sum of the two shares; what a tree compressor adds per cherry is one pointer.
title: Reading one cherry

q: Which compressor’s punnet looks like the application’s picture of a small dictionary and uniform deltas?
a: The no-tree compressor 129 (dictionary share 0.01–0.04, every delta about two thirds of a cherry)
wrong: Compressor 109, with every cherry in the dictionary
why: A tree compressor’s dictionary is half the punnet, made of the cherries themselves, and about 80 % of its deltas are empty.
title: Reading one cherry

q: What did the toolbox expect to set a ceiling on stretch length, and did one appear?
a: The drift of the data; no ceiling appeared up to 32 768 tokens, and a bound says a whole sequence is better still
wrong: The amortization rule 8w/b; it appeared at 4096
why: The tree keeps gaining 0.010–0.020 per doubling from 16K to 32K. The right scope is the whole sequence, sequence scope.
title: Reading one cherry

q: Replaying Qwen3.5-2B with the same code, checkpoint, torch build and GPU reproduced how many value bytes exactly?
a: 50 331 648, every one that was checked
wrong: None; floating-point arithmetic is never repeatable
why: Values are an exact function of the text and the weights. Same program, same machine, same libraries, same tokens: the same bytes.
title: Where the bits come from

q: What happens to the stored FP8 bytes when the LLM is replayed under a different torch build, or in float32?
a: About 28 % of cells move one grid step, and 1.2–1.4 bits per value are left to pay (ratio 0.15–0.17)
wrong: Nothing changes; the bytes are deterministic
why: A different arithmetic path orders the rounding differently. The wobble is about 1 % of the spread, but FP8 cells are narrow, so a quarter of the bytes land in a neighbouring cell.
title: Where the bits come from

q: In the memory table, what did the intact LLM pay per value, and what did it pay with far attention cut and the linear-attention state reset?
a: 1.35 bits intact; 5.16 bits with both removed, about what compressor 102 pays with no LLM at all (5.13)
why: What a punnet compressor cannot predict is what the LLM remembers from far earlier text. The equality holds for the six-layer mean on one window; per layer the two differ by about a bit.
title: Where the bits come from

q: Of the 4.89 bits per value left after a good punnet compressor, how much did knowing the token id save?
a: About 0.004 bit
why: Role saved 0.0003, the previous token 0.007, the other five KV layers 0.025. After a good compressor, the leftover looks the same whatever the token is.
title: Where the bits come from

q: Why may no compressor use the prediction rule computed from the LLM’s weights alone, although it would take compressor 102 from 0.6407 to 0.6326?
a: It is a shared table, which the human ruled legitimate but allowed only once an independent training dataset exists
wrong: It needs more reads than the leash allows
It was shown to fail on target 02
why: Both sides would have to hold the weights in advance. The ruling is yes in principle and not yet in practice.
title: Where the bits come from

q: How much does one compressor’s score move from one sequence to another, and how much does the paired difference of two compressors move?
a: About 0.012 between sequences; 0.0001–0.001 for the paired difference
why: Two compressors rise and fall together on the same punnets, so their difference is ten to a hundred times steadier than either score.
title: Signal or noise

q: Why is “35 of 35 parts of a screen agree” weaker evidence than “5 of 5 sequences agree”?
a: Punnets of one sequence are correlated; the campaign took sequences as its independent samples
wrong: Parts of a screen are measured with a worse compressor
It is stronger, since 35 is more than 5
Parts of a screen are always shuffled
why: Parts of the same text share its hardness. Only separate conversations are separate draws.
title: Signal or noise

q: The layer screen read 0.6449 and the token screen 0.6461. What did the same-window comparison say?
a: v[t, :, :, :] cherries are better by 0.0043, on 20 of 20 sequences; the token screen simply held harder punnets
wrong: v[t, l, :, :] cherries are better by 0.0012
why: The token screen sampled punnets 0.0046 harder for every compressor. Scores from two different screens can never be subtracted.
title: Signal or noise

q: What single thing explains 97 % of how hard a punnet is to compress?
a: One number per token window, shared by all KV layers and heads, that follows the share of repeated tokens (r = −0.91)
