wrong: Which KV layer the punnet comes from
The punnet’s position in the sequence
why: Hardness belongs to the text. A compressor’s gain, by contrast, belongs to the layer (99 % of its variance is between layers).
title: Signal or noise

q: Which three decisions did the human make during and after the campaign?
a: The leash limits every single cherry; delta lengths are not counted; a shared table is legitimate but no compressor may use one until an independent training dataset exists
wrong: Use fewer researchers; use BF16; stop at a stretch of 4096
Charge delta lengths; sample 8 cherries per punnet; ban shared tables
Verify nothing; count the mean reads; publish immediately
why: Each decision changed the rules of scoring without changing any score; the first changed 4 of 19 winners and no headline.
title: Signal or noise

q: The napkin expected most of the gain in a few pre-RoPE key furrows and about nothing in values. What did the campaigns measure?
a: Values compress to 0.63 at a stretch of 4096 and 0.62 at 16 384, about 1.1–1.3 bits below solo; keys compress like values
wrong: Values stayed at solo; keys gave 1 bit
why: The prior was wrong on values. The gain came from repeated tokens (reference cherries) and the fixed geometry of the weights (linear prediction), neither of which is a furrow effect.
title: The scorecard

q: What was the verdict on the fixed rotations, the Compass?
a: They lose by 0.28–0.32 bit per element; rotating then rounding pays a tax of about 0.25 bit, and prediction without rounding wins
why: Element numbers carry no neighbourhood, so a DCT has nothing to work with, and any rotation leaves the grid and pays the lattice constant on the way back.
title: The scorecard

q: Which of the hypotheses was untested by the campaigns?
a: The Lucky Louis property; the campaigns measured bytes, never which picks an indexer names
why: Deployment and the indexer were out of the campaign’s scope. Which picks are wanted and what is inside them remain two different questions.
title: The scorecard

q: How did fallen-apple similarity fare?
a: Half wrong; repeats are the axis, with distance mattering only in the middle KV layers, and adjacent tokens are nearly useless at KV layers 0, 4 and 5
wrong: Entirely wrong, no cherry predicts any other
why: Mutual information with the adjacent token is 0.058 bit per element at KV layer 0; the references that pay point at the same token again, often far away. Middle layers form chains along the text.
title: The scorecard

q: What do the measurements say about the gain the project needs?
a: Go, since the gain over solo is about 1.1–1.3 bits per element, far above a 0.75-bit line; but at sequence scope, because longer stretches always won and the stretch-scope gain the project bet on is negative in the old sense
wrong: No go, the gain is under 0.25 bit
Go at stretch scope, as hoped
The rule cannot be applied at all
why: The whole sequence is the best scope found. The gain is real; where to fit the dictionary is the part the data changed.
title: What it means for kvblockdiff

q: Why does the two-rates gap of V.11 still have to be paid or avoided?
a: Every compressor in the campaigns uses an entropy coder (rANS); the fixed-length rate the application wants for the miss path was never measured
wrong: Because the deltas were measured in BF16
Because the gap was measured at zero
why: For Laplace-shaped residuals at 5–7 bits the fixed-length rate runs about one bit above the entropy rate. Whether these residuals behave the same is unmeasured.
title: What it means for kvblockdiff

q: Feed the light no-tree compressor’s delta share, about 0.69, into the square-root rule of the application. What does lever 1 alone buy at each system’s best hot-cache size?
a: About 1.2×, in the “worth it only if it comes almost for free” band
why: The square root of 1/0.69 is about 1.2. The assumed 0.75 gave 1.11×; the measured share moves it by a tenth, and an entropy-coded share is optimistic for a fixed-length store.
title: What it means for kvblockdiff

q: Why must a tree compressor’s dictionary be resident on the GPU?
a: A cold decode of one cherry reads about 100–300 cherries’ worth of dictionary; in GPU memory that is nothing, over the link it would be ruinous for a single miss
wrong: Because all its deltas are empty
Because the link is faster than GPU memory
why: Half the punnet sits in the dictionary as the cherries themselves. That is a compressed orchard on the GPU, lever 2 territory, rather than a light dictionary loaded once.
title: What it means for kvblockdiff

q: What single measurement did the campaign’s supervisor most want repeated, and why does the next campaign start there?
a: The memory table, on many windows; if it holds, it settles what any stretch-scope compressor can ever reach
why: It rests on one 2048-token window of one sequence. The whole reading of “the wall” depends on it.
title: What it means for kvblockdiff

q: Compressor 121 scores 0.636 = dictionary share 0.525 + delta share 0.112. Why does the 0.525 look like a measure of shared information?
a: The score’s square drew the dictionary as the shared summary and the delta as the private remainder, so a big dictionary reads as a lot shared
wrong: Because 0.525 is close to one half
Because the delta share is the mutual information
Because the dictionary was trained on other sequences
why: The square’s axes are the dictionary share and the delta share, two byte counts that sum to the score. The page shows that the dictionary share does not track information.
title: What the half says, and what it does not

q: Moving every cherry of a tree compressor into its dictionary, so that every delta was empty, did what to the ratio?
a: It moved by +0.00004
why: A reference cherry costs the same per element inside the dictionary as outside (5.84 against 5.85 bits). The share records where the bytes were filed.
title: What the half says, and what it does not

q: The light compressor 129 has a dictionary of about 2 % of the punnet. What does that 2 % buy?
a: About 0.09 of ratio, 0.686 against solo coding’s 0.778
wrong: Nothing; 2 % is too small to matter
why: A short summary (a mean and a scale per furrow and a prediction rule) carries most of what a per-punnet compressor knows. Dictionary size and information gained point in opposite directions here.
title: What the half says, and what it does not

q: What is the punnet redundancy of a punnet of cherries?
a: The sum of the cherries’ solo entropies minus their joint entropy, per element; the most any per-punnet compressor can save over solo coding
wrong: The dictionary share of the best tree compressor
The delta share of the best tree compressor
The entropy of the dictionary’s bytes
why: It is the redundancy of the punnet’s elements, the mutual information among the cherries plus the fixed relations among a cherry’s elements. A compressor’s gain over solo is a lower bound on it; a dictionary’s size says nothing about it.
title: What the half says, and what it does not

q: How much of a cherry’s solo bits did the campaigns show to be shared across a punnet?
a: About a fifth, between 18 % (the best verified compressor at a stretch of 4096) and 23 % (a code-length floor at 16 384)
wrong: About half, as the dictionary share says
About 2 %, as the light compressor’s dictionary says
why: Solo is 6.22 bits per element; the tree compressor pays 5.09 (1.13 bits less) and the punnet floor is about 4.80 (1.4 bits less). Both are lower bounds on the punnet redundancy.
title: What the half says, and what it does not

q: Solo coding pays 6.22 bits per element and the best verified tree compressor 5.09. What share of solo’s bits is saved?
why: 6.22 − 5.09 = 1.13, and 1.13 / 6.22 ≈ 0.18. The light compressor saves 0.73 bit (12 %); only the intact LLM saves 4.87 (78 %).
title: Shared across the stretch, in bits

q: Which step of the ladder is not shared information at all?
a: The 1.78 bits from raw 8 to solo 6.22, the uneven use of the FP8 codes by each furrow coded alone
wrong: The tree compressor’s 0.40 bit over the light compressor
The punnet floor’s 0.3 bit over the tree compressor
The intact LLM’s 4.87 bits over solo
why: Solo coding knows nothing about other cherries. Its saving is the bit budget of V.1: a bell-shaped furrow uses 253 codes unevenly.
title: Shared across the stretch, in bits

q: Joining the two heads of a KV layer saved 0.0322 of ratio. Joining all six KV layers after that saved how much more?
a: 0.0043, about 0.03 bit per element
why: Given everything else, adjacent KV layers share 0.03 to 0.08 bit per element and distant layers about 0.01. Joining adjacent tokens is what loses 0.037.
title: Shared across the stretch, in bits

q: Why does a tower of adjacent KV layers add so little once each layer has its own reference cherry?
a: The reference is a repeat of the same text, and the same pair of tokens repeats at every layer, so the layer above tells the reference little it did not already carry
wrong: Because adjacent layers are rotated copies of each other
Because the leash forbids joining layers
why: Layers also group by kind (KV 0, 4, 5 against 1, 2, 3), so adjacency was the wrong axis for a cherry shape anyway.
title: Shared across the stretch, in bits

q: Of the 5.16 bits per value the LLM pays when it keeps only one 2 048-token window, how much is about text outside that window?
a: About 3.8 bits; the intact LLM pays 1.35
why: Cutting attention beyond 16 384 tokens alone costs 2.14 bits (1.35 → 3.49); with the running state reset as well and attention kept inside the 2 048-token window, 5.16, next to a punnet compressor’s 5.13. One window, code-length estimate.
title: Shared across the stretch, in bits

q: How much of that outside-the-stretch information can a compressor without the LLM recover at sequence scope?
a: About 0.26 to 0.45 bit per element, the part that returns as literal repeats (a bound, one window)
why: The rest is the LLM’s memory of far text, reachable only by a receiver who holds the weights, which the human has ruled a shared table.
title: Shared across the stretch, in bits

q: What does the “What it says about our scenario” section of a paper page contain?
a: Three lists: what in Parts IV–VIII the paper supports, what it contradicts and who we believe, and what it suggests trying
wrong: A summary of the paper’s abstract
The paper’s numbers converted to dollars
A list of the paper’s co-authors
why: Builds on, conflicts with, suggests. Every item links to the scenario page, the stage, the hypothesis or the measurement it touches.
title: How we read papers

q: Which part of a paper does the trust rule rank highest?
a: The background its introduction treats as known, and any result that is a formula or a count
wrong: The headline ratio in the abstract
The throughput on the authors’ own rig
why: Background is what the field agrees on; a count can be redone. A ratio on a private rig can be checked by nobody.
title: How we read papers

q: Which data path does this project live on?
a: The miss path of sparse decoding: scattered single cherries that must each be rebuilt alone
wrong: The bulk transfer of a prompt’s orchard from the prefill GPU to the decode GPU
The network fetch of a stored prefix from another machine
The orchard kept compressed in GPU memory and decoded inside attention
why: On the Pin, per layer per decode step, about 274 scattered 640-byte picks cross the link, each rebuilt from its own delta and a dictionary already on the GPU.
title: How we read papers

q: Why can a compressor that is excellent for bulk transfer still be the wrong shape for the miss path?
a: It may decode only a whole stream front to back, so one cherry cannot be rebuilt cold
wrong: Bulk compressors cannot run on a GPU
Bulk transfers move fewer bytes than the miss path
why: The access pattern decides the form. A stream compressor carries state from one value to the next; the miss path needs one cherry, decoded cold, under the leash.
title: How we read papers

q: On the map, where does almost every lossless result sit?
a: On the bulk-transfer path
why: SplitZip and the float compressors ship whole tensors once. The GPU-memory path is full of lossy work, and the miss path has a cache that moves raw bytes and no compressor yet.
title: How we read papers

q: What does HiSparse change about decoding?
a: Where picks live, host memory or GPU memory, and nothing about their bytes
wrong: The numbers stored in each cherry
How many picks attention reads per step
why: HiSparse keeps the orchard in host DRAM and a hot cache of raw picks in HBM. Attention reads the same bytes as before, so the LLM’s outputs are unchanged.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: Which fact does HiSparse’s introduction treat as known, and which we lean on most?
a: Sparse attention reads a few thousand picks per layer per step, but every cherry of the orchard must stay available
wrong: Picks arrive in order of position
why: Everything must be kept, and only a little is read. That is the background of the paper, and the premise of the whole scenario.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: At 4096 slots, LRU misses 13.4 % of picks and Bélády’s clairvoyant policy 8.2 %. What does the gap tell us?
a: A perfect eviction policy would remove only about 5 points of misses; the eviction lever is nearly used up
wrong: LRU is a poor policy and should be replaced
Doubling the cache would not reduce misses
Bélády’s policy can be built from the indexer’s scores
why: Bélády’s policy knows the future, so no real policy can beat it. To cut misses much further you need a bigger cache, or cheaper misses.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: How many traces are HiSparse’s locality numbers (30 / 13.4 / 6.7 % misses) measured on?
a: One: a single 100 384-token LongBenchV2 prompt on GLM-5.1, averaged over decode steps
why: The trace is one sequence with 1 799 decode steps over 78 sparse layers; the means cover the first 1 000 steps.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: Which of our open questions does HiSparse leave unanswered, by design?
a: Where the misses land, spread over the orchard or piled into a few heavy stretches, and what is inside the picks
wrong: Whether the hot cache can hold 4096 slots
why: Every number it reports is about which picks are wanted. None is about their bytes, and none is broken down by stretch.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: HiSparse’s “hot device buffer” is which object on this site?
a: The hot cache
why: Its per-sequence, per-layer GPU buffer of raw picks, managed LRU, is the hot cache of Part III. The dictionary shelf is ours and does not exist in HiSparse.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: In the toy step, what changes when the selector is switched from DSA to Quest or NSA with the same budget?
a: The picks arrive in runs of consecutive positions inside fewer stretches, at some cost in precision
wrong: Attention reads twice as many positions
The picks become single scattered tokens
why: Group selectors score runs of positions and take whole runs. The toy’s readout shows fewer stretches touched and fewer of the true top 8 caught.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.1

q: What do all five selectors assume, and this project relies on?
a: Each names, per layer, which positions attention will read before any orchard bytes are touched
wrong: Each picks single tokens one by one
Each must be trained together with the LLM
Each stores the orchard in compressed form
why: That announcement is the demand signal a hot cache, or a delta store, serves. Everything else about the selectors can differ.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.1

q: How does Quest score a stretch of 16 positions without reading every key in it?
a: It keeps each element’s smallest and largest key value over the stretch and computes an upper bound of the query–key score
wrong: It reads one trained summary key per stretch
It averages the keys of the stretch
It reuses the previous step’s attention weights
why: For each element, whichever end (min or max) gives the larger product with the query’s element bounds every key in the stretch; summing over elements bounds the whole score.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.1

q: Under DeepSeek-V4, what does one pick cover?
a: One row that squeezes 4 consecutive tokens into one; the indexer picks the top 512 or 1024 of those rows
wrong: One token at one layer, as in DSA
One token for a group of layers
why: V4 first squeezes every 4 tokens into one row and then selects among the rows. The thing a cache or a delta store serves is the squeezed row.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.1

q: Why does GLM-5.1’s shared selection call for a different scenario from DSA’s?
a: One pick covers one position for a whole group of layers, so one ask must return several layers’ cherries, served by one dictionary or by a multi-layer cherry
why: What a pick covers decides what one ask returns, hence the cherry shape and what a dictionary must serve. DSA’s per-layer pick maps to one-layer cherries with a dictionary per layer.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.1

q: Quest’s “page” is which object on this site?
a: A stretch of 16 tokens
why: A page is 16 consecutive positions scored and picked together: a stretch, with the stretch length fixed at 16 by the selector rather than chosen by us.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.1

q: Which part of each BF16 number does SplitZip store raw?
a: The sign and the 7 mantissa bits, one raw byte per number
wrong: Nothing: every bit goes through the 4-bit code
why: The low mantissa bits are close to noise, so SplitZip keeps that byte as it is and codes only the exponent byte.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: What does SplitZip’s introduction take as known about the numbers in an orchard?
a: Their exponents are concentrated in a few values and their mantissas are close to uniform
why: That is the physics every lossless float compressor cashes in. SplitZip adds nothing conditional on top of it.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: Escapes aside, what is the most a 4-bit exponent code can shrink BF16 numbers?
wrong: 2×, because half the bits are exponent
why: Each number keeps 8 raw bits and spends 4 on the exponent code, so 16 bits become at least 12. The measured 1.324× sits right under that ceiling.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: Why does SplitZip’s 3-bit code expand E4M3 data instead of shrinking it?
a: It saves only 1 bit of the 4-bit exponent, and the escapes for uncovered values cost more than that
wrong: E4M3 values cannot be split into bit fields
The mantissa grows when the exponent is coded
why: Even at 96 % coverage, 4 % of values × several dozen bits per escape is more than the 1 bit per value the code saves.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: The campaigns’ solo compressor reaches 0.778 on E4M3 values where SplitZip’s code expands them. What is the difference?
a: Solo uses one entropy-coded table per furrow; SplitZip uses one fixed-length table for every element
wrong: Solo uses a dictionary per stretch
The Bench’s values are not E4M3
why: Per-furrow tables see that each element position has its own spread; an entropy coder spends fractional bits. Both gains are gone in a single 3-bit code.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: SplitZip calls its table of the 16 most frequent exponents a “codebook”. What is it on this site?
a: A fixed-length code with escapes, fit once on calibration data and shared by every sequence
wrong: A probability table an arithmetic-coding stage updates as it reads
why: On this site “codebook” means VQ centroids only. SplitZip’s table maps 16 exponent values to 4-bit codewords; everything else is escaped.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: Draw numbers from one bell curve and store them in BF16. About how many bits of information does the 8-bit exponent field carry?
a: About 2.5 bits
why: Most values fall in a few binades around the curve’s width; the exponent’s entropy works out to 2.54 bits. That leaves about 5.5 of its 8 bits as redundancy for an entropy coder to remove.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: What do all six compressors take as known about LLM numbers?
a: They are roughly bell-shaped, so their exponents are skewed and their mantissas nearly uniform
wrong: Their low bits carry most of the information
why: One recipe fits all of them because the background is the same. A bell curve on a log grid is the whole explanation.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: Why does LZ4, a byte-string matcher, shrink BF16 tensors by only about 2 %?
a: Floats almost never repeat as exact byte strings; their redundancy is in the uneven use of exponent values
wrong: LZ4 cannot run on a GPU
why: LZ matching copies earlier byte strings. LLM numbers share a skewed exponent distribution, not repeated strings, so an entropy coder finds what LZ cannot.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: ZipNN’s 1.515× in SplitZip’s comparison table is suspicious for which reason?
a: It beats the ceiling of any exponent-only compressor on that workload (about 1.42× at 3.29 bits of exponent entropy)
wrong: ZipNN does not code exponents at all
why: With 8 raw bits of sign and mantissa, 3.29 bits of exponent gives 16 / 11.29 ≈ 1.42×. Either ZipNN squeezes the other byte too, or its row was measured on other data.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: What does this family of papers say about the campaigns’ choice to compress FP8 rather than BF16?
a: It supports it; at BF16 the mantissa’s seven noise bits cap lossless work near 1.5×, and the campaigns saw the low four BF16 bits behave as noise
wrong: It contradicts it; BF16 compresses better
It says FP8 cannot be compressed losslessly
why: The float compressors stop near 1.3–1.5× on BF16 for one reason, the mantissa. Moving to 8-bit storage removes most of that noise before any dictionary is tried.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: At what granularity does DFloat11 decode the LLM’s weights, in our words?
a: Per layer
why: The paper names the unit with a word this site retires for data and token ranges; it is one transformer layer, whose weights are decoded together.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: In KVFetcher’s layout, what does the previous video frame hold, relative to the current one?
a: The neighbouring token, so predicting from the previous frame is predicting a cherry from the token before it
wrong: Another KV head of the same token
why: Frames follow the token axis. A video compressor’s favourite move, “same place, one frame back”, becomes fallen-apple prediction at token distance 1.
title: KVFetcher (2026)

q: What does KVFetcher take as known about the orchard?
a: That consecutive tokens have similar values within one furrow, enough for a video compressor’s predictions to pay
wrong: That keys and values are identical
why: The whole design rests on the video analogy, and the analogy rests on neighbouring tokens looking alike. It is assumed, then exploited; not measured in bits.
title: KVFetcher (2026)

q: Which step of KVFetcher throws information away?
a: Rounding the orchard’s numbers to integers before the video compressor sees them
wrong: The H.265 compressor in lossless mode
Decoding on the GPU’s video chip
why: The video compressor runs in its lossless mode, so the integers come back exactly; the original BF16 numbers do not. “Lossless accuracy” means the benchmark scores did not drop.
title: KVFetcher (2026)

q: Swapping half of the numbers between KV heads made the ratio 2.4× worse. What does that show?
a: Which numbers sit next to each other inside a frame decides how well a neighbour-predicting compressor works
wrong: Heads are identical to each other
why: The swap leaves the token order alone and scrambles each frame’s picture, so much of the ratio must come from structure inside one token’s numbers, not from its neighbour.
title: KVFetcher (2026)

q: What did the campaigns measure about the token-distance-1 prediction KVFetcher leans on?
a: Nearly useless at the Bench’s layers 0, 4 and 5 (0.058 bit per element of mutual information at layer 0) and modest in the middle layers
why: Fallen-apple similarity came out weak except in the middle layers; the axis that mattered was repeats of the same token far away, not distance.
title: KVFetcher (2026)

q: KVFetcher’s “frame” is which object on this site?
a: One token’s values at one or more layers, laid out as a small picture; close to one cherry
why: One frame holds one token’s numbers; three layers are its colour planes. A run of thousands of frames must be decoded together, which no cherry on the miss path may require.
title: KVFetcher (2026)

q: KIVI lays its key rulers along which numbers, in this site’s words?
a: One furrow over a run of 32 tokens, a column of the table
wrong: All the numbers of one token’s key vector (a row)
All keys of one layer at once
One head’s keys and values together
why: A furrow is one element position followed along the token axis. Per-furrow rounding computes the ruler (smallest value and step) over tokens, separately for each position.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: What does KIVI’s introduction take as known about keys and values?
a: A few fixed furrows of the keys are very large, token after token; the values show no such pattern
wrong: Keys and values are both bell-shaped with equal spread
why: Magnitude plots of a few layers are the paper’s background. The whole design, rulers along furrows for keys and along cherries for values, follows from it.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: Counting a 16-bit smallest value and a 16-bit step per scale group of 32 numbers, what does “2-bit” KIVI cost per number?
a: About 3 bits
why: 2 bits of code plus 32 bits of ruler shared by 32 numbers = 1 more bit each. Our count, under a stated assumption about how the ruler is stored.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: KIVI shows that keys survive 2-bit rounding. What does that tell us about an exact copy of 8-bit keys?
a: Little; it is about what the LLM tolerates, not about how much of each number is predictable
wrong: That 8-bit keys compress losslessly to about 2 bits
That keys have no noise below the second bit
why: Rounding throws away the six low bits; a lossless compressor must reproduce them, noise included. What it can save depends on the variance a predictor explains, which KIVI does not report.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: KIVI lays a fresh ruler every 32 tokens, as if a furrow’s level drifted. What did the campaigns find about drift in the Bench’s values?
a: No drift ceiling; longer stretches kept winning up to 32 768 tokens, and a whole sequence is best
wrong: That values drift faster than keys
That drift explains most of the bits
why: Per-stretch dictionaries would beat long-scope ones only if furrow levels moved along the text. On the Bench they did not move enough to show.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: KIVI’s “per-token quantization” of values is which rounding on this site?
a: Per-cherry rounding, one ruler for one token’s vector
why: One token’s values at one layer are one cherry; a ruler over that vector is a per-cherry ruler.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: Why are keys easier to round per furrow before RoPE than after it?
a: RoPE turns each pair of elements by an angle that grows with position, so a furrow with a steady large value starts to swing
wrong: RoPE adds random noise to every key
RoPE makes all furrows the same size
why: Before RoPE a furrow can sit near 9 token after token; after RoPE the same number is shared between the two elements of its pair in proportions that change with position.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: Which fact does KVQuant take over from KIVI as known?
a: Keys have large persistent furrows and values do not, so keys get per-furrow rulers and values per-cherry rulers
wrong: Values are bell-shaped with no outliers
RoPE can be undone exactly in floating point
why: The ruler directions are inherited; KVQuant’s contributions are pre-RoPE rounding, a fitted grid and escapes on top.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: According to KVQuant’s appendix, if keys are rounded per cherry (not per furrow), is rounding before RoPE still better?
a: No; with per-cherry rulers, rounding after RoPE did better
wrong: Yes, always, by a wide margin
It makes no difference at all
The paper did not try per-cherry rulers
why: LLaMA-7B, 3-bit uniform, per-token in their words: perplexity 10.87 after RoPE versus 14.68 before (16-bit: 5.68). Pre-RoPE pays off only together with per-furrow rulers.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: KVQuant’s “dense-and-sparse” step stores the largest ~1 % of numbers separately. Which idea from this site is that?
a: Escapes; rare values stored in full, with their positions, outside the fixed-width code
why: The rest of the vector then needs a much narrower ruler. Fixed-length codes with an escape stream make the same trade, losslessly.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: The Bench’s dump stores keys before RoPE. What did the campaigns find about them?
a: Pre-RoPE keys compress like values at the same depth, with the same compressor family and the same order of mechanisms
wrong: Keys compress twice as well as values
why: One night of C1 on pre-RoPE keys, FP8 and BF16; C2 never touched keys. KVQuant’s advice to store keys before RoPE is what made that night possible.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: KVQuant’s “pre-RoPE quantization” means, on this site, that the exact target is which object?
a: The 8-bit keys before RoPE, with the GPU applying RoPE after each cold decode
wrong: The post-RoPE keys, re-encoded for free
The values, which have no RoPE
why: In floating point a rotation is not bit-exactly undone, so “store pre-RoPE” is a design choice made up front about what the contract reproduces.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: In this site’s vocabulary, what is the “PCA decorrelation” step of KVTC?
a: A KLT, a rotation onto the axes along which the data spreads most, fitted once on calibration data
why: PCA and the KLT are the same mathematics. KVTC fits the axes once, offline, and reuses them for every orchard, a dictionary of global scope.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: What does KVTC’s setup take as known about the orchard’s statistics?
a: That its variance is concentrated on a few directions, so a rotation makes most coordinates small
why: Transform coding pays only on a steep spectrum. The paper assumes one, and its 20× says it found one, for a lossy purpose.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: How does a lossy transform compressor like KVTC reach ratios like 20×?
a: It gives zero bits to the many small axes below a “water level” and drops them
wrong: It codes every axis exactly with fewer bits
why: Bits go to an axis in proportion to the log of its variance above the water level; below it, nothing is stored at all.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: What does the same rotation save in a lossless compressor?
a: The transform coding gain, ½ log₂ (AM/GM) of the variances, in bits per element, on standardized data
wrong: The same ratio as the lossy compressor
Nothing; rotations never help lossless coding
log₂ of the number of axes dropped
why: A lossless compressor cannot drop axes; every one still costs bits down to the stored grid. Only the uneven spread of variance is saved, and only logarithmically.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: What did the campaigns find when they rotated the Bench’s values and rounded?
a: Fixed rotations lost 0.28–0.32 bit per element; rotating then rounding costs about 0.25 bit, and linear prediction, which never rounds the vector, won
wrong: A KLT saved 2 bits per element
Rotations tied with the reference tree
why: On an 8-bit grid the rounding after a rotation is a tax the lossy recipe never pays. Prediction subtracts a guess and keeps the grid.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: KVTC’s final DEFLATE step is which kind of stage on this site, and why is it wrong for the miss path?
a: A stream entropy coder; a stream must be decoded from its start, and the miss path reads one cherry cold under the leash
why: Offloading a whole orchard reads it all anyway; a cold decode of one 512-byte cherry cannot wait for the stream before it.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: What is sparse coding, in one sentence?
a: Describing a vector as a weighted sum of a few atoms chosen from a large fixed dictionary, storing only which atoms and their weights
wrong: Storing only the non-zero elements of a vector
Rotating a vector onto its principal axes
why: VQ is the special case of one atom with weight 1; a KLT uses every axis with a weight.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: What does Lexico take as known that makes one dictionary per LLM plausible?
a: That the vectors an LLM produces lie near a few directions out of many, whatever the text
wrong: That every text has its own alphabet
That atoms must be refitted per sequence
That keys and values share one alphabet
why: The dictionary is trained once on Wikipedia text and never retrained; the bet is that the geometry belongs to the LLM, not to the prompt.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: With 8 atoms per vector, a dictionary of 4096 atoms and 8-bit weights, how many bits does one vector cost?
a: 160 bits, 8 × (12 index bits + 8 weight bits)
why: Naming one of 4096 atoms takes log₂ 4096 = 12 bits. A 128-number vector at 16 bits is 2048 bits, so 160 bits is about 8 % of it.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: For a lossless compressor using Lexico-like atoms (8 per vector, 4096 atoms, 8-bit weights, 128 elements per vector), what share of variance must the atoms explain just to break even?
a: About 82 %
why: The tax is 160 bits / 128 elements = 1.25 bits per element; ½ log₂ 1/(1−R²) = 1.25 needs 1−R² = 2^−2.5 ≈ 0.18.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: What did the campaigns find about structure that belongs to the LLM rather than to the text?
a: A linear prediction rule fit on another sequence recovers 91–96 % of the gain, and the shuffle control barely moves it
wrong: A codebook of 4096 centroids beat every other stage
why: Geometry belongs to the LLM; repeats belong to the text. That is Lexico’s bet, measured in bits, for the prediction stage.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: Lexico’s “universal dictionary” is, on this site, which kind of dictionary?
a: A dictionary of global scope, one per LLM
why: Fit once on a calibration corpus and shared by every sequence; charged to nobody per punnet. “Universal” means across prompts and tasks, not across LLMs.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: In CacheGen, what is each non-reference token stored as?
a: Its difference from the first token of its stretch of 10, same layer and furrow
wrong: Its difference from the immediately preceding token
Its difference from the layer below
why: Referencing one shared token lets all nine differences be computed and decoded in parallel. The first draft said “adjacent-token deltas”; that was not quite right.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: What does CacheGen’s first insight take as known?
a: That within one layer and one furrow, nearby tokens have similar values
wrong: That the orchard repeats byte strings
That keys are harder than values
That the LLM tolerates any rounding
why: Fallen-apple similarity, stated as a fact and measured as a variance ratio. It is the premise of the differencing step.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: Subtracting a neighbour that carries its own independent noise does what to the noise variance?
a: Doubles it
why: The difference of two numbers with independent noise of variance σ² has noise variance 2σ². Differencing pays off only when slow drift dominates the fast noise.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: If the differences’ 2.4× smaller variance is measured against each furrow’s own typical value, at least how much of a furrow’s variance must be slow drift?
a: About 79 %
why: The difference keeps at least twice the noise, so 2(1−f) ≤ 1/2.4, which gives f ≥ 0.79.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: What did the campaigns measure about the token-distance prediction CacheGen relies on?
a: Weak except in the middle layers; references pointed at far repeats of the same token, and joining two adjacent tokens into one cherry made the ratio worse by 0.037
wrong: A variance ratio of 2.4× at every layer
Nothing; the token axis was never tried
That adjacent tokens are the best reference everywhere
why: On the Bench, repetition mattered and distance mostly did not. CacheGen’s premise holds, if at all, in the middle layers.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: CacheGen’s “group of 10 tokens with an anchor” has the shape of which objects on this site?
a: A stretch of 10 whose dictionary is one reference cherry, weight 1
why: Every token is rebuilt from the reference plus its own difference. Then the arithmetic coding turns each run of tokens into a stream, which breaks the cold decode.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: What does KVComp’s “cache-resident decompression” mean, in plain words?
a: Decoded numbers go straight from fast on-chip memory into the attention dot products, never written back to GPU main memory
wrong: The orchard is decompressed once at the start of decoding
Only the hot cache is compressed
why: Writing decoded numbers back to GPU memory and reading them again would cost the very bandwidth compression saves.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: Which of KVComp’s choices are KIVI’s ruler directions?
a: Keys rounded with per-furrow rulers in runs of tokens, values with per-cherry rulers
wrong: Keys per cherry, values per furrow
why: The same background, key furrows have sizes of their own and values vary by token, used before a Huffman code.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: What does KVComp show that this project needs from it?
a: That a variable-length code can be decoded on the GPU at attention speed, hundreds of GB/s
wrong: That the orchard has no structure
That Huffman beats rANS in ratio
why: Entropy coders have a reputation for being slow and sequential. KVComp is the counter-example; every compressor of Part VIII uses an entropy coder and none has been timed on a GPU.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: In the grid figure (R² = 75 %), how does a predictor’s saving change from an 8-bit-like grid (σ = 32 steps) to a coarse one (σ = 1 step)?
a: Fewer bits saved (1.00 → 0.69) but a larger share of the total (14 % → 33 %)
wrong: More bits saved and a larger share
why: A coarse grid shrinks every cost, the predictor’s saving included, but the order-0 cost shrinks faster. The grid alone does not make predictors useless.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: What did the campaigns find that a predictor is worth on the Bench’s 8-bit values?
a: About 1.2–1.3 bits per element over solo at stretches of 4096–16 384 tokens, from reference cherries and linear prediction
wrong: Nothing; rounding had absorbed it all
why: Solo is 0.778; the best verified compressor reached 0.636 at 4096 and 0.618 at 16 384. The gap is prediction, which KVComp’s pipeline leaves out.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: KVComp rounds keys with one ruler per element position within a run of tokens. What is that on this site?
a: Per-furrow rounding with one scale group per furrow per run of tokens
why: One ruler per furrow within a run of tokens; the run is a scale group along the token axis, not a stretch of ours.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: The receiver knows Y, which equals X or differs from it in one of three bits. Without knowing Y, how many bits must the sender spend on X?
a: 2 bits, the index of X’s bin
wrong: 0 bits: the receiver can guess X from Y
why: Bins pair each 3-bit string with its complement. The two members differ in all three bits, so only one of them can be within one flip of Y.
title: The classics we lean on

q: What do Slepian–Wolf’s bins assume that a 512-byte cold decode cannot offer?
a: Very long runs of symbols and good statistics of how X and Y differ
wrong: That X and Y are independent
why: The theorem’s rate is reached in the limit of long codes. One cherry decoded alone under the leash is the opposite regime.
title: The classics we lean on

q: Why can one pass over a trace give an LRU cache’s misses at every size at once?
a: An ask misses exactly when its stack distance is at least the cache size, so counting distances answers every size
wrong: Because every cache size has the same miss rate
why: LRU’s contents at size B are always contained in its contents at size B + 1 (Mattson’s inclusion property), which is what makes the stack distance meaningful.
title: The classics we lean on

q: On the toy trace, LRU with 3 slots misses 7 times and Bélády’s policy 6 times. What does the 6 mean?
a: No eviction policy whatsoever can miss fewer than 6 times with 3 slots on this trace
wrong: LRU can be tuned to reach 6
Bélády’s policy is what HiSparse uses
why: Bélády’s policy knows the future and evicts the item needed furthest ahead; it is optimal for equal-cost misses, so it is a floor, not a design.
title: The classics we lean on

q: In kvblockdiff the sender builds each punnet dictionary itself. What is the formal home of coding cherries against it?
a: Ordinary conditional coding; both ends know the dictionary, and Slepian–Wolf is needed only for side information the sender cannot see
wrong: Slepian–Wolf coding, because only the GPU holds the dictionary
Wyner–Ziv coding, because the deltas are lossy
Rate–distortion theory with no side information
why: Slepian–Wolf’s surprise is that the sender may lack Y. When the sender has Y, our case for dictionaries, the H(X | Y) of Part II already applies.
title: The classics we lean on

q: Why is the step x → x + round(a · y) exactly reversible on integers?
a: The step leaves y unchanged, so the decoder recomputes the same round(a · y) and subtracts it
wrong: Because rounding never changes an integer
Because a is always an integer
why: That is lifting. Three such shears make a rotation; a PLUS factorization makes any matrix with determinant ±1 out of such steps.
title: The classics we lean on

q: Which kind of evidence do the lossy papers (KIVI, KVQuant, KVTC, Lexico, CacheGen) give us?
a: Where structure lives and what the LLM tolerates, not how many bits an exact copy needs
why: Their yardsticks are accuracy and perplexity at a memory budget. Lossless gains are set by variance explained, which none of them reports.
title: What would be new

q: Which published compressor counts bits for an exact copy at 8 bits, and what is missing from it?
a: SplitZip, but only context-free: no neighbours, no dictionaries beyond one global table
why: SplitZip’s 6.19-bit order-0 bound on E5M2 is a bit count; it says nothing about what a reference cherry or a punnet dictionary would add.
title: What would be new

q: What did the campaigns deliver on claim 1, the measurement?
a: Bits for an exact copy of 8-bit values on one LLM, with a shuffle control: stereo 0.85 bit per element, echo the axis that mattered, fallen-apple weak, upstairs small
wrong: Nothing yet; the measurement is still planned
A lossy compressor with a higher ratio
why: Part VIII is claim 1 for values of Qwen3.5-2B on one kind of text. Keys, other text, a second LLM and the sequence scope are still open.
title: What would be new

q: What is the honest caveat on claim 2, the random-access lossless delta store?
a: Its parts are known; only the combination and the target are new, and its worth depends on the leash’s cost, which the campaigns found small at 4096
wrong: It has already been published by HiSparse
why: Fixed-length codes, escapes, reference cherries and punnet dictionaries all exist. A cold decode within 293 cherries’ worth cost nothing at stretch 4096; at 137 it cost 0.023 of ratio.
title: What would be new

q: Why might the novelty claims be narrower than they look?
a: We checked papers through abstracts and summaries, and saw newer related titles we have not read
why: Being honest about the search is part of the claim. A measurement is still a result even if a neighbouring paper turns up.
title: What would be new

q: Which of these did the campaigns answer with a measured number?
a: How much joining the two KV heads of a layer into one cherry saves (0.032 of ratio on 20 of 20 sequences)
wrong: How often a pick is a δ-miss on the Bench
Whether keys and values share bits
Whether prose compresses like coding transcripts
why: Stereo similarity was measured by a same-window comparison of cherry shapes. The other three need a pick trace, a K+V scenario or a second corpus, none of which exists yet.
title: Where we stand

q: Why is every application-side number (misses, popularity, δ-miss fraction) still unmeasured on the Bench?
a: No indexer ever ran on the Bench; the dump holds keys and values of prefill tokens and nothing about which positions would be picked
wrong: Because the Bench has no GPU
Because the campaigns ran out of time
Because HiSparse’s numbers already cover it
why: Picks come from queries scored against keys. The dump has no queries, so there is no pick, no miss and no popularity to count.
title: Where we stand

q: What is a big-picture question, on this site?
a: An open-ended question the project exists to get closer to, too wide to settle with one experiment
wrong: A question with a yes-or-no answer from one scenario
A question about one compressor’s score
A question a paper has already answered
why: Q1 to Q3 name the three big questions; each experiment of this Part is a small, decidable step towards one of them.
title: Where we stand

q: Two compressors score 0.636 and 0.629 on two different screens. What can be said about which is better?
a: Nothing: two screens read different punnets, so the scores cannot be subtracted; only a paired run on the same punnets ranks them
wrong: The first is better, because its screen was harder
why: The campaigns learned this the hard way. The frontier compressor beat its parent by 0.0088 on every one of 5 sequences with a spread of 0.0001, and only a paired comparison could show it.
title: Principles: speed first

q: What is an experiment question, on this site?
a: A question asked together with its scenario line, its controls and the meaning of each possible reading, all written down before any data
wrong: Any question an experiment could answer
A question about the harness’s code
One of the three big questions
why: The scenario line fixes what is measured, the controls fix what would expose a mistake, and the pre-written readings stop every curve from meaning “promising”.
title: Principles: speed first

q: Why does every experiment of this Part carry a rough cost in hours?
a: Because the experiments are ordered by speed to a result, and an hour estimate is what makes that ordering checkable
wrong: Because the harness refuses jobs without one
To compare compressors by their run time
why: Speed first is the ruling principle of this plan; an experiment that cannot say how long it takes cannot be placed in the queue.
title: Principles: speed first

q: What does the Bench dump hold for each token?
a: Its values and its pre-RoPE keys at each of the six KV layers, two heads of 256 elements, in BF16, plus its token kind
wrong: Its hidden state at every layer
Its queries and the indexer’s picks
why: The dump is k and v of shape (n_tokens, 6, 2, 256) as captured in BF16; FP8 is derived on read with one power-of-two scale per layer and tensor. Nothing about queries was kept.
title: The dataset we have, and what to add cheaply

q: Why is “prefill only” a limit of the dump?
a: Every token was shown to the LLM, none was written by it; tokens the LLM writes itself might grow different keys and values
wrong: Because prefill tokens have no keys
Because the hot cache only holds decode tokens
why: The orchard of a serving sequence is mostly prompt, so prefill is the right first measurement, but the newest stretch, the one attention reads most, is written during decode and is not in the dump.
title: The dataset we have, and what to add cheaply

q: What does computing the queries for the dump cost?
a: One forward pass per sequence, the same pass that produced the dump, plus about 200 MB per sequence to store the queries of the last 8192 positions
wrong: Nothing, they are already in the dump
why: Queries are a linear projection of the same hidden state as keys and values; the pass that computed one computed the other and threw it away.
title: The dataset we have, and what to add cheaply

q: Which scenario comes first in the queue, and why?
a: Keys, K at one KV layer, k[t, l, :, :] · stretch 4096 · leash 293: the harness only needs to read k instead of v, and C1’s one-night keys result predicts the reading within about 0.05
wrong: Sequence scope, because it promises the biggest gain
A second LLM, because transfer is the biggest risk
The GPU decode, because speed decides everything
why: Speed first. Keys need no new data and almost no new code; the others need a corpus, a tree over 225K cherries, or a kernel.
title: Next in the harness

q: What would a (k[t, l, :, :], v[t, l, :, :]) score below the byte-weighted mean of the K-only and V-only scores mean?
a: That one token’s keys and values share bits, a new axis of neighbour similarity, and that a pick should be coded as one cherry
wrong: That keys are harder than values
why: The two halves alone are the control; any saving beyond their mean can only come from predicting one half from the other.
title: Next in the harness

q: Why is the whole-sequence scenario not simply run with the frontier compressor as it is?
a: Its reference tree is built from pairwise distances, which grow with the square of the punnet size; 225K cherries is 3 000 times the work of 4096
wrong: Because sequence scope is not a scenario
Because the harness cannot read a whole sequence
why: At 55 CPU seconds per 4096-token punnet, a quadratic tree over a whole sequence is days; a nearest-neighbour index or a 32K-then-64K extrapolation is the cheap road.
title: Next in the harness

q: What is the output of the pick-trace subproblem?
a: For each decode step and each KV layer, the set of k token positions attention would read: picks[step][layer_id]
wrong: The compressed bytes of each pick
why: The trace records which positions are wanted and nothing about their bytes. Miss rates come later, from replaying it; a trained indexer is what the exact top-k stands in for.
title: Queries and picks: a stand-in indexer

q: Why can the trace be computed inside the same forward pass that made the dump?
a: Queries are a projection of the same hidden state as keys and values, and the pass applies RoPE itself, so the scores against pre-RoPE keys need no re-rotation
wrong: Because the dump already contains queries
Because RoPE does not apply to keys
why: The pass computed q for every token and threw it away. Keeping it, or the scores, is a flag in the dump script.
title: Queries and picks: a stand-in indexer

q: Why is an exact top-k only a stand-in for a trained indexer?
a: A DSA indexer is a separate small network trained to approximate attention’s ranking, with its own keys and learned head weights, and GLM-5.1 selects once for a group of layers
wrong: Because trained indexers pick fewer positions
why: The stand-in reproduces the ranking the indexer is trained to copy, so stretch-level statistics should carry over; exact miss rates are checked against HiSparse’s published ones.
title: Queries and picks: a stand-in indexer

q: What does the replay subproblem take in and give out?
a: A pick trace, a cache size B, a policy and a stretch length; out come counts: miss rate, misses per stretch, popularity, the δ-miss fraction and dictionary loads
wrong: A compressor and a punnet; out comes an MDL ratio
The orchard’s bytes; out comes a dictionary
A GPU and a kernel; out come cherries per second
why: The replay only counts which positions are wanted. Bytes enter only afterwards, when the counts are multiplied by cherry and delta sizes in the napkin.
title: Replaying the hot cache

q: In the replay, when does a miss count as a δ-miss?
a: When the dictionary of the missed pick’s stretch was already on the shelf at the moment of the miss
wrong: Whenever the stretch has a dictionary somewhere on the host
When the pick was in the hot cache at some earlier step
why: Dictionaries are loaded after a step’s misses, for later steps. A miss is cheap only if its dictionary was already on the GPU.
title: Replaying the hot cache

q: What must happen to the δ-miss fraction when the trace’s positions are relabelled by a random permutation?
a: It must fall to about the share of stretches on the shelf, because every stretch is now an even slice of the picks
wrong: It must rise, because the hot cache warms faster
It must stay the same, because hits are unchanged
why: The relabelling keeps which picks repeat (the hot cache’s hits are untouched) and destroys where they sit, so any concentration into stretches that survives is a bug.
title: Replaying the hot cache

q: Why does the replay drop its first thousand steps from every count?
a: Until the hot cache has filled, every pick misses; counting those steps would report a miss rate no serving system sees
wrong: Because the trace’s first steps are corrupt
Because the shelf is empty only then
why: The counts describe a steady state. A warm-up of warm steps is dropped in the loop before misses, δ-misses and loads are tallied.
title: Replaying the hot cache

q: Why must a decoder on the miss path run at least ten times faster than the link?
a: So that decoding a layer’s misses takes a small fraction of the 0.38 ms in which the link is already busy delivering them
wrong: Because the GPU is ten times faster than the host
Because each delta is decoded ten times
Because ten sequences share one decoder
why: At the Pin 110 sequences × 274 misses × 640 B ≈ 19 MB per layer per step; the link needs the whole 0.38 ms for that, and a 500 GB/s decoder adds 39 µs, a tenth.
title: How fast must the decoder be?

q: Which two decoders does the speed test compare?
a: A GPU decode of the frontier compressor (reference tree, linear prediction, entropy coder) and of a fixed-length variant with the same tree and prediction
wrong: The CPU harness and a Python script
why: The entropy coder is serial within a cherry; the fixed-length variant trades bytes for parallelism. Which one clears 500 GB/s decides the delta format.
title: How fast must the decoder be?

q: What is measured, in which units?
a: Cold-decoded cherries per second at the miss batch sizes, converted to bytes of rebuilt cherries per second, against the link’s bytes per second
wrong: The MDL ratio of the decoded punnet
The number of CUDA cores used
Seconds per punnet on the sender’s side
why: The decoder competes with the link for the same window; the only comparable unit is bytes per second of what it hands to attention.
title: How fast must the decoder be?

q: Which of the frontier compressor’s three decode stages is the worry for a GPU?
a: The entropy-coder stage, one rANS stream per cherry read symbol by symbol, 512 serial decodes per cherry
wrong: The linear prediction, a small matrix-vector
why: The gather and the prediction have known GPU shapes; the serial symbol decode is why the fixed-length variant is built as the control.
title: How fast must the decoder be?

q: Why is a dump from DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp’s own indexer not simply the next step?
a: It has hundreds of billions of parameters and needs a multi-GPU node; only a rented node for a few hours could produce its pick trace on our transcripts
wrong: Because its indexer is not open
Because its picks cannot be replayed
why: The weights are open and the indexer is exactly the real thing; what is missing is the machine. The trace itself would be small, about a gigabyte per sequence.
title: Beyond the harness

q: What is the cheapest way to get a trained indexer’s picks on the Bench?
a: Train a small DSA-style indexer on Qwen3.5-2B’s own attention, the way DSA trains its indexer, then record its picks
wrong: Download GLM-5.1’s indexer and attach it to Qwen3.5-2B
Use the exact top-k and call it trained
Train a new LLM from scratch
why: DSA’s indexer is trained to match attention’s distribution. Doing that on the Bench’s attention costs hours on one GPU and yields a selector that ranks like a real one, with its errors.
title: Beyond the harness

q: What does the shared-selection simulation change about the trace?
a: One pick set serves a group of KV layers, built from the summed scores of the group, as GLM-5.1 selects once for a group of layers
wrong: Every layer gets the same k random picks
why: The grouped trace is derived from the per-layer one and replayed the same way; its hit rate against the per-layer trace and its f_D are the readings.
title: Beyond the harness

q: What must a synthetic trace with planted concentration show under the replay?
a: The planted δ-miss fraction and loads per step, and their collapse to the even-spread values once the trace is shuffled
wrong: A miss rate of exactly zero
The same f_D before and after the shuffle
why: A control has a known answer; recovering it, and losing it under the shuffle, is what makes the real replay’s numbers believable.
title: Beyond the harness

q: Where does the victim tier’s value come from without a second replay?
a: From the reuse-distance curve of the trace: the share of misses whose reuse distance lies between B and B + B_V
why: A victim tier catches re-picks that fell just out of the hot cache; the reuse-distance curve counts exactly those.
title: Beyond the harness

q: What is a decision rule, on this site?
a: A table fixed before any data that maps an experiment’s possible readings to what happens next
wrong: The rule by which the harness ranks compressors
A threshold learned from the data
why: Written afterwards, every reading means “promising”; written before, a reading is evidence for one row.
title: What each outcome would mean

q: The replay reads fD​≥0.8 with 8 dictionaries on the shelf and 0.6 loads per step. Heavy dictionaries (w = 256): affordable?
a: No: 0.6 × 256 ≈ 154 cherries’ worth of loads per step, more than half the miss traffic the deltas save
wrong: It cannot be judged without ρ
why: Loads must satisfy n_load × w ≪ the misses per step (274 at the Pin); for w = 256 that is under about 0.1 loads per step.
title: What each outcome would mean

q: Which three numbers decide whether the project is worth a system?
a: ρ on the miss path, f_D with n_load on the Bench, and the decoder’s bytes per second against the link
wrong: The MDL ratio, the dictionary share and the delta share
Miss rate, hit rate and TPOT
The stretch length, the leash and the cherry shape
why: They are the three inputs of the napkin that are still assumed; each experiment of this Part supplies one of them.
title: What each outcome would mean

q: How would we find out that the Bench’s results do not transfer to the Pin?
a: From H8 on a second LLM, and from a rented trace or orchard of an MLA LLM; the Pin keeps one latent per token and has no head axis, so stereo cannot even be asked there
wrong: From the miss rate at 4096 slots
why: Transfer is a question about another LLM, and only another LLM answers it. Stereo is the one finding that has no counterpart in an MLA orchard.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: The exact top-k gives miss rates far below HiSparse’s. What does that mean, and what is the pivot?
a: The stand-in is more local than a trained indexer; scale the stretch statistics by the ratio and move the small trained indexer up the queue
why: A trained indexer approximates attention’s ranking with errors; the calibration reading exists to catch exactly this.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: What is the pivot if no decoder clears 500 GB/s?
a: Decode off the miss path, on promotion into a victim tier, where one cherry’s latency is the constraint instead of a layer’s throughput
why: The victim tier rebuilds a re-picked cherry from its delta already on the GPU; it needs latency well under a step, not 500 GB/s.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: What is the next action of the plan?
a: Add the query flag to the dump script, run keys through the harness, replay the first trace
why: Each of the three is hours of work on data that exists; together they fill the first rows of the decision table.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: In what order does this Part build its numbers?
a: A dump with queries, a stand-in indexer, a pick trace, a replay of the hot cache and the shelf, a rule that carries the counts to the Pin, then the napkin at equal GPU memory
wrong: A compressor, a punnet, an MDL ratio, then a trace
A trained indexer, a GPU kernel, then a benchmark
The napkin first, then the trace that confirms it
why: Each step uses only the one before it. Bytes enter at the very end, from the campaigns of Part VIII; everything before that counts which picks are wanted.
title: The result on one page

q: Which LLM produced the pick traces of this Part?
a: Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct, over five coding-agent sequences of 24.5K to 30K tokens
why: Its dump kept the queries; the Bench’s did not. Its numbers reach the Pin through scaling rules measured inside the dump.
title: The result on one page

q: At the Pin, extrapolated, what share of the misses does a shelf of 4 dictionaries of 4096 positions catch?
a: 36–54 %, not the 85 % Part VI assumed
why: On the Bachelor’s 27K context that shelf catches 94 %, but it spans 60 % of the context. Misses spread as the context grows (b / t^1.27), so at 100K it catches far less.
title: The result on one page

q: At the Pin, each design at its best hot-cache size, how many sequences per GPU does a solo code on every miss serve, against HiSparse resized?
a: 141 against 127
why: The solo code keeps no bytes per sequence on the GPU, so every byte it removes from a miss raises the link bound. It needs a GPU decoder of at least 500 GB/s.
title: The result on one page

q: What is the most any compression of the miss path can add at the Pin, with this miss curve and rig?
a: About +31 %: 166 sequences per GPU for a global code at the whole-sequence floor of 0.57, against 127
wrong: Nothing; the link is not the bottleneck
why: The hot cache turns about half of any compression gain into a smaller cache: sequences per GPU grow as about 1 / √r, not 1 / r.
title: The result on one page

q: What grade does a number of this Part carry when it is read at the Pin’s 100K context?
a: Extrapolated, carried from the Bachelor’s 8K–30K by a fitted rule
why: Measured: an exact replay of the traces. Derived: arithmetic or a fit on measured numbers. Extrapolated: carried to the Pin by a rule. HiSparse’s own numbers are their measurement.
title: The result on one page

q: After this Part, which application-side number on the site is still unmeasured on the Bench?
a: Its miss rates, because the pick traces ran on another LLM
why: The traces come from Qwen 2.5 1.5B, the Bachelor. The Bench (Qwen3.5-2B) kept no queries, so its pill still reads “not measured” for miss rates.
title: The result on one page

q: What is the Bachelor?
a: A dump of Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct over five coding-agent sequences of 24.5K to 30K tokens, with keys, values and queries of all 28 layers
wrong: A third reference setting next to the Pin and the Bench
The Bench’s orchard with queries added
GLM-5.1’s pick trace from the HiSparse paper
why: It is a stand-in LLM’s dataset. Its numbers reach the Pin only through the scaling rules of the next page; the pill in the top bar does not switch to it.
title: The Bachelor: a dump with queries

q: Which tokens of the Bachelor are “decode-like”?
a: Assistant text and tool calls (token kinds 3 and 4), the tokens a server would generate
wrong: Only the last 8192 tokens of each sequence
why: Qwen’s template puts tool responses in the user role (kind 2). Kinds 3 and 4 are 17–25 % of positions in four sequences and 69 % in sequence 3.
title: The Bachelor: a dump with queries

q: How does the stand-in indexer score a candidate position j at step t?
a: By the LLM’s own attention probability on j, averaged over the 12 query heads of the layer
wrong: By the cosine between the key at j and the key at t
By the sum of the values at j
why: The softmax is causal over j ≤ t; the self position is in the softmax but never a candidate; the 12-head mean gives one score per position, and the top k by that score are the picks.
title: The Bachelor: a dump with queries

q: Why are smaller budgets prefixes of larger ones in the trace?
a: The trace stores each step’s candidates in rank order, not as a set, so the top 512 are the first 512 of the top 2048
wrong: Because the indexer was run once per budget
Because the hot cache keeps only the top 512
Because the window removes the rest
why: One ranking serves every budget from 64 to 2048, so the sweep of budgets needs no new pass over the dump.
title: The Bachelor: a dump with queries

q: With 512 picks per layer, what share of the attention mass (self excluded) do the picks hold on the Bachelor?
a: About 87 %
title: The Bachelor: a dump with queries

q: Where does most of a step’s attention go, apart from the picks’ tail?
a: To four sink positions at the start (24 % of the non-self mass) and to the last 128 positions (40 %)
why: Misses come from what is left: the far, diffuse tail. Layers 0, 1 and 27 have almost no sink; layer 0 puts 39 % of its attention on the token itself.
title: The Bachelor: a dump with queries

q: In the trace of sequence 2, layer 9, which positions are picked at every one of the 600 steps?
a: The first 256 positions, which hold the attention sinks, and the positions just before the step
wrong: Only the positions of the current tool response
No position is picked at every step
why: The first 256 positions get 6.6 picks per step and 1.5 % of the misses. The 256 positions before the step get 91 picks per step; a position picked for the first time always misses.
title: A trace, up close

q: What happens in the trace when the assistant starts writing after a tool response, at step 19 489?
a: A band of picks appears about 550 to 1800 positions back, and the next step misses 220 of its 512 picks
wrong: Every pick moves to the first 256 positions
The step misses no pick at all
why: Picks in positions 17 664 to 18 943 jump from 28 to 127 at step 19 490. Their stretches are on the shelf, so 190 of the 220 misses are δ-misses.
title: A trace, up close

q: Where in the trace do misses happen most often, relative to the picks?
a: Where picks are thin; densely picked positions almost always hit
wrong: In the densest band of picks
why: Cells of 256 positions with 60 or more picks in a step miss 7 % of them; cells with a single pick miss 36 %. The five most-picked bins hold half the picks and a fifth of the misses.
title: A trace, up close

q: How often does the dictionary shelf change in the 600 steps shown?
a: Three of its four stretches never leave; the fourth slot changes 38 times, mostly between two stretches
why: Stretches 16, 17 and 18 stay for all 600 steps. The fourth slot alternates between stretch 15 and stretch 4; stretch 19 enters for good at step 19 746.
title: A trace, up close

q: Is the 600-step window typical of its layer?
a: Yes: it misses 19.1 % and catches 58 % of misses on the shelf, against 19.4 % and 60 % for the whole layer
wrong: No, it was chosen for its extreme miss rate
why: Layer 9 has the median miss rate of the 28 layers; the window was chosen around a change of token kind, and its averages match the layer’s.
title: A trace, up close

q: What is the budget share φ?
a: The share of the context one layer’s picks cover at step t: φ = k / t (k·g / t for squeezed rows)
wrong: The share of misses that are δ-misses
The share of the hot cache taken by dictionaries
The share of the attention mass the picks hold
why: On the Pin it is 2048 of 100 384, 2.0 %. The pin-scaled configuration keeps it: 512 of about 25K on the Bachelor.
title: Carrying numbers from a small LLM

q: Why does the hot-cache size scale with the budget k, as B/k?
a: The hot cache exists to hold picks that repeat, and there are k picks per step
wrong: Because GPU memory is proportional to k
Because the link moves k picks per step
Because B and k are both powers of two
why: HiSparse quotes its sizes as 2048, 4096 and 8192 slots for k = 2048: B/k = 1, 2 and 4. The replay uses the same ratios.
title: Carrying numbers from a small LLM

q: What does the “pin-absolute” configuration test?
a: HiSparse’s literal numbers, k = 2048, on a context about four times shorter, so a budget share of 7–8 % instead of 2 %
wrong: The Pin’s budget share on the Bachelor
A hot cache with no guard
why: Pin-scaled keeps the share (k = 512); pin-absolute keeps the count. Which one reproduces HiSparse’s miss rates says which quantity carries.
title: Carrying numbers from a small LLM

q: Which difference between the Bachelor and GLM-5.1 cannot be measured inside the dump?
a: The size and training of the LLM, a 1.5B dense LLM against a frontier LLM trained with sparse attention
wrong: The number of query heads in the selection
why: Context, heads, window, indexer error and depth all vary inside the dump. LLM size needs a size ladder or a second LLM; neither has run.
title: Carrying numbers from a small LLM

q: At the Pin’s budget share (512 picks, about 2 %), what does the stand-in’s hot cache miss at B/k = 1 / 2 / 4?
why: HiSparse measured 30 / 13.4 / 6.7 % on GLM-5.1: the stand-in is 1.2–1.5× higher, inside the pre-registered 2× rule. 28 / 10 / 2.5 % is pin-absolute, at four times the share.
title: The hot cache, replayed

q: Why does pin-absolute (k = 2048 on the Bachelor) fail the 2× rule at B/k = 4?
a: At 2048 of about 27K positions its budget share is 7.5 %, not 2 %, and miss rates follow the share
wrong: Because its hot cache is smaller
Because it uses a resident window
why: At B/k = 4 it misses 2.5 %, 0.37× HiSparse’s 6.7 %. The next page shows that the miss rate is a function of the share φ = k/t.
title: The hot cache, replayed

q: What is the burst factor?
a: The 99th percentile of one layer’s misses per step divided by their mean
wrong: The share of steps with more misses than the mean
The ratio of LRU to Bélády misses
The misses of the worst layer divided by the best layer’s
why: Pin-scaled at B/k = 2: mean 97 misses of 512 picks, p99 263, a burst factor of 2.9 (2.2–3.8 across layers).
title: The hot cache, replayed

q: What does a resident window of 128 positions do to the miss rate at the Pin’s share?
a: It raises it by 13–20 %
why: The window takes the easiest hits (recent positions that would hit anyway) and pushes the 512 picks to farther positions, which repeat less.
title: The hot cache, replayed

q: HiSparse’s Pin has “274 misses per layer per step”. What does the replay say about that number?
a: It is an average of unequal layers: per-layer miss rates span 11–29 % (p10–p90) at B/k = 2
why: In layers 0–11 even layers miss about twice as often as odd ones (24 % against 13 %); layer 0 is local.
title: The hot cache, replayed

q: Miss rates for budgets k = 64 … 2048, binned by context length t, fall on one curve when plotted against what?
a: The budget share φ = k / t
why: If the count k carried, each budget’s line would be flat in t and the lines would stack by k. They lie on one curve in s instead; at fixed s, adding log k changes the fit by −0.05 [−0.17, 0.14] at B/k = 2.
title: The share carries, not the budget

q: What miss rates does the share rule predict for the Pin at B/k = 1 / 2 / 4, and what did HiSparse measure?
a: 36 / 21 / 12 % predicted, against 30 / 13.4 / 6.7 % measured on GLM-5.1
why: The stand-in’s curve at φ = 2048 / 100 384 gives 36 / 21 / 12 %. The count rule (k = 2048) would give 30 / 12 / 3 %. GLM-5.1’s trained indexer churns less than exact attention on a 1.5B LLM.
title: The share carries, not the budget

q: How does the slope of the reuse curve change with the budget share?
a: It rises: 0.63 at k = 64, 1.07 at k = 512, 2.2 at k = 2048 on the Bachelor
wrong: It stays at 1.08 for every budget
It falls as the budget grows
why: At a larger share the picks cover more of the context, so a few more slots catch a larger part of what repeats. HiSparse’s 1.08 sits at s ≈ 2 %, next to pin-scaled’s 1.07.
title: The share carries, not the budget

q: To read the stand-in’s miss rate for another LLM’s setting, which two quantities must match?
a: The budget share φ = k·g / L and the hot-cache ratio B / k
wrong: The number of layers and the head dimension
The budget k and the hot-cache size B
The context length and the stretch length
why: The collapse says the miss rate is a function of s at fixed B/k. A different count of picks at the same share gives the same miss rate.
title: The share carries, not the budget

q: With stretches of 1024 positions at the Pin’s budget share and B/k = 2, what share of a step’s misses does its heaviest stretch hold?
a: 31 %, against 9 % in the shuffled twin
why: The heaviest four hold 71 % against 31 %. Misses do pile into stretches, about 3× above what an even spread gives.
title: Where misses land

q: What does the shuffled twin of a trace keep, and what does it destroy?
a: It keeps which picks repeat (the hot cache’s misses are unchanged) and destroys where they sit (every stretch becomes an even slice)
wrong: It keeps where misses sit and destroys which repeat
It keeps nothing; it is a random trace
why: One fixed permutation of the positions of each sequence relabels every pick. Any concentration into stretches that survives it is chance.
title: Where misses land

q: Which shelf policy had the highest δ-miss fraction in every cell of the replay?
a: Popularity over the last 32 steps, with hysteresis
wrong: An LRU of stretches touched by a miss
The stretches with the most picks in the hot cache
why: It also loaded 2–4× fewer dictionaries than popularity over 8 steps. The LRU of touched stretches, the loop of X.6, was the worst: lift ≤ 2.7 and 0.5–9 loads per step.
title: Where misses land

q: Why does the replay count net loads rather than gross loads?
a: A dictionary loaded and dropped within the same step would never be shipped by any implementation
wrong: Because gross loads are always zero
why: Net loads count the dictionaries that are still on the shelf after the step. For the heaviest and popularity policies gross equals net; for the touched LRU it does not.
title: Where misses land

q: What is the shelf coverage?
a: n_D · stretch_len / t: the positions the stretches on the shelf hold, over the context so far
wrong: The share of misses that are δ-misses
The share of the hot cache taken by dictionaries
The number of dictionaries per layer
why: If misses landed evenly, f_D would equal the coverage. The shuffled twin gives exactly that value, so f_D is always read next to the twin’s.
title: The shelf, replayed

q: On the Bachelor, with the popular policy, what does a shelf of 4 dictionaries of 4096 positions catch, and why is that not the Pin’s number?
a: f_D 0.94, but the shelf spans 60 % of the 27K-token context; the twin catches 0.60
wrong: f_D 0.94, and it carries to the Pin unchanged
f_D 0.57, because the stretches are too short
why: At 100K tokens four stretches of 4096 span 16 % of the context. What a stretch catches must be carried at its share of the context, and faster than that.
title: The shelf, replayed

q: At a fixed budget share, f_D at a fixed (n_D, stretch length) collapses on which quantity?
a: The stretch length over t to the power 1.27, b / t^1.27
why: Absolute b leaves a logit residual of 0.42, plain b / t 0.15, b / t^1.27 0.12. Misses spread over more of the context as it grows, faster than the context itself.
title: The shelf, replayed

q: Extrapolated to the Pin’s 100K, what does a shelf of 4 dictionaries of 4096 positions catch, and at how many loads per step?
a: f_D 0.36–0.54, at 0.10–0.13 net loads per step
why: The range comes from the two ends of the fitted exponent, 0.93 and 1.44. 0.85 is outside it.
title: The shelf, replayed

q: Read with the pre-registered decision rule of X.9, what does a shelf of stretches of 4096 say at the Pin?
a: “Partly” at best (0.54 at 4 × 4096, with loads at the 0.1 limit), “spread” at worst
wrong: The rule cannot be read without a GPU
why: f_D ≥ 0.8 at n_D ≤ 8 with n_load ≤ 0.1 was “affordable”; 0.5 ≤ f_D < 0.8 “partly”; below 0.5 “spread”. At the Pin only the upper end of 4 × 4096 reaches 0.5.
title: The shelf, replayed

q: Which compressor has the lowest MDL ratio the campaigns verified at stretches of 4096, and how does it split?
a: The reference tree with linear prediction, compressor 121: 0.636 = dictionary share 0.525 + delta share 0.112
why: About half of its bytes are reference cherries kept in the dictionary; each delta is about a ninth of a cherry on average.
title: The other half of the bill

q: How does the MDL ratio of the best compressors change with the stretch length?
a: It falls as the stretch grows (0.689, 0.636, 0.618 at 512, 4096, 16 384), with the dictionary share staying near 0.4–0.5
wrong: It rises with the stretch length
It is the same at every stretch length
It falls because the dictionary share falls to zero
why: A longer stretch spreads the dictionary over more cherries and holds more repeats to point at; the best split keeps about half of the bytes in the dictionary throughout.
title: The other half of the bill

q: What are the floors 0.60 and 0.57, and what grade do they carry?
a: 0.60 is a code-length estimate inside a punnet of 16 384 positions; 0.57 extrapolates it to a whole sequence. Neither is a compressor
wrong: The ratios of solo coding with and without escapes
why: The 0.60 comes from four punnets of two sequences; the 0.57 continues a trend of about −0.007 per doubling for 3.8 more doublings. The best verified ratio at 16 384 is 0.618.
title: The other half of the bill

q: In the MDL ratio a dictionary is spread over its punnet. What is it in serving?
a: Resident GPU memory: w cherries’ worth for as long as it is on the shelf, whether or not its stretch is fetched
wrong: Link bytes, spread over the misses of its stretch
Nothing; only deltas cost anything in serving
why: A tree dictionary of a 4096-position stretch is 2150 slots’ worth per layer, 45 % of a resized hot cache; at 16 384 positions it is 8090, more than the whole cache.
title: The other half of the bill

q: Why is the stretch length that is best for the MDL ratio the worst for the shelf?
a: A longer stretch lowers the ratio by spreading the dictionary thinner, but the dictionary on the GPU grows with the stretch
wrong: Because long stretches have more misses
Because long stretches break the leash
Because the shelf cannot hold long stretches
why: At a dictionary share near one half, the memory a shelf of one dictionary holds is half the stretch, whatever share of it is ever fetched.
title: The other half of the bill

q: What is the slot price?
a: The link bytes one more hot-cache slot saves per decode step: about α·m·k·e / B
wrong: The bytes of one hot-cache slot
The exchange rate from variance explained to bits
why: With m ∝ B^−α, one more slot removes a share α/B of the misses, α·m·k/B misses per layer per step. At HiSparse’s resized cache that is about 0.05 misses, 32 bytes.
title: The slot price

q: When does one more dictionary on the shelf beat the same memory spent on hot-cache slots?
a: When (1 − ρ) · [f_D gained by that dictionary] · B / w > α
wrong: Whenever its delta share is below 1
When w is less than B
why: The dictionary saves (1 − ρ)·e on each extra δ-miss; its w cherries’ worth of memory would hold w slots, each saving α·m·k·e/B. Loads only make the dictionary’s side worse.
title: The slot price

q: Tree dictionaries (w ≈ 2150 per 4096 positions, ρ = 0.112) at B ≈ 4740: how much must each one raise f_D to beat the slots?
a: More than 0.5, which no shelf at the Pin reaches
why: α·w / ((1 − ρ)·B) ≈ 2150 / (0.888 × 4740) ≈ 0.5. The first dictionary of 4096 positions catches 0.11–0.20 at the Pin.
title: The slot price

q: At the Pin, each design at its best hot-cache size: which serves the most sequences per GPU?
a: A solo code on every miss with no per-sequence bytes: 141 (ρ = 0.804, verified)
