why: It keeps no dictionary on the GPU, so every byte it removes from a miss raises the link bound. It needs a GPU decoder of at least 500 GB/s, unmeasured.
title: The slot price

q: Tree dictionaries on a shelf at the Pin: how do sequences per GPU change from stretches of 4096 to 16 384?
a: They fall, from 88–97 to 55–59
wrong: They rise, from 88–97 to 120–130, because the ratio improves
why: The ratio improves only from 0.636 to 0.618, while each resident dictionary grows from 2150 to about 8090 slots’ worth per layer.
title: The slot price

q: Which dictionary loses least when the stretch grows from 4096 to 16 384 positions?
a: The light one (dictionary share 0.02): 127–132 at 4096, 126–130 at 16 384
wrong: The tree (0.5): it gains the most from longer stretches
They all lose the same share
why: The memory a dictionary holds is its share times the stretch length; at 0.02 even 16 384 positions make only about 350 slots.
title: The slot price

q: At 4096 slots HiSparse is bound by the link. What does it serve once its hot cache is resized so both bounds meet?
a: 127 sequences per GPU at about 4740 slots, with no compression
why: More slots mean fewer misses and more memory per sequence; the link bound rises and the memory bound falls until they cross. Every gain of kvblockdiff is quoted against 127.
title: The ceiling of the miss path

q: What is the half-gain rule?
a: For a code with no bytes per sequence and ratio ρ on every miss, sequences per GPU at the best hot-cache size grow as ρ^(−1/(1+α)) ≈ 1/√ρ
wrong: Half of the misses become δ-misses
A dictionary of half the punnet halves the misses
why: Balancing the link bound (∝ B^α/ρ) against the memory bound (∝ 1/B) gives B* ∝ ρ^(1/(1+α)) and N* ∝ ρ^(−1/(1+α)). With α ≈ 1, about half of the gain in log terms goes into a smaller cache.
title: The ceiling of the miss path

q: A solo code shrinks every miss to 0.804 of a pick (1.24× fewer link bytes). By how much does it raise sequences per GPU at the Pin?
a: About 1.11×: from 127 to 141
why: 0.804^(−0.48) ≈ 1.11. The other half of the gain lowers the best hot-cache size from about 4740 to about 4250 slots.
title: The ceiling of the miss path

q: What is the most a global code could add at the Pin, at the whole-sequence floor of 0.57?
a: +31 %: 166 sequences per GPU against 127
why: The floor is an extrapolated code-length estimate that no compressor has met, and approaching it today needs a per-sequence dictionary, which the rule does not allow for.
title: The ceiling of the miss path

q: An indexer with recall 0.64 against exact attention: what does it do to the miss rate at B/k = 2?
a: It depends on the errors: drawn afresh each step they double it (×2.04); fixed per position they lower it (×0.85)
wrong: It always lowers it by a third
Nothing; recall does not affect misses
why: A persistent error keeps picking the same wrong positions, which then sit in the hot cache. A per-step error brings new positions at every step, and new positions miss.
title: What the indexer can change

q: What should a trained indexer for HiSparse-style serving be judged on, besides recall?
a: How stable its picks are from step to step
why: Two indexers with the same recall of 0.80 differ by a factor of 1.35 / 0.95 = 1.4 in misses. A plausible reason GLM-5.1 misses less than the stand-in is that its picks repeat more (70 % against 65 %).
title: What the indexer can change

q: How many of their top-512 picks do the Bachelor’s two KV heads share?
a: About 45 %
why: Each KV head’s own 6-query-head selection shares 71–74 % with the 12-head selection, and replayed it changes the miss rate by −1 to +6 %.
title: What the indexer can change

q: GLM-5.1 picks once for a group of layers. How much of a layer’s own top-512 does the selection of the layer below cover?
a: About half (53 % of all picks; 44 % outside the sinks and the last 128 positions)
why: Adjacent layers share 53 % of their picks; layers two apart share 51 %. One selection for two layers covers about half of the second layer’s own choice.
title: What the indexer can change

q: How do decode-like steps differ from the average step?
a: They miss 1–9 % more, and their δ-miss fraction is 0.02–0.04 lower
why: Assistant text and tool calls are the tokens a server would generate; prefill queries stand in for decode queries everywhere else in this Part.
title: What the indexer can change

q: What should be done to HiSparse before any compression is compared with it?
a: Resize its hot cache to about 4740 slots, which raises it from 109.5 to 127 sequences per GPU on the Pin
wrong: Shrink its hot cache to 2048 slots
why: At 4096 slots HiSparse is link-bound with memory to spare. Every kvblockdiff gain is quoted against 127.
title: What it means, and what is next

q: Why is the campaigns’ best ratio (0.636) the wrong target for a GPU-resident application?
a: Its dictionary is 52 % of the punnet, and as GPU memory it saves fewer link bytes than the same memory would as hot-cache slots
wrong: Because its deltas are too large
why: Each tree dictionary would have to raise f_D by more than 0.5 to beat the slots its memory would hold. A solo code, 0.804 with no dictionary, serves 141 sequences per GPU at the Pin.
title: What it means, and what is next

q: A compression search moves the ratio of a global code from 0.804 to 0.70, 13 % fewer bytes per miss. What does that add at the Pin?
a: About 7 % more sequences per GPU, 141 to 151
wrong: About 13 %, the same as the bytes
Nothing, the link is not the bottleneck
why: By the half-gain rule sequences per GPU grow as about 1/√ρ; the hot cache shrinks to take the other half of the gain. The whole bytes side is bounded at +31 % (166 at 0.57).
title: What it means, and what is next

q: Which open question would change the conclusion first?
a: Whether a GPU decodes a solo code at 500 GB/s or more; without it, the 141 is not reachable
why: The solo code is the best design measured only if its deltas are decoded about ten times faster than the link delivers them.
title: What it means, and what is next

q: What would a pick trace of Qwen3.5-2B at 225K tokens add?
a: It would put the Pin’s 100K inside the measured contexts, turning the 4.4× extrapolation of f_D into an interpolation
wrong: It would measure the decoder’s speed
Nothing; the share rule already settles f_D
why: f_D at the Pin is read at 22.5K and carried by the b / t^1.27 rule. A 225K-token trace would measure it directly, on the LLM whose values the campaigns compressed.
title: What it means, and what is next

q: Which caveat sets the largest extrapolation in this Part?
a: f_D at the Pin is carried 4.4× in context, from the Bachelor’s 22.5K to 100K
wrong: The stand-in indexer churns 1.2–1.5× more than GLM-5.1’s
why: The shelf’s catch is read at the 20K–24K bin and carried by the b / t^1.27 rule; a trace of Qwen3.5-2B to 225K would turn it into an interpolation.
title: What it means, and what is next

q: In one sentence, what is the compression scenario?
a: A sender holds one sequence’s orchard; a receiver asks for one cherry at a time, at random, and must rebuild it bit for bit from that cherry’s delta plus a dictionary it held in advance
wrong: Compress a whole orchard with zstd and ship it once
Quantize the orchard to fewer bits per element
Keep the most-used picks in a bigger hot cache
why: One ask at a time, at random, decoded cold. Everything else (the leash, the score, the punnet) follows from that access pattern.
title: The one-page summary

q: What does kvblockdiff change in HiSparse, and what does it leave alone?
a: It serves a hot-cache miss as a delta against a dictionary kept on the GPU; hits, evictions and the LLM’s outputs are untouched
wrong: It replaces the indexer with a cheaper one
It drops the least-used tokens from the orchard
It retrains the LLM to need fewer KV layers
why: The δ-miss moves fewer bytes over the link and the GPU rebuilds the pick exactly. Lossless and invisible to the LLM.
title: The one-page summary

q: Which hypothesis turned out to be the strongest structure the campaigns measured?
a: Stereo similarity; the two KV heads of a layer share about 0.85 bit per element though their cosine is near zero
wrong: Fallen-apple similarity, cheaper the closer the neighbour
why: Joining the two heads into one cherry saved 0.032 of ratio on 20 of 20 sequences. Distance lost; repeats and the head axis won.
title: The one-page summary

q: On the Pin, why must a tree compressor’s dictionary sit on the GPU rather than be loaded per miss?
a: One cold decode reads about 120 cherries’ worth of dictionary; cheap from GPU memory, ruinous over the link for one miss
wrong: Because its deltas are all empty
Because the link is faster than GPU memory
Because the dictionary is only 2 % of the punnet
why: Half the punnet sits in the dictionary as reference cherries. Resident, it is lever 2, a compressed orchard on the GPU, and GPU memory is what the Pin runs out of first.
title: The one-page summary

q: Which three measurements come first in the plan, in order of how fast they return a result?
a: More scenarios in the harness; queries and a stand-in indexer for the dump we have; a replay of the hot cache
wrong: A GPU decoder, then a paper, then a product
A new harness, then new text, then keys
why: Each uses the data that exists today. The replay is what turns the assumed δ-miss fraction and load rate into measured ones.
title: The one-page summary

q: Which quantities does the Bench lack that the Pin has?
a: Picks per step, the miss rates and the time per output token; no indexer ever ran on it
wrong: The cherry size and the number of KV layers
The link bandwidth and the GPU memory
The stretch length and the storage format
why: The Bench is the data-side setting. It has shapes, bytes, stretch lengths and measured ratios; the miss side of the economics needs an indexer and a decode loop.
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: The best verified compressor at 4096 tokens scored 0.636. In bits per element, that is about…
a: 5.1 bits of 8
why: Bits per element are 8 × the MDL ratio: 8 × 0.636 ≈ 5.1. Solo sits at 6.22 (0.778), raw at 8.
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: A number on this page is graded “code-length estimate”. What does that mean?
a: A code length computed from a probability table on the data without building the compressor; a lead, not a verified result
wrong: Every cherry was rebuilt bit for bit in a separate process
The number was confirmed on all 30 sequences
The compressor ran in exact integer arithmetic
why: Four grades appear here: verified, quick, code-length estimate and bound. Only a verified score can hold a record.
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: In the Pin at 4096 slots, how many misses does one layer have per decode step, and what does the link then feed?
a: About 274 misses; about 110 sequences per GPU
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: Which three LRU miss rates did HiSparse measure on its GLM-5.1 trace, at 2048, 4096 and 8192 slots?
why: Bélády’s clairvoyant policy at 4096 misses 8.2 %, so better eviction can win at most about 5 points.
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: Part VI assumes a shelf of 4 dictionaries of 4096 positions catches 85 % of the misses. What does the pick-trace replay give for the Pin?
a: 36–54 %, extrapolated from Qwen 2.5 1.5B, at 0.10–0.13 loads per step
why: On the Bachelor’s 27K context the same shelf catches 94 %, but spans 60 % of the context. What a stretch catches scales as b / t^1.27, so at 100K it catches far less.
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: How many distinct non-negative values does FP8 E4M3 (the “fn” variant) represent?
a: 127, zero, 7 subnormals and 15 binades of 8 values, minus the one NaN pattern
why: With the sign, that is 253 distinct values plus −0, which the dump canonicalizes to +0.
title: FP8 E4M3 facts used by compressors

q: Why do compressors reason in index space?
a: So that a residual of 1 means one representable step, whatever the size of the step
wrong: Because indices are always smaller than values
Because E4M3 has no negative numbers
why: On a logarithmic grid, equal value differences are very different numbers of steps near zero and far from it.
title: FP8 E4M3 facts used by compressors

q: What did the campaigns find when they estimated shared bits on the FP8 code index instead of on the values?
a: The estimate read 0.104 against 0.278 on the values, three times too low; the linear structure is in the values and the log grid hides it
wrong: The index-space estimate was three times too high
why: The winning compressors predict in value and integrate the probability over the FP8 cell; subtracting a prediction in index space throws the structure away.
title: FP8 E4M3 facts used by compressors

q: Which related work is lossless AND serves one-cherry-at-a-time random access on the sparse-decode miss path?
a: None of them; that combination is what would be new
why: SplitZip is lossless but bulk and solo; KVTC and CacheGen are lossy; HiSparse moves raw picks.
title: Prior-art map

q: CacheGen codes nearby tokens as deltas against a group reference. What did the campaigns measure for that idea at 8 bits, lossless?
a: Joining two or four adjacent tokens into one cherry costs +0.037 and +0.063 of ratio; the reference that pays is a far repeat of the same token
wrong: Nothing could be measured under a leash
why: At quantized precision nearby values look close; counted in bits, the adjacent token shares 0.058 bit per element at KV layer 0. Echo, not distance.
title: Prior-art map

q: Which classic results formalize “the receiver already has side information”?
a: Slepian–Wolf (1973) and Wyner–Ziv (1976)
why: Mattson’s stack distances and Bélády’s policy are about caches; Huffman is about prefix codes.
title: References

q: Where do the trial ids quoted in the receipts of Part VIII (env-t0096, r25-t0003) come from?
a: The ledgers of the experiment repository kv-compress-roofline, one JSON line per trial, which no agent may edit
wrong: The site’s own figure data, made up for illustration
why: The harness wrote them during the campaigns of 29–30 October 2026; the site’s figure data is extracted from those ledgers.
title: References

q: The first draft used one word for the thing the indexer names and the thing the receiver asks for. What are the two words now?
a: A pick (what the indexer names) and a cherry (what the receiver asks for and the sender answers with a delta)
wrong: A slice and a cherry shape
why: A pick is one unit of demand, (layer_id, token_pos_id); it is served with one or more cherries, by the scenario’s cherry shape.
title: Old words, new words

q: The ledger names a screen s-layer-b4k-r293. Written as a scenario, that is…
a: V · all · cherry v[t, l, :, :] · stretch 4096 · leash 293, on the screen’s sample of punnets
wrong: K · layer 4 · cherry v[t, l, h, :] · stretch 4096 · leash 293
V · one head · stretch 4096 · no leash
why: “layer” is the ledger’s name for the cherry shape that stacks both heads of one layer; “b4k” is the stretch length; “r293” is the leash.
title: Old words, new words

q: KIVI rounds keys with one scale per position in the head vector, and values with one scale per token. In this site’s words?
a: Keys per furrow, values per cherry
wrong: Keys per stretch, values per punnet
Keys per element, values per layer
Keys per pick, values per slice
why: A furrow is one element position followed along the token axis; a cherry is one token’s vector (or vectors) at one layer.
title: Old words, new words
